chapters.title: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: OSTEP describes the operating system as three easy pieces. Which trio is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Virtualization, concurrency, and persistence

choices.label: B
choices.body: Compiling, linking, and loading

choices.label: C
choices.body: Kernel, shell, and web browser

choices.label: D
choices.body: Processes, threads, and deadlocks

easy.hint: Think V-C-P: the illusion of private resources, juggling many things at once, and remembering data forever. Which trio covers all three?
easy.explanation: OSTEP organizes the OS into three easy pieces: virtualization (illusions of private resources), concurrency (many activities at once), and persistence (data that survives crashes and reboots).
easy.deepDive: Think of the OS as a theater company: virtualization is the stage illusion where every play feels like it owns the whole stage, concurrency is the stage manager juggling overlapping performances, and persistence is the archivist who keeps every script safe after the lights go out. This course returns to these three pieces again and again, so naming them now gives you a map for everything ahead. Why it matters: whenever you meet a new OS feature, asking which piece it serves tells you what problem it is really solving.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Compiling, linking, and loading are toolchain steps that produce a program, not the three OS themes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The shell and browser are programs that run on the OS, not the three conceptual pieces.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Processes, threads, and deadlocks are all subtopics inside the first two pieces, not the full trio.

easy.prompt: You run a music player, a text editor, and a browser at the same time on a single CPU, and each program behaves as if it owns the processor. Which piece of the OS provides this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Persistence: keeping files safe across crashes

choices.label: B
choices.body: Compiling the program from source

choices.label: C
choices.body: Virtualization of the CPU

choices.label: D
choices.body: Rendering the user interface

easy.hint: Many programs, one CPU, each feeling like it is alone on the machine. Which piece creates that illusion?
easy.explanation: Running many programs on fewer CPUs so each believes it owns the processor is CPU virtualization (time-sharing).
easy.deepDive: Picture ten toddlers and one swing: the OS pushes each one briefly and rotates so fast that everyone feels like the swing is theirs alone. That time-sharing rotation is CPU virtualization, and the mechanism behind it is rapid context switching between processes. Why it matters: this single illusion is what lets your music player, editor, and browser all feel alive on one processor.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Persistence is about data surviving reboots and crashes, not about sharing the CPU.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Compiling happens once before the program runs and does not share the processor.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The interface is just one application; the sharing illusion underneath it is virtualization.

easy.prompt: What is the difference between virtualization and concurrency?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Virtualization gives each program its own illusion; concurrency is about correctly handling many overlapping activities and their interactions

choices.label: B
choices.body: They are synonyms and can be used interchangeably

choices.label: C
choices.body: Virtualization is about disks while concurrency is about CPUs

choices.label: D
choices.body: Concurrency applies only to multi-core machines

easy.hint: One idea is the private-room illusion, the other is the rules for sharing the kitchen safely. Which choice keeps both ideas?
easy.explanation: Virtualization creates private-resource illusions; concurrency deals with the correctness problems of many things happening at once on shared state.
easy.deepDive: Imagine private dressing rooms versus a shared kitchen: virtualization hands every actor a private dressing room, while concurrency writes the rules so cooks sharing one kitchen do not spoil each other's soup. Mixing the two ideas up makes later bugs mysterious, because a sharing bug and an illusion bug demand different fixes. Why it matters: naming the layers correctly tells you whether to reach for scheduling tools or synchronization tools.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: If they were synonyms, locks and semaphores would be pointless; sharing introduces correctness problems that illusions alone do not solve.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both ideas apply to CPUs, memory, and more; the split is illusion versus safe sharing, not disk versus CPU.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Even a single core interleaves threads and interrupts, so concurrency problems appear with or without many cores.

easy.prompt: Your laptop battery dies while you edit a document. When you reboot, the latest auto-saved version is intact. Which piece of the OS is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Recompiling the editor after an update

choices.label: B
choices.body: The editor auto-saving your document so it survives a power outage

choices.label: C
choices.body: Two editor windows redrawing at the same time

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each editor window believing it owns the screen

easy.hint: Which scenario is about data surviving after the machine dies and restarts?
easy.explanation: Persistence means data outlives processes, crashes, and power loss; durable auto-save is the textbook example.
easy.deepDive: Think of persistence as a librarian who writes every borrowed book into a fireproof ledger before the library closes for the night. The file system journals or carefully orders its writes so a crash mid-save still leaves either the old version or the new one, never gibberish. Why it matters: users forgive a slow program far more easily than a program that eats their thesis during a blackout.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Recompiling builds a new binary and says nothing about surviving a crash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Redrawing two windows at once is concurrent activity, not durable storage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A private-screen illusion is virtualization, not crash survival.

easy.prompt: What does it mean to virtualize the CPU?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each program behaves as if it has its own private CPU, even though the OS shares the real one

choices.label: B
choices.body: The OS physically duplicates the CPU for every program

choices.label: C
choices.body: Programs take turns owning the hardware permanently

choices.label: D
choices.body: The CPU runs only one program per boot

easy.hint: One real CPU, many programs, each fooled into feeling alone. Is hardware being duplicated or is an illusion being staged?
easy.explanation: CPU virtualization is the illusion of many private processors multiplexed onto fewer physical ones by time-sharing.
easy.deepDive: A good illusionist never reveals the trapdoor: the OS swaps programs so quickly that each one perceives continuous private execution. Under the hood there is still exactly one processor being time-sliced among all runnable programs. Why it matters: believing the illusion lets programmers write simple sequential code while the OS handles the messy sharing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No duplication happens; silicon stays fixed while the OS multiplexes time on it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ownership is temporary slices of milliseconds, never permanent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Modern machines routinely run hundreds of processes per boot thanks to this illusion.

easy.prompt: What does it mean to virtualize memory?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each process sees its own private address space, isolated from other processes

choices.label: B
choices.body: All processes share one visible pool of physical addresses

choices.label: C
choices.body: Programs directly name RAM chips and bytes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Memory is used only while powered and never abstracted

easy.hint: Your program uses address 1000 and your friend's program uses address 1000, yet neither crashes the other. What must each of them own?
easy.explanation: Memory virtualization gives every process a private address space; the OS and hardware translate virtual addresses to physical frames.
easy.deepDive: Think of apartment numbers versus one shared dormitory: every process gets address zero through the top of its own building, and the OS plus page tables quietly translate those numbers to different physical rooms. A bug writing to address 1000 in one program therefore cannot scribble on another program's address 1000. Why it matters: this isolation is the foundation of both protection and the simple programming model you rely on daily.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A single visible pool would let any program read or smash any other program's data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Programs name virtual addresses; only the OS and memory hardware know the physical placement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Virtual memory is precisely the abstraction layer over raw powered RAM.

easy.prompt: What machinery maintains the virtualization illusion while programs run?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Rapid context switches by the OS plus hardware support such as timers and address translation

choices.label: B
choices.body: Faster CPUs that finish each program before the next starts

choices.label: C
choices.body: Programmers politely pausing their own code

choices.label: D
choices.body: Storing every program on a separate disk

easy.hint: Something must forcibly pause a running program and swap its CPU and memory state. Is that the program's job or a partnership of OS plus hardware?
easy.explanation: The illusion is maintained by the OS multiplexing the CPU (context switches driven by timer interrupts) together with hardware address translation.
easy.deepDive: Watch the magician's hands: a timer interrupt periodically yanks control back to the OS, the OS saves one program's registers and restores the next, and the memory hardware flips to the new address space. Each grab-and-restore takes microseconds, so programs perceive smooth continuous execution. Why it matters: the illusion is engineered, not accidental, and every piece of that machinery becomes a topic of its own later in the book.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed alone never shares; without switching, the first program would hog the CPU forever.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Relying on politeness fails the moment one program loops forever or turns malicious.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Separate disks change storage, not how the CPU and memory are shared at runtime.

easy.prompt: Why does the hardware provide separate user mode and kernel mode?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To protect the OS and programs from each other by restricting what user code can touch directly

choices.label: B
choices.body: To make user programs run faster than the kernel

choices.label: C
choices.body: To give every program its own physical machine

choices.label: D
choices.body: To remove the need for system calls

easy.hint: If any program could rewrite OS memory or seize the disk, whose bug could crash everything? What barrier stops that?
easy.explanation: Dual-mode operation exists for protection: user code runs restricted, and only the kernel runs with full hardware privilege.
easy.deepDive: Think of a bank with a lobby and a vault: customers handle their business in the lobby, and only badged staff enter the vault where the money and master keys live. User mode is the lobby and kernel mode is the vault, with the processor badge-checking every sensitive instruction. Why it matters: without this wall, any buggy or malicious program could rewrite the OS itself and crash the machine.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Kernel crossings cost time, so modes trade a little speed for safety rather than granting it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Modes divide privilege on shared hardware; they do not clone the machine.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Modes are exactly what make controlled system calls necessary.

easy.prompt: What can code running in kernel mode do that user-mode code cannot?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Execute privileged instructions and directly access hardware and all of memory

choices.label: B
choices.body: Run JavaScript in a browser tab

choices.label: C
choices.body: Draw pixels without any driver

choices.label: D
choices.body: Skip scheduling and own the CPU forever

easy.hint: One mode holds the master key to interrupts, page tables, and devices. Which choice names that kind of raw power?
easy.explanation: Kernel mode can run privileged instructions (interrupt control, MMU configuration, device I/O) and touch any memory; user mode cannot.
easy.deepDive: Picture a master key that opens the electrical room, the server closet, and every locked door: kernel mode holds that key for instructions like disabling interrupts, switching page tables, and driving devices. User programs hold ordinary room keys that work only on their own space. Why it matters: concentrating raw power in a small trusted kernel keeps the blast radius of any application bug tiny.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Browser scripting runs firmly inside restricted user mode, far from hardware privilege.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Drawing always passes through drivers and the kernel; no mode lets apps bypass them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Even the kernel yields the CPU on timer interrupts so sharing continues.

easy.prompt: How does the CPU switch from user mode to kernel mode?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A trap, system call, or interrupt transfers control to the kernel

choices.label: B
choices.body: The program runs faster and promotes itself

choices.label: C
choices.body: The program edits its own mode bit directly

choices.label: D
choices.body: Modes switch only when the machine reboots

easy.hint: User code cannot promote itself, so some hardware event must carry it across. What kind of event acts as the guarded gate?
easy.explanation: Only guarded events (traps, system calls, interrupts) switch the CPU into kernel mode at a vetted handler address.
easy.deepDive: Follow one keystroke: the keyboard raises an interrupt, the hardware flips to kernel mode and jumps to the OS handler, and the OS later returns the waiting program to user mode. System calls ride this same trapdoor in reverse, with the program knocking to request entry. Why it matters: every crossing is a guarded gate, so the kernel inspects each request instead of trusting the caller.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed never changes privilege; only a hardware gate can raise it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The mode bit is protected, so user code attempting this faults instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Machines cross into the kernel thousands of times per second without rebooting.

easy.prompt: A user program attempts a privileged instruction, such as disabling interrupts. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The hardware traps to the OS with a fault instead of obeying

choices.label: B
choices.body: The instruction quietly succeeds anyway

choices.label: C
choices.body: The program is silently upgraded to kernel mode

choices.label: D
choices.body: The CPU shuts down permanently

easy.hint: The vault door does not open for a lobby badge. Does it open quietly, upgrade the visitor, or beep and call security?
easy.explanation: Privileged instructions attempted in user mode raise a processor exception (trap/fault) to the kernel instead of executing.
easy.deepDive: Imagine a lobby visitor swiping a fake badge at the vault door: the reader beeps, denies entry, and alerts security rather than opening. The CPU does the same when user code attempts a privileged instruction, raising a fault that hands the OS the decision. Why it matters: this refusal is the enforcement behind the whole protection story, turning attacks and accidents into catchable errors.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Silent success would destroy all protection guarantees the modes exist to provide.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Privilege is never granted just because it was attempted; that would reward every attack.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Faults are routine handled events, not hardware death sentences.

easy.prompt: What is a system call?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A controlled request from a program to the kernel, executed with privilege on the program's behalf

choices.label: B
choices.body: Any function call inside an application

choices.label: C
choices.body: A phone call to the computer vendor

choices.label: D
choices.body: A jump between two user functions

easy.hint: It crosses the user-kernel wall through a guarded gate, running with privilege but on your behalf. Which choice crosses that wall?
easy.explanation: A system call is the guarded gateway through which user programs request privileged kernel services such as file, process, and network operations.
easy.deepDive: Think of a courtroom where citizens pass written petitions to the judge instead of grabbing the gavel themselves: the system call is that petition window into the kernel. The program states what it wants, the kernel validates the arguments, performs the privileged work, and hands back a result. Why it matters: this gate is where protection meets usefulness, letting programs do powerful things without holding power.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ordinary function calls stay inside user mode and never cross into the kernel.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Vendors are not involved; the call goes to the locally running kernel.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: User-to-user jumps never change privilege or enter the OS.

easy.prompt: How does a library call like printf differ from a system call like write?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Library calls run in user mode and may or may not invoke kernel system calls underneath

choices.label: B
choices.body: They are identical with different names

choices.label: C
choices.body: Library calls are more privileged than system calls

choices.label: D
choices.body: System calls run in user mode while libraries run in the kernel

easy.hint: printf feels instant and cheap while write crosses into the kernel. Could one be the lobby concierge and the other the vault visit?
easy.explanation: Library calls are ordinary user-mode functions; they wrap, buffer, or simplify work and call into the kernel only when privileged service is needed.
easy.deepDive: Picture a helpful concierge in the lobby who handles simple requests herself but walks vault errands through the guarded door when needed: the C library buffers and formats in user mode, then issues a write system call only when the buffer fills. That is why printf can run a dozen times while the kernel sees a single write. Why it matters: the split explains both performance (fewer costly crossings) and portability (same library face over different kernels).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: If they were identical, there would be no user-kernel boundary left to protect.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Privilege flows the other way: libraries are unprivileged and system calls are the privileged ones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: This swaps the modes exactly backwards from how real systems work.

easy.prompt: Why can't applications write directly to the disk device?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Direct access would let any bug or malware corrupt data and other programs, so the OS mediates every request

choices.label: B
choices.body: Disks are too fast for programs to handle

choices.label: C
choices.body: Programs prefer slower indirect access

choices.label: D
choices.body: The kernel has nothing better to do

easy.hint: If every program scribbled on the disk freely, whose typo could eat your files? What does a gatekeeper prevent?
easy.explanation: The OS must mediate hardware access for protection (permissions, isolation), correct sharing, and crash-consistent ordering.
easy.deepDive: Hand every stranger the bank vault combination and losses become a matter of when, not if: one wild pointer could overwrite anyone's files. Forcing all disk traffic through system calls lets the kernel check permissions, order writes for crash safety, and share the device fairly. Why it matters: mediation is the price of a machine where your files survive your neighbor's bugs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Disks are slower than CPUs, and sharing plus safety are the real reasons for mediation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Nobody prefers slower paths; programs accept the gate because unchecked access is unsafe.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mediation is essential protection work, not busywork for an idle kernel.

easy.prompt: What does separation of policy and mechanism mean in OS design?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The mechanism provides how something works; the policy decides what should be done

choices.label: B
choices.body: Policy is code and mechanism is paperwork

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mechanism decides goals and policy implements them

choices.label: D
choices.body: They are the same thing in OS design

easy.hint: One is the steering wheel, the other is the choice of destination. Which choice keeps how apart from what?
easy.explanation: Separation of policy and mechanism means building flexible low-level operations (mechanism) apart from the decisions about how to use them (policy).
easy.deepDive: Think of a car: the steering linkage and brakes are the mechanism, while the driver choosing the route is the policy. Swapping in a new driver never requires rebuilding the steering column. Why it matters: this split lets researchers invent new scheduling or paging policies for decades without rewriting the delicate low-level machinery.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This flips the terms: mechanism is the implemented machinery and policy is the decision rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: This swaps the roles; mechanisms implement and policies decide.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Merging them forces a rewrite of fragile machinery every time a goal changes.

easy.prompt: Which of these is a mechanism rather than a policy?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The context switch that saves and restores a process

choices.label: B
choices.body: The rule choosing which process runs next

choices.label: C
choices.body: The goal of keeping interactive programs responsive

choices.label: D
choices.body: The decision to favor short jobs

easy.hint: Which item is the machinery that swaps runners on the track, rather than the judge's decision of who runs next?
easy.explanation: Context switching is mechanism (how to swap processes); the scheduling choice of who runs next is policy built on top of it.
easy.deepDive: Consider chess equipment versus tournament rules: the context switch is the board and clock that make any game playable, while the scheduler is the rulebook deciding pairings. You can run a round-robin evening or a knockout final on the same board. Why it matters: spotting the machinery-versus-decision split tells you exactly which file to edit when a scheduling idea changes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Choosing the next process is the classic scheduling policy decision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Responsiveness is a goal that policies aim at, not machinery that performs a swap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Favoring short jobs is a policy rule, implementable atop the same switching machinery.

easy.prompt: Why is separating policy from mechanism valuable?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Administrators can change scheduling goals without rewriting the delicate switching code

choices.label: B
choices.body: It makes the kernel run with fewer instructions

choices.label: C
choices.body: It removes the need for any scheduler

choices.label: D
choices.body: It lets policies touch hardware directly

easy.hint: If the dining room stays the same but the seating rules change nightly, what did the split buy you?
easy.explanation: Separating the two lets policies evolve (fairness, latency, energy) while the hard-to-get-right mechanism stays stable.
easy.deepDive: Imagine swapping a restaurant's seating rules from first-come to reservations without rebuilding the dining room: the tables and kitchen keep working while only the host's rulebook changes. Operating systems want the same freedom, tuning fairness or latency by editing policy while the context switcher stays untouched. Why it matters: this flexibility is why one kernel can serve phones, laptops, and servers with different policies atop shared machinery.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The kernel executes the same machinery either way; the win is flexibility, not fewer instructions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A scheduler is still required; only its decision rule is now cleanly replaceable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Policies stay above the machinery and never gain direct hardware access.

easy.prompt: Which goals does an OS designer try to balance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Performance, protection and security, and reliability

choices.label: B
choices.body: Compiling speed, font rendering, and battery color

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only raw CPU clock rate

choices.label: D
choices.body: The number of installed applications

easy.hint: Fast, safe, and dependable: which trio sounds like what you demand from the machine under all your apps?
easy.explanation: OS designers chase several goals at once, classically performance, protection/security, and reliability, plus concerns like energy and portability.
easy.deepDive: Think of an OS as a city government juggling fast highways, safe streets, and bridges that never collapse: travelers want speed, residents want safety, and everyone assumes the lights stay on. OSTEP adds portability and efficiency across devices to the same balancing act. Why it matters: every design argument in the book is secretly an argument about which of these goals wins in a given situation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fonts and colors are application details, not the OS-level goals OSTEP discusses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clock rate is one hardware input; OS goals span far beyond raw speed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: App count measures a market, not the quality tensions inside the OS itself.

easy.prompt: Why can't an OS maximize performance, security, and reliability all at once?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Improving one goal often costs another, so designers trade off deliberately

choices.label: B
choices.body: All goals improve together with no conflicts

choices.label: C
choices.body: Goals are independent and never interact

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only performance matters in practice

easy.hint: Armor slows a race car but saves the driver. Do OS safety features come free, or do they charge a speed toll?
easy.explanation: OS goals conflict: stronger protection, reliability, or efficiency measures typically cost performance and vice versa.
easy.deepDive: Consider armoring a race car: every steel plate adds safety but steals speed, so engineers choose the balance per race. Extra permission checks, redundant writes, and encryption behave the same way inside an OS. Why it matters: recognizing a trade-off stops you from demanding the impossible and starts you negotiating which goal wins this time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: If everything improved together, design would be trivial and this chapter unnecessary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Shared machinery means every check, copy, or replica touches the same budget of time and energy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A blazing machine that leaks data or eats files fails its users completely.

easy.prompt: Which file-system choice shows the reliability-versus-performance tension?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Syncing every write to disk immediately: safest against crashes but slowest

choices.label: B
choices.body: Keeping data only in RAM forever

choices.label: C
choices.body: Never checking user permissions

choices.label: D
choices.body: Running all programs in kernel mode

easy.hint: One setting never loses a byte but waits on the slow disk every time. Which choice names that safety-versus-speed knob?
easy.explanation: Eager durability (fsync per write) maximizes crash safety at a steep latency cost; batching is faster but risks losing recent work.
easy.deepDive: Imagine signing and photocopying every letter before mailing it: nothing is ever lost, but the post office line crawls. A file system that flushes each write pays the same price in disk waits for its crash-proof guarantee. Why it matters: this single knob, how eagerly to make data durable, is where reliability and performance visibly wrestle in every storage system.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: RAM-only storage abandons reliability entirely instead of balancing it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Skipping permission checks trades security, not crash reliability, for speed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Running everything privileged destroys protection rather than tuning durability.

easy.prompt: What is the difference between a program and a process?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bytes on disk plus a recipe, while a process is one live cooking session with its own counter, registers, and kitchen state.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A process is the compiled binary, while a program is the running instance in RAM.

choices.label: C
choices.body: They are identical and the kernel uses the words interchangeably.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A program is a thread pool, while a process is a single function call.

easy.hint: Compare something static on disk with something alive that the CPU steps through.
easy.explanation: A program is static bytes on disk; a process is one running instance with CPU and memory state.
easy.deepDive: Think of a program as a recipe card and a process as one active cooking session with its own counter, ingredients, and timer. The OS creates that session when you run the recipe, giving it a private address space, an open-file table, and a program counter that says where it is. That is why one recipe can have many simultaneous sessions that fail or finish independently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This swaps the definitions: the binary on disk is the program and the live instance is the process.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The kernel tracks live instances separately from on-disk files, so the terms are not interchangeable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Threads and function calls live inside a process rather than defining the program versus process split.

easy.prompt: Which best describes the process control block (PCB)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The full video framebuffer of the desktop.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only the process exit code after it finishes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: PID, process state, saved registers and stack pointer, page-table pointer, open-file table, and scheduling priority.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The source code text of the program.

easy.hint: Ask what the kernel must save to pause one process and resume it later without confusion.
easy.explanation: The PCB is the kernel record that lets the OS pause, schedule, and resume each process exactly.
easy.deepDive: Think of the PCB as the folder the coach keeps for each player with jersey number, position, and current injury status. When the OS pauses a process it files the registers, stack pointer, and page-table pointer in that folder so it can resume exactly. Without that folder the OS could not tell a ready process from a blocked one or restore its CPU context.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The framebuffer belongs to the display system, not to per-process kernel metadata.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The exit code is one small field kept at termination, not the whole control block.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Source text lives in files, while the PCB holds live kernel bookkeeping about the running instance.

easy.prompt: What do the ready, running, and blocked process states mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ready means waiting for a CPU, running means executing now, and blocked means waiting for an event such as disk I/O.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Ready means terminated, running means booting, and blocked means powered off.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All processes are always running and states are only a debugging myth.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ready means holding the disk, running means holding the printer, and blocked means holding memory.

easy.hint: Think waiting room, exam chair, and lab queue.
easy.explanation: Ready, running, and blocked describe whether a process wants the CPU, has it, or waits on I/O.
easy.deepDive: Picture a clinic with a waiting room for ready patients, one exam chair for the running patient, and a lab queue for blocked patients awaiting test results. A process moves from ready to running when dispatched, from running to blocked when it requests slow I/O, and from blocked back to ready when the event completes. The PCB state field is the wristband that tells the scheduler which room each process is in.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Terminated, booting, and powered off are machine or lifecycle conditions, not the three scheduling states.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The OS multiplexes one CPU across many processes, so states are required to track who can run.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: States describe CPU and event readiness, not which physical device a process owns.

easy.prompt: What does fork() return after a successful call?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 0 to the child, the child PID to the parent, and -1 on failure with no child created.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The parent PID to both parent and child on success.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 0 to both parent and child so they are symmetric.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The child PID to the child and 0 to the parent.

easy.hint: The two return values must let each side tell who it is.
easy.explanation: fork returns twice: 0 in the child and the child PID in the parent.
easy.deepDive: Think of fork as a phone call that splits one caller into two identical callers with different name tags. Right after the split both resume at the same line, but the tag reads 0 for the child and the new PID for the parent so each knows its role. That split return value is the only first clue about who is who, and every later trace depends on branching on it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The parent receives the child PID, not its own PID, and the child receives 0.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Symmetric zeros would leave neither side able to tell parent from child.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: This reverses the real convention and would break the standard parent-waits-for-child pattern.

easy.prompt: Trace: int x = 10; fork(); x += 5; printf("%d", x); What prints?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both print 10 because fork resets all variables to zero.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Parent prints 10 and child prints 15 because only the child ran the increment.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Parent prints 15 and child prints 15 because they share one variable.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Parent prints 15 and child prints 10 because the parent increments after the child exits.

easy.hint: Ask whether the increment after fork touches one shared variable or two private copies.
easy.explanation: Each process has a private copy of x, so both increment from 10 to 15.
easy.deepDive: Trace it line by line with x starting at 10 in the parent before the split. After fork both copies resume after the call with x equal to 10, then each adds 5 to its own private copy. Think of photocopying a worksheet mid-lesson where later pencil marks stay on separate sheets, so both print 15. The key lesson is that memory is duplicated, not shared, after fork.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: fork duplicates memory rather than resetting it, so x starts at 10 in both.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both processes execute every line after fork unless code branches on the return value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: There is no ordering guarantee here and both run the increment in their own address space.

easy.prompt: Trace: rc = fork(); if (rc == 0) printf("CHILD"); else printf("PARENT"); What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both print PARENT because the child skips the branch.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both print CHILD because fork returns 0 twice.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Child prints CHILD and parent prints PARENT, each taking its own branch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only the parent prints because the child terminates immediately at fork.

easy.hint: Substitute rc = 0 for the child and rc > 0 for the parent, then follow each path.
easy.explanation: Branching on rc separates child work from parent work.
easy.deepDive: Label the return value rc and walk each twin separately from the line after fork. The child sees rc equal to 0 and enters the first branch, while the parent sees a positive PID and enters the else branch. Think of a forked trail sign that sends the 0-tagged hiker left and the PID-tagged hiker right, so exactly one message comes from each side.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The child receives 0, so it enters the first branch instead of skipping it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Only the child receives 0, while the parent receives a positive PID.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The child continues executing after fork and reaches its branch normally.

easy.prompt: What does wait() do for the parent?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It returns immediately with the parent PID and never blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It blocks until a child changes state and returns that child PID to the parent.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It terminates the calling process and returns its exit code.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It creates a new child process like fork does.

easy.hint: Which call lets a parent pause until its child is done?
easy.explanation: wait sleeps for a child exit and reports which child finished.
easy.deepDive: Think of wait as a parent pausing at the school gate until one child walks out with a report card. The gate pause blocks the parent from prompting too early, and the returned PID says exactly which child arrived. That pairing of a blocking pickup with a PID ticket is what turns raw forks into ordered shell commands.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: wait blocks rather than returning instantly, and it reports the child PID.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Terminating with a code is the job of exit, not wait.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Creating children is the job of fork, while wait collects already-created children.

easy.prompt: What happens to a running child when its parent exits first?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A live child whose parent exited first, now adopted by init which will reap it.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A dead child whose parent refuses to call wait.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A process with no address space at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A process that forked twice in a row.

easy.hint: Who adopts a still-running child when its parent is gone?
easy.explanation: Orphans keep running under init instead of becoming zombies.
easy.deepDive: Think of a lost child at a fair being walked to the information booth that never closes. When a parent exits first, the kernel reparents each live child to the init process as the booth guardian. The child keeps running normally, and init routinely waits so no lingering ticket row remains.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes a zombie, which requires a dead child and a living non-waiting parent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Orphans keep a normal address space and continue executing code.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fork count is unrelated to whether the parent is alive.

easy.prompt: What must the kernel save and restore on a context switch?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Copy the whole disk image of each process to swap them.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Save registers, stack pointer, and page-table base of the old process, then load those of the new one.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Recompile both programs and relink their libraries.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only change the shell prompt string.

easy.hint: What three things must change for another address space to run correctly?
easy.explanation: A context switch swaps CPU context plus address-space pointer.
easy.deepDive: Think of swapping drivers in a rally car while keeping the race clock running. The crew saves seat position, mirror angles, and the map book pointer for one driver, then loads the next driver settings. Registers plus stack pointer plus page-table base are those three adjustments, all filed in the PCB.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Switches move register and mapping state, not entire disk images.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Programs are already loaded, so no recompilation happens during a switch.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The prompt is shell state, while context switches move kernel CPU state.

easy.prompt: What is the basic shell execution loop?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Compile every command from C source before running it.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Loop over read a line, parse it, fork a child, exec the program, wait, then repeat.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exec itself into each command without ever forking.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Keep all commands as threads inside the shell process.

easy.hint: Which loop lets one surviving shell launch many transient commands?
easy.explanation: The shell is a loop around fork, exec, and wait.
easy.deepDive: Think of a short-order cook who takes one ticket, shouts the recipe, and waits for the plate before taking the next ticket. Reading the line is taking the ticket, forking hires a helper cook, exec hands over the recipe, and wait holds the counter until pickup. That loop is why the shell survives every command and always returns to its prompt.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Shells launch existing binaries rather than recompiling source per command.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Exec without fork would replace the shell on the first command.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Commands run as separate processes for isolation, not as threads sharing shell memory.

easy.prompt: Three jobs A, B, C all arrive at t=0 with bursts A=4, B=2, C=6. They run FCFS in order A,B,C with no preemption. What is the turnaround time of A? Recall turnaround = completion − arrival.
easy.hint: First find when A completes (it runs 0→4), then subtract its arrival time 0.
easy.explanation: A completes at 4 and arrived at 0, so turnaround = 4 − 0 = 4.
easy.deepDive: Turnaround measures total time from arrival to completion, including any waiting. Here A never waits, so its turnaround equals its burst. Later jobs will add waiting to this same formula. This metric matters most for batch jobs where end-to-end latency counts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 0 is the arrival time, not completion minus arrival; turnaround is never 0 for nonzero burst.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 12 is C's completion (total of all bursts), not A's completion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 2 is B's burst, which is irrelevant to A's turnaround.

easy.prompt: Three jobs all arrive at t=0 with bursts A=3, B=5, C=2. FCFS order A,B,C, no preemption. What is the turnaround time of C?
easy.hint: Add the three bursts to get C's completion, then subtract arrival 0.
easy.explanation: C completes at 3+5+2=10, arrived at 0, so turnaround = 10.
easy.deepDive: A later job's turnaround accumulates every earlier burst as waiting plus its own burst. C waits 8 and runs 2, totaling 10. This shows why job order controls average turnaround. The same Gantt will next let us separate response from turnaround.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 2 is only C's burst; it ignores the 8 units C waited behind A and B.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 8 is B's completion (and C's start), not C's completion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 7 is neither start nor completion; it subtracts incorrectly.

easy.prompt: Three jobs all arrive at t=0 with bursts A=4, B=3, C=5. FCFS order A,B,C. What is the response time of C? Recall response = first-run − arrival.
easy.hint: Find when C first starts (after A and B finish), then subtract arrival 0.
easy.explanation: C first runs at 4+3=7, arrived at 0, so response = 7.
easy.deepDive: Response measures time until first service, which matters for interactivity. It excludes C's own execution, unlike turnaround. Here C's response is 7 but its turnaround is 12. Schedulers that interleave jobs target exactly this gap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 12 is C's turnaround (completion), not first-run; response stops at start.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 5 is C's burst; response counts waiting before start, not execution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 0 is A's response only; later jobs wait behind earlier ones.

easy.prompt: Three jobs all arrive at t=0 with bursts A=2, B=4, C=5. FCFS order A,B,C. What is the waiting time of C? Use wait = start − arrival (no preemption).
easy.hint: Compute C's start (A+B bursts), then subtract arrival 0; check with turnaround minus burst.
easy.explanation: C starts at 2+4=6, so wait = 6; equivalently turnaround 11 minus burst 5 = 6.
easy.deepDive: Wait isolates queueing from service by removing the job's own burst. With no preemption and simultaneous arrival, wait equals response. This distinction becomes sharp once preemption splits waiting across slices. Optimizing wait and turnaround both push toward short-first orders.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 11 is turnaround (wait plus burst), not wait alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 5 is the burst; wait excludes own execution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 2 is A's burst, only part of C's waiting.

easy.prompt: Three jobs arrive at t=0 with bursts A=6, B=2, C=2. FCFS order A,B,C. What is the average turnaround time?
easy.hint: List completions (6, 8, 10), add them, then divide by 3.
easy.explanation: Completions are 6, 8, 10; average = 24/3 = 8.
easy.deepDive: Averages summarize a whole schedule in one number so policies can be compared. Note 3.33 is just average burst and ignores waiting entirely. The gap between 8 and the short-first average motivates smarter ordering next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 3.33 is average burst (6+2+2)/3, which omits all waiting time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 4.67 is average response/wait (0+6+8)/3, not turnaround.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 10 is only C's turnaround, not the mean of all three.

easy.prompt: Jobs: A arrives 0 burst 8, B arrives 1 burst 2, C arrives 2 burst 2. Scheduler is FCFS nonpreemptive (runs each job to completion in arrival order). When does B complete?
easy.hint: Run A fully 0→8 first (B waits even though it arrived at 1), then run B 8→10.
easy.explanation: FCFS runs A 0–8, then B 8–10, so B completes at 10.
easy.deepDive: FCFS commits to arrival order and never preempts, so a late short job cannot jump ahead. B's turnaround is 9 despite burst 2 because it absorbed A's residue. This head-of-line blocking is the convoy effect previewed quantitatively next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 3 would require preempting A at 1, which FCFS never does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 4 assumes B and C run immediately at arrival, ignoring A's monopoly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 8 is A's completion (B's start), not B's completion.

easy.prompt: Three jobs all arrive at 0: L=8, S1=2, S2=2. FCFS order L,S1,S2. What is average turnaround?
easy.hint: Completions are 8, 10, 12 — average them.
easy.explanation: Completions 8, 10, 12 average to 30/3 = 10.
easy.deepDive: Putting the long job first forces every short to carry its 8 units. The short-first order would complete at 2, 4, 12 for average 6. That gap of 4 is the convoy penalty in one number. Schedulers beat FCFS by avoiding exactly this ordering.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 6 is the short-first (SJF) average, not FCFS with L first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 4 is average burst (8+2+2)/3, ignoring waiting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 12 is the maximum turnaround, not the mean.

easy.prompt: Jobs all arrive at 0: L=7, S1=2, S2=2. FCFS order L,S1,S2. What is the waiting time of the last job S2?
easy.hint: S2 starts after L+S1 finish (7+2); that start minus arrival 0 is its wait.
easy.explanation: S2 starts at 9, so wait = 9; its turnaround is 11 minus burst 2.
easy.deepDive: A 2-unit job waits 9 units — over 4x its service — purely due to position. This disproportionality is why convoy hurts interactive workloads. Any policy that lets shorts bypass the long job directly attacks this wait.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 11 is turnaround (9 wait + 2 burst), not wait alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 2 is the burst; wait counts time before first run.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 0 would mean S2 ran first, contradicting L-first FCFS.

easy.prompt: A 20-unit job arrives at 0; five 1-unit interactive jobs arrive at 1,2,3,4,5. Under FCFS, what happens and what does it motivate?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shorts wait ~20 units behind the long job; motivates shortest-first to cut average turnaround.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shorts preempt the long job; motivates larger quanta to stop preemption.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Average turnaround is already optimal; motivates keeping FCFS forever.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Response equals burst for shorts; motivates fixed priorities by PID.

easy.hint: Ask who runs 0→20 under nonpreemptive FCFS, then what each short's wait becomes.
easy.explanation: The long job monopolizes 0–20, so each short waits ~15–19 units; running shorts first would slash the average.
easy.deepDive: FCFS is fair in arrival order but blind to burst length, so one long job convoys many shorts. The shorts' turnaround is dominated by waiting, not service. This exact pathology motivates SJF, which orders by burst to minimize average turnaround.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: FCFS never preempts; shorts cannot interrupt the running long job.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Long-first is pessimal for average turnaround, not optimal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Shorts' response is ~20, not 1; PID ordering does not fix length blindness.

easy.prompt: Jobs all arrive at 0 with bursts A=6, B=2, C=4. Nonpreemptive SJF picks the shortest available job first. Which runs first?

choices.label: A
choices.body: B (burst 2)

choices.label: B
choices.body: A (burst 6)

choices.label: C
choices.body: C (burst 4)

choices.label: D
choices.body: Whichever has the latest deadline

easy.hint: Compare the three burst numbers and pick the minimum — ignore arrival order.
easy.explanation: Shortest burst is B=2, so SJF runs B first.
easy.deepDive: SJF reorders by predicted service instead of arrival, attacking convoy at its root. With simultaneous arrival the rule is simply ascending burst. Staggered arrivals add an availability constraint handled in SRTF next. Note SJF targets average turnaround, not maximum.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A first is FCFS thinking; SJF explicitly overrides arrival order by length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: C is the median, not the minimum; SJF picks the true shortest.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deadlines belong to EDF real-time scheduling, not SJF.

easy.prompt: Jobs arrive at 0 with bursts A=5, B=2, C=3. Compare FCFS order A,B,C vs SJF order B,C,A. What is SJF's average turnaround?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 5.67 (completions 2, 5, 10)

choices.label: B
choices.body: 7.33 (completions 5, 7, 10)

choices.label: C
choices.body: 3.33 (average burst)

choices.label: D
choices.body: 10 (maximum turnaround)

easy.hint: Order B,C,A: B 0→2, C 2→5, A 5→10; average 2, 5, 10.
easy.explanation: SJF completions are 2, 5, 10, so average = 17/3 ≈ 5.67.
easy.deepDive: Short-first drops the average from 7.33 to 5.67 with identical work, a pure ordering win. SJF is provably optimal for average turnaround among nonpreemptive policies. The catch, taken up next, is that it assumes burst lengths are known.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 7.33 is the FCFS average, showing exactly what SJF improves upon.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 3.33 is average burst with zero waiting, unachievable under any order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 10 is the max (A's turnaround); SJF optimizes the average, not the max.

easy.prompt: Which is a genuine limitation of SJF (and a common misconception to avoid)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It needs burst estimates and long jobs can starve if shorts keep arriving.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It optimizes maximum turnaround, so averages stay high.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It needs no quanta because it is a multilevel feedback queue.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It guarantees deadlines even when total utilization exceeds 1.

easy.hint: Ask what SJF must know before choosing, and what happens to a 100-unit job facing endless 1-unit arrivals.
easy.explanation: SJF cannot pick the shortest without knowing bursts, and continuous shorts indefinitely delay longs.
easy.deepDive: Burst prediction uses history (e.g., exponential averaging) but is never exact, so SJF is an ideal more than an implementation. Starvation is structural: any strict shortest-first rule sacrifices fairness. These two flaws motivate Round Robin and MLFQ, which avoid prediction and add aging.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: SJF optimizes average turnaround, not maximum; minimizing the max is a different objective.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MLFQ is a separate scheduler; SJF has no queues or quanta at all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No scheduler meets all deadlines when overloaded; that misconception belongs to EDF.

easy.prompt: Process P runs `int main(){ return f()+1; }`. Where does the compiled machine code for `main` and `f` live in P's address space?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Heap — code is allocated with malloc at runtime and grows as functions run.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Code (text) segment — fixed-size, low virtual addresses, holds compiled instructions.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stack — one frame per instruction, pushed on every loop iteration.

choices.label: D
choices.body: PCB — the process control block stores the machine code itself.

easy.hint: Ask: which region never changes size during the run? Code is known at compile time; heap/stack are dynamic.
easy.explanation: Compiled instructions live in a fixed-size code segment at low addresses, separate from dynamic heap/stack.
easy.deepDive: Think of the address space like a printed book: the story text (code) is printed once and never changes length, while margin notes (stack) and pasted-in inserts (heap) come and go. That is why the OS maps code low, marks it read-only/executable, and never mallocs it — protection and sharing depend on it staying fixed. This split is what lets two processes share one physical copy of code later.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Code is not malloc'd — heap is for runtime-sized data, not fixed instructions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stack holds frames/locals, not the instructions themselves.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: PCB (Ch1-2) holds pointers/metadata, not the program's code bytes.

easy.prompt: The heap starts just above globals. When malloc needs more space and calls sbrk/brk, which way does the heap grow?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It grows down toward lower addresses, same direction as the stack.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It stays fixed — only the stack ever grows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It grows up toward higher addresses (via sbrk/brk when malloc needs more).

choices.label: D
choices.body: It grows in both directions at once to balance fragmentation.

easy.hint: Heap sits just above code/globals. Which way is the open gap — toward higher or lower addresses?
easy.explanation: Heap starts above globals and grows up to higher addresses when the allocator requests more memory.
easy.deepDive: Picture heap and stack as two piles starting at opposite ends of an empty shelf, growing toward each other — the gap is free space either can claim. Heap grows up because it starts just above code/globals and extends into that gap via sbrk. If both grew the same way they would collide immediately instead of sharing flexibly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Same-direction growth is the classic misconception — heap grows up, stack grows down.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Heap is dynamic by definition; code/globals are the fixed regions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only one growth direction per region; bidirectional growth is not how sbrk works.

easy.prompt: Heap grows up. Stack starts near the top of the address space and grows down. Why opposite directions?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both grow up, so the OS places heap low and stack just above it.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Heap grows up and stack grows down — toward each other — so either can use the middle gap.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both grow down from the top of the address space.

choices.label: D
choices.body: They grow away from each other to avoid ever meeting.

easy.hint: Combine Q2 with the stack fact: stack starts high and grows down. Draw both arrows — do they point the same way?
easy.explanation: Opposite growth lets heap and stack share the middle free gap flexibly without a fixed split.
easy.deepDive: The toward-each-other design is a poor-man's flexible partition: instead of pre-splitting memory 50/50, the OS leaves one big middle gap and lets the needier side take it. A deep call chain eats stack space; a big malloc workload eats heap space — neither starves the other prematurely. Meeting in the middle means out-of-memory, which is exactly the signal to trap or deny.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Heap-up/stack-up would stack them rigidly — the standard layout is opposite to share the gap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Heap does not start at the top; it starts above globals and grows up.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Growing apart wastes the middle and forces fixed limits; growing together shares flexibly.

easy.prompt: `main` calls `f()`. What happens to the stack?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Call pushes a new frame (return address + locals); return pops it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Call mallocs heap for locals; return leaks it until exit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Call overwrites the single shared frame in place.

choices.label: A
choices.body: The kernel copies the entire address space to disk on every call.

easy.hint: Locals die on return without free(). What push/pop discipline gives that for free?
easy.explanation: Each call gets a fresh pushed frame; return pops it, auto-reclaiming locals.
easy.deepDive: Think of frames like cafeteria trays stacked per call: each caller leaves a return-address note on the new tray, the callee eats (runs) on it, then the tray is removed on return. That push/pop discipline is why locals vanish automatically and why the stack pointer just moves — no allocator search needed. It also previews overflow: too many trays topple the stack.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Locals live in stack frames, not malloc'd heap — no free() needed on return.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Overwriting one frame would destroy the caller's locals and return address.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: PCB switch happens on context switch (Ch1-2), not on every function call.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Calls never touch disk; frames are just pushed/popped in memory.

easy.prompt: Hardware has base and bound (limit) registers per process. What do they do on each memory access?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It compiles virtual addresses into physical ones at build time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It stores the stack pointer so returns find their caller.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hardware computes physical = virtual + base, after checking virtual < bound; else it traps.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It pages memory to disk whenever the heap grows.

easy.hint: Two jobs: let every process use address 0 AND stop it touching other memory. Which register does each job?
easy.explanation: Base relocates (add offset); bound protects (trap if virtual >= bound).
easy.deepDive: Base-and-bounds is two ideas in one piece of hardware: relocation (add base, so every process can use address 0) plus protection (compare against bound, so no process touches neighbors). Trace it: virtual 100 with base 5000 becomes physical 5100, but virtual 9999 with bound 1000 traps before touching memory. That trap is the isolation motive from Ch1 enforced by silicon.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No recompilation needed — translation happens at runtime in hardware, that is the point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Stack pointer is a separate register; base/bound are relocation + limit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Paging to disk is swapping (later chapter), not base/bounds translation.

easy.prompt: Process with bound=1000 accesses virtual address 5000. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It wraps around to address 0 and continues silently.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It returns NULL to the program like a failed malloc.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It extends the bound automatically to fit the access.

choices.label: D
choices.body: CPU raises a fault/trap to the OS, which typically kills the process (segfault).

easy.hint: Protection must act BEFORE memory is touched. What hardware action stops a bad access and involves the OS?
easy.explanation: Illegal virtual addresses trap to the OS instead of touching чужой memory — typically a segfault kill.
easy.deepDive: The trap is the enforcement half of isolation: without it, a stray pointer in one process could scribble on another process's memory or the kernel. That is why out-of-bounds is not a quiet wrap or a NULL — hardware stops the access before it touches DRAM and hands control to the OS. Ch1's protection motive becomes a real exception you can observe as 'Segmentation fault'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Wrap-around would silently corrupt address 0 — the opposite of protection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Auto-extending the bound lets any program grab all memory; bounds are OS-set, not self-extending.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: NULL is a software malloc convention, not what MMU hardware does on a bounds violation.

easy.prompt: `char *p = malloc(64); free(p);` What does `free(p)` guarantee?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It immediately returns the memory to the OS and zeroes it.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It returns the block to the user-level allocator's free list for reuse; the OS may still have the pages mapped.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It deletes the pointer variable so it can never be used again.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It compacts all of memory to remove fragmentation.

easy.hint: Two levels: allocator (library) vs OS (kernel). Which one does free() talk to directly?
easy.explanation: free() recycles to the allocator's free list; OS-level return (sbrk down/munmap) is rare and separate.
easy.deepDive: Think of malloc/free as a librarian (allocator) managing books lent from the library (OS): returning a book goes to the reshelve cart (free list), not back to the publisher (OS) each time. That is why free is fast and why freed memory is reusable by the next malloc but still counts against the process until the OS reclaims pages. Confusing these two levels is the root of 'free gives back to OS immediately' bugs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Immediate OS return + zeroing is the misconception — reuse comes from the free list, zeroing is not guaranteed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The pointer variable still holds the old address (now dangling); free touches the block, not the variable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No compaction happens; fragmentation persists — that is a later problem, not free's job.

easy.prompt: What is internal fragmentation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wasted space INSIDE an allocated unit — e.g., a 12-byte request in a 16-byte size class, or a 1-byte file in a 4KB page.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Free gaps BETWEEN allocated blocks/segments too scattered to reuse.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delay caused by the scheduler switching between processes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Corruption caused by writing past a malloc'd buffer.

easy.hint: Parse the word: INTERNAL = inside the allocation. Which option describes waste you already own but cannot use?
easy.explanation: Internal fragmentation is padding waste inside an allocated chunk/page that the owner cannot use.
easy.deepDive: Internal means inside: you asked for a small box but the warehouse only rents fixed-size crates, so padding sits empty but billed to you. Rounding every allocation up to a size class or page causes it, and no amount of rearranging free blocks fixes it — only smaller quanta or different splitting. Contrast with external, where the waste is outside, in unusable gaps between live blocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Gaps between blocks is external fragmentation — the mirror image.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scheduler delay is a CPU-scheduling concept, not memory waste; classic distractor.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overflow corruption is a malloc bug, not a fragmentation category.

easy.prompt: Why give each segment (code, heap, stack) its own read/write/execute bits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To make memory accesses faster by caching permissions.

choices.label: B
choices.body: So the scheduler can prioritize code over data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: So illegal uses trap: e.g., code is R-X (execute but not write), data/stack are RW- (write but not execute).

choices.label: D
choices.body: So every segment shares one permission for simplicity.

easy.hint: Think intent: should a program ever WRITE its own instructions, or EXECUTE its stack bytes? What enforces that?
easy.explanation: Per-segment R/W/X lets hardware trap writes to code and execution of data/stack.
easy.deepDive: Permissions turn each segment's intent into hardware law: code should run but never be overwritten, data should be read/written but never jumped into as code. A write to the code segment or a jump into the stack then traps instead of silently succeeding — stopping both accidents and code-injection attacks. One uniform permission would force a choice between self-modifying code and an exploitable stack.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Permissions check legality, not speed — caching is a TLB/MMU speed trick, separate idea.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scheduler priority is Ch-scheduling; protection bits do not schedule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Uniform permissions defeat the purpose — code and data need opposite rights.

easy.prompt: A system uses 4-KB pages. How many bits of the virtual address are the page offset, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 8 bits, because 4 KB ≈ 1000 bytes

choices.label: B
choices.body: 10 bits, because addresses are 32 bits

choices.label: C
choices.body: 12 bits, because 2^12 = 4096

choices.label: D
choices.body: 20 bits, because 32 − 12 is VPN

easy.hint: Ask: what power of 2 equals the page size? That exponent is the offset width.
easy.explanation: 4 KB = 4096 = 2^12, so 12 offset bits address each byte in the page.
easy.deepDive: The offset must index every byte in a page, so offset bits = log2(page size). This is why 4-KB pages always mean a 12-bit offset regardless of VA width. Once the offset is fixed, the remaining VA bits are the VPN. That split is the single idea every later translation builds on.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Confuses decimal 1000 with binary 1024; page sizes are powers of 2, and 4 KB is 4096.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 10 bits is 1 KB; it also mixes up VA width with page size.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 20 bits is the VPN count for 32-bit VAs, not the offset — you computed the complement.

easy.prompt: With 32-bit virtual addresses and 4-KB pages, how many bits are VPN vs offset?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 12 bits VPN + 12 bits offset

choices.label: B
choices.body: 20 bits VPN + 12 bits offset

choices.label: C
choices.body: 32 bits VPN + 0 bits offset

choices.label: D
choices.body: 20 bits VPN + PID in the top 12 bits

easy.hint: Subtract the 12 offset bits from 32. Where does the PID live — in the address or in OS state?
easy.explanation: 32 − 12 = 20 VPN bits; PID lives in OS state (page-table register), not in the address.
easy.deepDive: A 32-bit VA names 2^32 bytes. Reserving 12 bits for the offset leaves 20 bits for the VPN, giving about 1M virtual pages. The PID is not encoded in the VA; the OS switches page tables per process. This fixed split motivates why linear page tables have 2^20 entries.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Halves the address; VPN gets all remaining bits after the offset, not an equal split.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zero offset bits would mean byte addressing inside a page is impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: the PID is not part of the VA; the OS switches the page-table base register on context switch.

easy.prompt: VA = 0x12345678, 4-KB pages. What are the VPN and offset?

choices.label: A
choices.body: VPN = 0x12345, offset = 0x678

choices.label: B
choices.body: VPN = 0x123, offset = 0x45678

choices.label: C
choices.body: VPN = 0x678, offset = 0x12345

choices.label: D
choices.body: VPN = 0x2345678, offset = 0x1

easy.hint: With 12-bit offsets, how many hex digits stay at the bottom? Split 0x12345678 there.
easy.explanation: Low 12 bits (3 hex digits) = 0x678 offset; upper 20 bits = 0x12345 VPN.
easy.deepDive: Because 12 hex digits are 3 hex digits of offset, you can split a hex VA by eye: last 3 hex digits are the offset. The upper digits are the VPN used to index the page table. This mechanical split is exactly what hardware does by bit selection.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Takes 20 offset bits instead of 12 — that would be a 1-MB page.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Swaps the fields; the offset is always the low bits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Splits off only one hex digit (4 bits); that confuses a nibble with a page.

easy.prompt: VA = 0xABCDEFFF, 4-KB pages. Split into VPN and offset.

choices.label: A
choices.body: VPN = 0xAB, offset = 0xCDEFFF

choices.label: B
choices.body: VPN = 0xABCDEFFF, offset = 0x0

choices.label: C
choices.body: VPN = 0xFFF, offset = 0xABCDE

choices.label: D
choices.body: VPN = 0xABCDE, offset = 0xFFF

easy.hint: Cover the last 3 hex digits — that is the offset. What remains?
easy.explanation: Last 3 hex digits 0xFFF = offset; remainder 0xABCDE = VPN.
easy.deepDive: Same rule, new address: mask off the low 12 bits for the offset and shift right for the VPN. Checking a second address cements that translation never does arithmetic on the whole VA, only field extraction. The offset then passes through to the physical address unchanged.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Keeps only 8 VPN bits; you dropped most of the upper address.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Claims zero offset, which would mean the address is page-aligned — 0xFFF ≠ 0.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Swaps VPN and offset again; offset must be the low bits.

easy.prompt: From Ch4 (segmentation, fragmentation vocabulary): what placement problem does paging solve?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Paging reuses the inode to index pages, removing fragmentation

choices.label: B
choices.body: Paging splits memory into fixed-size frames so any free frame fits any page — no external fragmentation

choices.label: C
choices.body: Paging makes address spaces contiguous in RAM

choices.label: D
choices.body: Paging removes page faults with bigger tables

easy.hint: What made variable-sized segments hard to place? How does a fixed unit change that?
easy.explanation: Fixed-size pages/frames eliminate external fragmentation; any free frame fits.
easy.deepDive: Segmentation suffers external fragmentation because segments are variable-sized and must be contiguous. Paging fixes the unit at one page, so any free frame works and compaction is never needed. The cost is a table per page plus some internal waste, which the next questions quantify.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Real misconception: inodes index file blocks on disk, not virtual pages; paging uses page tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Paging does the opposite: virtual contiguity is preserved while physical frames scatter.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: table size never removes faults; faults depend on residency, not table capacity.

easy.prompt: What does the PTE valid bit tell the hardware?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The page is dirty and must be written back

choices.label: B
choices.body: The page is present in DRAM

choices.label: C
choices.body: The translation is legal; the VPN has a meaningful mapping

choices.label: D
choices.body: The process may write to the page

easy.hint: Which single bit should hardware check first to decide legal vs illegal address?
easy.explanation: Valid = 1 means this VPN is mapped for the process; valid = 0 traps.
easy.deepDive: Valid is the master legality switch checked first on every access. If valid = 0 the hardware traps even if other bits look plausible, and the OS typically delivers a segfault. Present, RW, and dirty refine a valid mapping with residency, permission, and write-back state.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the dirty bit, which records a write happened — not legality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the present bit (resident vs swapped); a page can be valid but swapped out.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is the read/write permission bit, checked after validity.

easy.prompt: Without a TLB, how many memory references does one load cost under single-level paging?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One extra read (PTE), then the data access — 2 memory refs total

choices.label: B
choices.body: Zero extra refs; the MMU computes PA arithmetically

choices.label: C
choices.body: One ref total; the PTE replaces the data access

choices.label: D
choices.body: Three refs: directory + table + data for single-level

easy.hint: To translate you must READ the PTE from memory first. Then what?
easy.explanation: Single-level: read PTE from the page table, then access data/instruction.
easy.deepDive: Every data access pays a translation tax without a TLB: fetch the PTE, then fetch the data. Single-level paging adds exactly one extra reference, which is why TLBs matter so much. Multilevel tables add one ref per level, covered in the stretch set.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Confuses translation with arithmetic; the VPN→PFN mapping lives in memory and must be read.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The PTE fetch is extra — it does not substitute for the data fetch.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Three refs describes two-level paging; single-level has one table only.

easy.prompt: What is internal fragmentation under paging?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Free gaps between variable segments

choices.label: B
choices.body: The whole linear page table wasting memory

choices.label: C
choices.body: Extra memory refs during a page walk

choices.label: D
choices.body: Wasted bytes in the last page of a segment (allocated but unused)

easy.hint: Think INSIDE the last page: what happens when segment size is not a page multiple?
easy.explanation: Fixed pages round each segment up; the tail of the last page is wasted.
easy.deepDive: Internal fragmentation is per-allocation rounding waste inside the last page, distinct from external fragmentation between allocations. With s segments the waste scales with s, averaging half a page each. Larger pages amplify it, which later questions compute numerically.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is external fragmentation, the segmentation-era problem paging fixed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is page-table space overhead, a separate cost from per-segment waste.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is translation time overhead (walk cost), not space waste.

easy.prompt: Why is a single linear page table wasteful for sparse address spaces?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because each PTE is 4 KB

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because it needs one entry per virtual page, even for never-used VPNs

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because the PID is stored in every PTE

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because pages are variable-sized

easy.hint: Does entry count track virtual pages or resident pages?
easy.explanation: Linear tables pay per VPN, not per used page — sparse regions still cost entries.
easy.deepDive: A linear table is indexed by VPN, so its size is proportional to the virtual space, not the used space. A 32-bit space with 4-KB pages forces ~1M entries per process regardless of actual allocation. That gulf between virtual size and physical use motivates multilevel and segmented tables.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Inverts sizes: PTEs are ~4–8 bytes; pages are KBs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real misconception: PIDs are not stored per PTE; one table per process implies the owner.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pages are fixed-size by definition; variable size describes segments.

easy.prompt: How do two processes share one physical code page under paging?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Two PTEs (in different tables) hold the same PFN, e.g. read-only for shared code

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two VPNs share one PTE entry

choices.label: C
choices.body: The inode points both processes at one page

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both processes embed the same PID in their VAs

easy.hint: If translation is VPN→PFN, how could two VPNs land on one frame?
easy.explanation: Sharing = alias PFN from two PTEs; permissions can differ per mapping.
easy.deepDive: Sharing is indirection: distinct VPNs map to one PFN, each with its own permission bits. Code can be mapped read-only/executable in both processes while data stays private. This page-granular control is finer than whole-segment sharing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Each process has its own table; entries are never shared across tables, only the PFN value is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real misconception: inodes are for files, not page aliasing; the PTE holds the PFN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: PIDs are not VA fields; tables are per-process.

easy.prompt: What is segmented (hybrid) paging at a high level?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One global page table indexed by PID + VPN

choices.label: B
choices.body: Paging the inode table

choices.label: C
choices.body: Segment base/bounds locate a per-segment page table; offset splits into VPN + page offset

choices.label: D
choices.body: One page table per byte of address space

easy.hint: Which step comes first: segment check or page lookup?
easy.explanation: Segment selects table; paging happens within the segment bounds.
easy.deepDive: Hybrid keeps segmentation's coarse structure (code/stack/heap) and pages within each segment. The segment register selects which page table to use, bounding table size to the segment. It inherits sharing and sparsity from both parents at the cost of two lookups.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No global table keyed by PID exists; the segment register + per-process tables do the job.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inodes are unrelated to address translation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tables are per page of virtual space, not per byte — that confuses offset with index.

easy.prompt: A program uses 3 tiny segments scattered across a 32-bit space. Which base scheme wastes less metadata and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Paging, because PTEs eliminate faults

choices.label: B
choices.body: Segmentation, because segments are fixed-size

choices.label: C
choices.body: Paging, because one linear table is smallest

choices.label: D
choices.body: Segmentation, because unallocated regions between segments cost nothing

easy.hint: Which scheme allocates metadata only for what exists vs for every VPN?
