easy.explanation: Segments describe only what exists; gaps are free. Linear tables pay per VPN including gaps.
easy.deepDive: With only base/bounds per segment, holes between segments need no backing store or table. Linear paging pays per VPN even in holes, which is exactly the sparsity penalty. This contrast sets up hybrid and multilevel designs that reclaim hole cost while keeping paging's placement ease.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Bigger/different tables never eliminate faults; also misstates the sparse case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reverses definitions: segments are variable-sized, pages fixed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The linear table is largest in the sparse case — one entry per VPN.

easy.prompt: What does the TLB cache?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Disk block numbers cached for file reads

choices.label: B
choices.body: Recent VPN-to-PFN translations plus valid/protection bits

choices.label: C
choices.body: Full page-table pages for all processes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Physical frame contents (data) of hot pages

easy.hint: Ask first: on a memory access, what mapping must the MMU know before it can form a physical address?
easy.explanation: The TLB caches recent address translations (VPN to PFN with permission bits), not data or disk blocks.
easy.deepDive: Think of the TLB as the CPU's sticky-note cache of recent translations. It sits beside the MMU, is tiny (64-1024 entries) and tagged by VPN plus ASID. On a context switch without ASIDs every sticky note must be tossed, which is why ASIDs were added. It never holds disk blocks or page data, only the mapping.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Disk blocks are cached by the buffer cache/page cache, not the TLB; confusing the two merges VM with filesystems.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Page tables live in memory; the TLB holds only a few cached entries from them, never whole tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Frame data lives in RAM/caches; the TLB holds only the translation to locate that data.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: On a TLB hit (page present, permitted), what happens next?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Walk the page table first, then probe the TLB to confirm

choices.label: B
choices.body: Trap to disk on every access, then refill both TLB and table

choices.label: C
choices.body: Probe TLB; on hit check protection and form PA with offset, no table walk

choices.label: D
choices.body: Flush the TLB, then fetch the data directly from swap

easy.hint: Sketch the two paths: what work can be skipped when the translation is already cached?
easy.explanation: A TLB hit avoids the page-table walk entirely: translate, check protection, and access memory.
easy.deepDive: The fast path is TLB-first: MMU probes the TLB in parallel with permission checks. A hit means the PFN is trusted immediately and concatenated with the offset. Only a miss pays for a memory-resident table walk. This is why hit rate dominates average access time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Walking first defeats the TLB's purpose; the TLB is probed before the table, not after.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Disk is touched only on a page fault (present=0), not on a TLB hit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Flushes happen on context switch or munmap, never as part of a successful hit.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: TLB lookup=1ns, memory=100ns, single-level table. Hit rate 90%. What is EAT?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 101 ns

choices.label: B
choices.body: 111 ns

choices.label: C
choices.body: 201 ns

choices.label: D
choices.body: 11 ns

easy.hint: List the cost of hit vs miss, then weight them: what does each access always pay?
easy.explanation: EAT is 111 ns: everyone pays TLB plus data, and 10 percent pay one extra walk.
easy.deepDive: Write EAT as base plus expected extra walks. Here every access pays TLB plus data for a base of 101. The 10 percent misses each add one table read, adding about 10 on average for 111 total. Think toll booths: everyone pays the main toll and only some pay the second booth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 101 forgets the TLB lookup cost; every access pays it even on a hit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 201 charges two full memories to every access instead of only to misses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 11 confuses ns units and drops the data access entirely.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: TLB=2ns, memory=100ns, single-level. Hit rate 96%. What is EAT?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 102 ns

choices.label: B
choices.body: 120 ns

choices.label: C
choices.body: 200 ns

choices.label: D
choices.body: 106 ns

easy.hint: Reuse the same formula: base (TLB+data) plus miss-rate times one extra memory read.
easy.explanation: EAT is 106 ns: base plus 4 percent times one extra memory read.
easy.deepDive: Reuse the hit/miss template with new numbers: base is 2+100=102. Misses (4%) add one 100ns walk, so 102+4=106. Notice a small miss-rate shift moves EAT only a few ns with RAM-speed walks. Disks later will swing it by millions, which is why working sets matter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 102 is only the hit cost; it ignores the expected extra walk on misses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 120 charges misses far too much, as if each miss cost 500ns.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 200 double-counts memory for every access, not just misses.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: Why do multilevel page tables save memory for sparse address spaces?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Allocate only second-level tables that have at least one valid page

choices.label: C
choices.body: Store all page tables on disk to save RAM

choices.label: D
choices.body: Use one giant flat table shared by all processes

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cache VPNs in the TLB so tables are unnecessary

easy.hint: Picture a mostly-empty flat table: which contiguous chunks could be omitted entirely?
easy.explanation: Multilevel tables save space for sparse address spaces by not allocating tables for unused regions.
easy.deepDive: A sparse address space (stack at top, heap in middle, code at bottom) leaves most of a flat table empty. Multilevel tables add a directory: invalid directory entries mean the whole second-level chunk is never allocated. You pay pointers for valid regions to avoid paying for empty ones. That is the core space trick.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tables must stay memory-resident for the walker; putting them on disk would fault on every translation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A shared flat table breaks isolation; each process needs its own mappings.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The TLB is only a cache; it cannot replace the authoritative tables and misses still walk them.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: 32-bit, 4KB pages, 10-bit directory + 10-bit index. How much does one second-level table cover?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 4 KB

choices.label: B
choices.body: 4 MB covering the whole process

choices.label: C
choices.body: 4 MB (1024 entries x 4KB pages)

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1 GB

easy.hint: Count entries in one second-level table, then multiply by page size.
easy.explanation: One second-level table holds 2^10 PTEs x 4KB = 4MB of coverage.
easy.deepDive: Split the 20-bit VPN into 10-bit directory plus 10-bit index. The index selects one of 1024 PTEs, each mapping a 4KB page, so one table spans 1024x4KB=4MB. The directory then covers 1024 such chunks to reach 4GB.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 4KB is a single page, not the whole table of 1024 pages.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 4MB per table is right but it does not cover a 4GB process; you need 1024 such tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1GB confuses page-directory coverage on PAE/huge variants with this classic split.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: FIFO, 3 frames, refs: 1,2,3,1,4,5. How many page faults?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 4 faults

choices.label: C
choices.body: 6 faults

choices.label: D
choices.body: 5 faults

choices.label: B
choices.body: 7 faults

easy.hint: Simulate step by step: keep a queue, evict the oldest only on a fault, hits change nothing.
easy.explanation: FIFO faults on 1,2,3,4,5 (1 hits on re-reference) = 5 faults with 3 frames.
easy.deepDive: Run FIFO with 3 frames on 1,2,3,1,4,5: faults on 1,2,3, then 1 hits, then 4 evicts 1 and 5 evicts 2, totaling 5 faults. The victim pointer moves only on faults, so the reused 1 is still evicted. FIFO ignores reuse, which later traces will punish.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 4 misses the compulsory fault on 5; every first use must fault.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 6 double-counts the re-referenced 1, but FIFO hits do not fault.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 7 faults on every access, forgetting the second 1 is a hit.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: LRU, 3 frames, refs: 1,2,3,1,4,5. How many faults and which pages are evicted first?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 5 faults

choices.label: B
choices.body: 7 faults

choices.label: C
choices.body: 4 faults

choices.label: D
choices.body: 6 faults

easy.hint: Track recency: on the hit to 1, which page becomes least-recently-used?
easy.explanation: LRU also faults 5 times here (1,2,3,4,5), but evicts 2 then 3 instead of FIFO's 1 then 2.
easy.deepDive: LRU on the same string: 1,2,3 fault, 1 hits and becomes MRU, 4 evicts 2 (LRU), 5 evicts 3. Total 5 here too, but the victim differs (2 vs 1). The trace habit is identical: maintain recency order, evict the tail on fault. Later strings separate LRU from FIFO clearly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 7 faults on every access; misses that 1 hits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 4 implies one first-touch hit, which is impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 6 miscounts by faulting on the repeated 1.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: What is Belady's anomaly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: LRU with more frames can fault more

choices.label: B
choices.body: OPT can be implemented with future prediction hardware

choices.label: C
choices.body: Clock always matches LRU exactly

choices.label: D
choices.body: FIFO with more frames can fault more (Belady's anomaly)

easy.hint: Which policy ignores recency, so extra capacity can preserve exactly the wrong pages?
easy.explanation: Belady's anomaly: FIFO can fault more with more frames; LRU/OPT cannot.
easy.deepDive: Belady showed FIFO breaks the more-frames-means-fewer-faults intuition on patterns like 1,2,3,4,1,2,5. Extra frames retain the wrong pages and shift eviction timing badly. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and immune. So Belady is specifically a FIFO (and random) hazard, a favorite exam trap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: LRU is a stack algorithm and never shows Belady; this is the classic misconception.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: OPT needs perfect future knowledge and is only a yardstick, not implementable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clock only approximates LRU with ref bits; it diverges on real traces.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

easy.prompt: What is thrashing?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Combined working sets exceed RAM, so pages ping-pong to disk and CPU idles

choices.label: B
choices.body: CPU overheats from too many TLB hits

choices.label: C
choices.body: Page tables grow larger than the address space

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disk fills up with zombie processes

easy.hint: What happens to CPU use when every process spends its quantum waiting on disk reads?
easy.explanation: Thrashing is excessive faulting because runnable working sets overflow memory, starving the CPU.
easy.deepDive: Thrashing is a feedback loop: each process's active pages (working set) no longer fit together, every timeslice faults, the pager steals pages from neighbors, and CPU utilization collapses while disk I/O spikes. The fix is admission control or fewer runnable processes, not faster disks. Watch for high paging plus low CPU as the signature.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: TLB hits speed things up; they never cause thrashing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tables are small relative to data; thrashing is about data pages, not table size.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Disk-full is a capacity error, not the fault-rate collapse of thrashing.

easy.prompt: What is the demand-paging page-fault sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Write victim to disk, then kill the process

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ignore the fault because the TLB will resolve it

choices.label: D
choices.body: Trap, find a free frame or evict one, read page from disk, update PTE, resume

choices.label: B
choices.body: Allocate a frame without updating any PTE

easy.hint: Order the steps: from trap to resume, when is disk read vs PTE update?
easy.explanation: A demand fault traps to the OS, pages in from disk into a frame, installs the PTE, and retries.
easy.deepDive: Demand paging faults follow a pipeline: hardware traps (present=0), OS locates the page on swap/disk, picks a victim frame if needed, issues the read, blocks the process, then installs the new PTE (present=1) and retries the instruction. TLB and tables are updated at the install step. Missing any step leaves an inconsistent mapping.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Victims are written back only if dirty, and the faulting process continues, not killed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Updating the PTE is mandatory; otherwise the retry faults again.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The TLB cannot satisfy a not-present page; only a disk read can.

easy.prompt: How does copy-on-write (COW) fork work?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Kernel copies all pages eagerly at fork time

choices.label: C
choices.body: Parent and child share read-only pages; a write fault copies the page privately

choices.label: D
choices.body: Child gets no address space until exec

choices.label: B
choices.body: Pages are compressed to halve memory use

easy.hint: When should the copy happen: at fork for every page, or lazily on first write?
easy.explanation: COW shares pages read-only after fork and copies only on a write fault.
easy.deepDive: Fork marks shared pages read-only with a COW flag and bumps reference counts. Reads proceed shared at full speed. The first write to a shared page traps, the OS allocates a fresh frame, copies contents, and remaps that PTE writable. This laziness makes fork+exec cheap, which is why shells fork constantly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Eager copy is what COW avoids; it would make fork O(address space).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The child gets a full (shared) address space immediately; exec comes later and optionally.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Compression is unrelated; COW is about sharing versus copying.

easy.prompt: A process creates two threads. Which memory do those threads share, compared to two separate processes?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each thread gets its own separate address space, like a forked process

choices.label: B
choices.body: All threads in a process share one address space (code, globals, heap, FDs)

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threads share only open files; code and heap are private per thread

choices.label: D
choices.body: Threads share nothing and communicate only through pipes

easy.hint: Recall fork gives a new address space. Ask: do threads fork the memory, or stay inside one memory?
easy.explanation: Threads of a process share the same code, globals, heap, and file descriptors; only stacks, PCs, and registers are private.
easy.deepDive: Processes isolate address spaces so one crash cannot corrupt another. Threads invert that choice inside one process to make sharing cheap and fast. The price is that any thread can corrupt shared globals or heap. That tradeoff is the single idea behind every sharing question that follows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This describes processes, not threads; threads were invented to avoid separate address spaces.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Code, globals, and heap are all shared; files are only one shared item.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pipes are for inter-process communication; threads share memory directly.

easy.prompt: Global int x = 0; two threads both do x++. What do they observe about x?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each thread sees a private copy of x starting at 0

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only the first thread to run sees x; the other sees uninitialized memory

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both threads read and write the same x, so one thread's update is visible to the other

choices.label: D
choices.body: The program fails to link because globals cannot be shared

easy.hint: Ask where globals live: per-process data segment or per-thread stack?
easy.explanation: A global lives once in the shared address space, so both threads access the identical location.
easy.deepDive: Globals live in the data segment, which belongs to the process, not to any thread. Both threads load and store the same address for x. That is why unsynchronized writes to globals race. Private state must live on the stack or be made thread-local.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Threads do not copy globals; that copy behavior is fork, not pthread_create.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: There is no first-wins rule; both threads map the same virtual address.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sharing globals is legal and common; it is the source of both power and races.

easy.prompt: Thread A mallocs a buffer and passes the pointer to thread B. Can B safely read it (assuming no free yet)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes: malloc returns pointers into the shared heap, visible to all threads

choices.label: B
choices.body: No: each thread has its own heap, so the pointer is invalid in thread B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes, but only after thread A exits and the heap is flushed to thread B

choices.label: D
choices.body: No: heap allocations are copied to each thread's stack on access

easy.hint: Ask: is the heap per-process or per-thread? Then decide if the pointer stays valid.
easy.explanation: The heap is process-wide and shared, so a malloc address is valid in every thread of the process.
easy.deepDive: malloc manages one process-wide heap shared by every thread. A pointer is just a virtual address in that shared space. So passing a heap pointer between threads works, but freeing it needs coordination. Contrast this with a stack address, which becomes dangerous once its frame returns.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: There is one heap per process, not per thread; no private heaps are created.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No flush or exit is needed; sharing is immediate because the address space is shared.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Heap memory is not copied to stacks; both threads dereference the same heap address.

easy.prompt: A process opens a log file, then two threads both write using that fd. What happens to the file offset?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The descriptor table is copied, so B writes to a different file offset

choices.label: B
choices.body: B gets EBADF because descriptors are per-thread private

choices.label: C
choices.body: B can write but starts at offset 0 while A continues elsewhere

choices.label: D
choices.body: B writes through the same open file description, sharing the file offset

easy.hint: Ask: did the process open the file, or did one thread? Process resources stay shared.
easy.explanation: File descriptors and offsets are process state, so both threads share the same open file description and offset.
easy.deepDive: Open file descriptors and their offsets live in process state shared by all threads. Writes from either thread advance the same offset. That makes concurrent logging easy but interleaved without locking. Private per-thread descriptors would defeat the purpose of shared I/O.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: fork copies descriptors, but thread creation does not copy anything.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Descriptors are not per-thread; EBADF would mean a closed fd, not a thread boundary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: There is only one offset per open description, so both threads advance the same one.

easy.prompt: Which state is private to each thread in the same process?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Nothing is private; threads share stacks, PCs, and registers too

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each thread has its own stack, program counter, registers, and thread ID

choices.label: C
choices.body: Each thread has its own heap and code segment

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each thread has its own file descriptors and globals

easy.hint: List what a thread needs to run different code: call stack plus where it is (PC) plus registers.
easy.explanation: Per-thread private state is the stack, PC, registers, and TID; everything else in the address space is shared.
easy.deepDive: Private execution state lets each thread run different code at different calls simultaneously. The shared address space lets them exchange data through globals and heap. This split of shared versus private is the definition to memorize. Every later bug, from stack overflow to races, follows from it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: If stacks and PCs were shared, threads could not run different functions at once.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Heap and code are shared; privatizing them would just be separate processes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Descriptors and globals are process-wide and shared, not per-thread.

easy.prompt: On a 2-CPU machine using the 1:1 threading model, two threads of one process can do what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: M user threads multiplexed on 1 kernel thread, so 2 CPUs can run 2 threads in parallel

choices.label: B
choices.body: M user threads on N kernel threads where N is fixed at 1 forever

choices.label: C
choices.body: Each user thread maps to its own kernel thread, so the OS can schedule them on 2 CPUs in parallel

choices.label: D
choices.body: Threads are emulated by the compiler with no kernel involvement at all

easy.hint: Ask: how many kernel-schedulable entities exist if each user thread has one? Then map them to CPUs.
easy.explanation: 1:1 gives every user thread its own kernel thread, so two CPUs can truly run two threads at once.
easy.deepDive: In the 1:1 model each pthread has a kernel schedulable entity. The kernel can place each on a different core, enabling true parallelism. That is why modern pthreads on Linux use 1:1. The cost is higher creation and context-switch overhead than pure user-level threads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes M:1, which allows only one kernel thread and hence no parallelism.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: M:N with N fixed at 1 is just M:1 under another name; N varies in real M:N.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Compiler emulation without kernel threads cannot achieve multiprocessor parallelism.

easy.prompt: After pthread_create(&t, NULL, fn, arg), what is guaranteed about execution order of creator and new thread?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The new thread runs concurrently with the creator; either may run next

choices.label: B
choices.body: The new thread waits until the creator exits before starting

choices.label: C
choices.body: The creator blocks until the new thread finishes, like wait()

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both threads merge into one execution stream immediately

easy.hint: Compare fork plus no wait: would you assume parent or child runs first? Apply that to threads.
easy.explanation: Create starts a concurrent peer with no ordering guarantee; the scheduler may run either thread next.
easy.deepDive: pthread_create only starts a concurrent peer; it does not wait. The scheduler interleaves creator and new thread arbitrarily. Any assumption about who runs first is a race. Explicit pthread_join is what adds ordering back when you need it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The new thread is runnable immediately; it never waits for creator exit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Create does not block; only pthread_join blocks like wait().
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Threads never merge; they remain independent execution streams sharing memory.

easy.prompt: What does pthread_join(t, &retval) do to the calling thread?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It kills the target thread immediately

choices.label: B
choices.body: It starts the target thread running

choices.label: C
choices.body: It switches the caller to the target's stack permanently

choices.label: D
choices.body: It blocks the caller until the target finishes and collects its return value

easy.hint: Think of wait() for processes: which call blocks the parent until the child is done? Join is its twin.
easy.explanation: pthread_join waits for the target to finish and retrieves its void* return value.
easy.deepDive: Join is the thread analogue of wait() for processes. It provides ordering: after join returns, the target has finished. It also provides communication via the void** return slot. Without join there is no guarantee the child finished before the parent uses its result.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No pthread call asynchronously kills; join only waits, like wait().
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: pthread_create starts threads; join only waits for an already-started thread.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Join does not steal stacks; each thread keeps its own stack throughout.

easy.prompt: Why do threads improve throughput for a server that blocks on network reads?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Threads make each individual I/O faster by splitting the disk

choices.label: B
choices.body: While one thread blocks waiting for I/O, another thread can run and overlap work

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threads eliminate context switches during I/O waits

choices.label: D
choices.body: Threads convert blocking I/O into busy-spin polling automatically

easy.hint: Recall process states: BLOCKED means waiting for I/O. Ask what the rest of the process could do meanwhile.
easy.explanation: Threads hide I/O latency by letting another thread run while one is BLOCKED waiting for the device.
easy.deepDive: Blocking puts only the waiting thread to sleep, not the whole process. The scheduler runs another ready thread during the wait. Total time drops from sum of waits to roughly the overlap. This is the main performance reason threads were adopted for servers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Latency of one I/O is unchanged; the win is overlapping waits, not faster disks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Overlapping needs more switches between threads, not fewer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The I/O still blocks that thread; nothing converts it to polling.

easy.prompt: Two threads each run `balance = balance + 10` on a shared `balance`. Which region must be the critical section protected by one mutex?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the lines that print the thread ID, since printing races.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The load, increment, and store of the shared balance — the read-modify-write sequence.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The entire main() function including thread creation, to add parallelism.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nothing; integer addition is always atomic on multicore.

easy.hint: Ask: which lines touch shared state, and what happens if two threads interleave between the load and the store?
easy.explanation: The critical section is exactly the shared read-modify-write; locking it makes the increment atomic without serializing private work.
easy.deepDive: The race window is the three-instruction sequence between load and store. Holding the lock only across that window serializes increments while leaving thread creation and private work parallel. Wider regions are correct but serialize independent work and inflate blocking time, which the scheduler then pays for as wakeups.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Printing uses private IDs; the race is on the shared balance, not the print.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Locks remove parallelism; locking thread creation serializes everything for no benefit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Load/increment/store is three steps and interleaves; it is not atomic.

easy.prompt: A thread increments a shared `requests` counter then writes a log line to disk. Where should the mutex go?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lock around the file write but not the counter update, because I/O is slower.

choices.label: B
choices.body: One lock around counter update plus file write together, to keep the log line matching the count.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Lock only around the shared counter update; do the file I/O outside the lock (or with a separate log lock).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Use two different mutexes both held only during the file write.

easy.hint: Compare how long each version holds the lock: what do other threads wait for while one thread writes to disk?
easy.explanation: Lock the shortest region that covers the shared invariant; holding a data lock across slow I/O serializes all threads needlessly.
easy.deepDive: Lock placement trades correctness against blocking time. I/O inside a data lock turns a nanosecond update into a millisecond serialization point and risks deadlock if the I/O path re-enters. The fix is minimal placement: guard shared state briefly, and use a dedicated lock only where a multi-variable invariant truly spans operations.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This leaves the actual shared update unprotected — the race remains.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct only if the spec demands count==log-line atomicity; otherwise it needlessly blocks on I/O.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct for the common case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Locking only I/O protects nothing about the counter.

easy.prompt: 1000 threads each increment a shared counter 1000× with one mutex around the increment. (Assume Threads: races.) What is true vs the no-lock version?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Threads serialize on the update but the final count is correct (2000000).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threads run fully in parallel and the count is correct because locks add parallelism.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The program deadlocks because two threads cannot hold one lock.

choices.label: A
choices.body: The final count is correct and runtime is faster than no lock, due to cache affinity.

easy.hint: Does the lock let both increments overlap, or force one to wait? What does waiting do to runtime?
easy.explanation: A correct lock makes the racy increment serial and correct — it does not speed it up; protection costs parallelism.
easy.deepDive: A mutex provides mutual exclusion, not speedup: the locked increment becomes serial and therefore slower than an unsynchronized (but wrong) run. The misconception that locks add parallelism comes from confusing protection with parallel execution. You pay blocking and wakeup cost precisely to buy a correct result.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct: serialized but right.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Locks remove overlap; they never add parallelism.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mutexes serialize holders one at a time; that is normal, not deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Serialization plus wakeup cost makes it slower, not faster.

easy.prompt: A consumer holds `mutex`, finds the work queue empty, and must wait for a producer. What is the correct next step?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spin in a tight loop re-checking the flag, keeping the mutex held.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sleep with a fixed 1-second delay, then re-lock and retry once.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Return immediately and drop the work item.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Atomically release the mutex and block until another thread signals new work.

easy.hint: What must happen to the mutex before sleeping, and what goes wrong if the wakeup arrives in between?
easy.explanation: When the queue is empty, atomically unlock-and-wait on a condition variable so the producer can enter and wake you.
easy.deepDive: Blocking atomically via a condition variable preserves both correctness and CPU: the unlock-plus-sleep is one atomic step so a wakeup cannot slip between them. Spinning while holding the mutex deadlocks the producer that needs the same mutex. Timed polling either wastes CPU or adds latency, the exact blocking-vs-spinning tradeoff from Scheduling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Holding the mutex while spinning blocks the producer forever.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fixed sleeps add latency and still race on re-check.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropping work is incorrect; waiting is required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

easy.prompt: What does a test-and-set (TAS) spinlock acquire loop do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It blocks in the kernel until the lock is free, never spinning.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It atomically sets flag to 1 and returns the old value; the caller loops while the old value was 1.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It compares two pointers and swaps them only during a context switch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It signals all waiting threads, like a condition-variable broadcast.

easy.hint: What single atomic fact does TAS return, and how does the loop use it to decide to retry?
easy.explanation: TAS atomically claims the flag and reports whether it was already held; spinning repeats until the claim succeeds.
easy.deepDive: Test-and-set gives an atomic acquire attempt; the spin loop retries until it observes 0, meaning it installed 1 from unlocked state. This is cheap when the wait is shorter than a context switch on a multicore, but wastes cycles and collapses under preemption. That observation motivates blocking locks for long or contended sections.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes a blocking mutex, not a TAS spinlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That confuses TAS with compare-and-swap and with scheduling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes CV broadcast, unrelated to TAS.

easy.prompt: You need an exact shared request counter with concurrent increments and reads. Which coarse-grained scheme is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wrap increment and read each in lock/unlock of one mutex; the final value is exact.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Give each thread a private counter and sum with no locks at the end, reading the shared total anytime.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Protect only increments, leave reads unlocked for speed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Use one mutex but initialize it after threads start, to save setup time.

easy.hint: Which operations touch shared state — updates only, or reads too?
easy.explanation: One mutex around every access (increment and read) makes the shared counter exact.
easy.deepDive: A single coarse lock around every access makes the counter linearizable: each operation appears to take effect instantaneously between lock and unlock. Unlocked reads tear the invariant because they can observe a half-updated value. Private counters without a merge protocol lose updates — the bridge to per-CPU approximate counters later.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Private counters with racy reads of a shared total still race; a disciplined merge is needed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Unlocked reads can see torn intermediate states.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Using an uninitialized mutex is undefined behavior.

easy.prompt: A sorted linked list has one global mutex. A teammate proposes a mutex per node. What is the core tradeoff?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One global list lock is always faster because it has no lock overhead.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Per-node locks remove all need for any global ordering.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A single global lock is simple and correct; per-node locks add concurrency but also overhead and ordering complexity.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No locks are needed if each thread uses a different head pointer variable.

easy.hint: If two threads insert at opposite ends, must they really wait for each other? What would that cost to arrange?
easy.explanation: Global lock: simple and correct; per-node locks: more concurrency but more overhead and a required acquisition order.
easy.deepDive: Coarse locking serializes whole-list operations with one ordering-free lock, while fine-grained locking lets disjoint segments proceed in parallel at the cost of lock overhead and a lock-coupling order. Threads still share the same nodes regardless of local pointer copies, so some synchronization is mandatory. This sets up hand-over-hand traversal as the disciplined fine-grained pattern.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: One lock serializes everything; it is simpler, not faster under contention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Shared nodes are still shared; local pointers do not privatize them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Per-node locking still needs a global acquisition order to avoid deadlock.

easy.prompt: A child thread must sleep until `done==1` set by the parent under a mutex. What is the correct waiter pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spin on the flag with the mutex held until it becomes true.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Unlock, spin without any lock, then re-lock and assume success.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Wait on a condition variable without holding the mutex.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hold the mutex, test the predicate in a while loop, and wait (atomically unlocking) when false.

easy.hint: Where can a wakeup get lost if you unlock and sleep as two separate steps?
easy.explanation: CV wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, so a setter can enter and no wakeup is missed.
easy.deepDive: Condition variables combine a mutex-protected predicate with atomic unlock-and-block, so no wakeup is lost between testing and sleeping. The mutex makes the test-and-sleep sequence atomic with respect to the setter. Spinning holds either the CPU or the lock hostage, which is exactly the blocking-versus-spinning cost from Scheduling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Spinning with the lock held blocks the setter — deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Unlocked spinning wastes CPU and races on the flag.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: CV wait requires the mutex to be held to make test-and-sleep atomic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

easy.prompt: A bounded buffer has N slots shared by producers and consumers. What synchronization state is fundamentally needed?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only a mutex, because producers and consumers never overlap.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A mutex for the buffer plus counting semaphores for empty slots and filled items.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Two mutexes, one for producers and one for the buffer size.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No synchronization; flow control is handled by the scheduler.

easy.hint: What two different waits exist: waiting for exclusive access vs waiting for an available slot or item?
easy.explanation: Count empty and full slots with semaphores for blocking flow control, plus a mutex for buffer mutual exclusion.
easy.deepDive: The bounded buffer has two independent constraints: mutual exclusion on indices and flow control on slot counts. Counting semaphores track empty and full slots so producers block when full and consumers block when empty. The mutex alone cannot count resources — the bridge to full semaphore and CV solutions next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: They do overlap on indices; mutual exclusion is still required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Buffer size is a constant, not lockable state.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The scheduler does not enforce buffer invariants.

easy.prompt: How do you use a binary semaphore `s` as a mutex around a critical section?

choices.label: A
choices.body: sem_init(&s, 0, 0) then sem_wait to enter.

choices.label: B
choices.body: sem_init(&s, 0, N) where N is the thread count.

choices.label: C
choices.body: sem_init(&s, 0, 1); sem_wait to lock, sem_post to unlock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: sem_init(&s, 0, -1) to indicate locked.

easy.hint: How many threads should the initial count admit before anyone posts?
easy.explanation: Initialize the binary semaphore to 1 so the first wait succeeds and later ones block until a post.
easy.deepDive: A binary semaphore initialized to 1 acts as a lock: the first waiter decrements to 0 and enters, others block until a post restores 1. Initializing to 0 deadlocks the first acquirer; initializing to N allows N concurrent holders. This models mutual exclusion but, unlike a mutex, carries no ownership — any thread may post.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Init 0 blocks the first locker forever.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Init N admits N holders — not mutual exclusion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Negative initial counts are invalid.

easy.prompt: A fixed pool of 8 database connections is shared by threads. Which semaphore models it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A counting semaphore tracking available pool entries, initialized to pool size.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A binary semaphore initialized to 0 used as a lock.

choices.label: C
choices.body: One mutex per waiting thread.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A condition variable with no associated counter.

easy.hint: What integer describes the pool, and which operation should change it in each direction?
easy.explanation: A counting semaphore holds the number of free resources; wait takes one, post returns one.
easy.deepDive: Counting semaphores generalize binary ones from 0/1 to 0..N, representing how many identical resources remain. Each wait consumes one unit, each post returns one, and blockers sleep until units exist. This is the natural model for connection pools and slot counts, distinct from the ownership-tracking role of a mutex.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Init 0 as a lock deadlocks immediately.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A mutex per waiter does not count free connections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A CV alone stores no count; the predicate would be missing.

easy.prompt: 4 threads compute partial sums, then combine them. They use a barrier for N=4. What is its guarantee?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The first thread to arrive proceeds immediately without waiting.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threads leave in the exact reverse order they arrived.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exactly one thread ever passes; the rest block forever.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No thread passes until all N have arrived; then all pass.

easy.hint: What must be true about arrivals before any thread may safely read the others' results?
easy.explanation: A barrier holds every thread until all N arrive, then releases them together into the next phase.
easy.deepDive: A barrier separates phases: arrival counting blocks early threads until the Nth arrival flips the gate. Implemented with a mutex-protected count plus a semaphore or CV gate, it guarantees all threads observe all pre-barrier work. Releasing early breaks the phase invariant and reintroduces races the barrier was built to remove.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is no barrier at all — early threads would read unwritten results.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Barriers impose no leave ordering, only that all arrive first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A reusable barrier releases everyone, not just one.

easy.prompt: Two threads need the same printer with exclusive access. Why is mutual exclusion a necessary condition for deadlock?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlock is impossible without exclusive access, because sharing removes blocking.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mutual exclusion guarantees threads run faster by avoiding context switches.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mutual exclusion means threads hold two locks at once.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mutual exclusion means the OS can preempt any lock at any time.

easy.hint: Ask: if both threads could use the printer at the same instant, would anyone wait?
easy.explanation: If the printer could be shared, neither thread would block, so exclusive access is what makes waiting possible.
easy.deepDive: OSTEP lists mutual exclusion as the first Coffman condition. It is necessary because if every resource were sharable, no thread would ever block waiting for another. Real locks are non-sharable by design, which is why this condition almost always holds. Prevention therefore targets the other three conditions instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Speed has nothing to do with it; exclusion is about blocking, not performance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Holding two locks is hold-and-wait, a different Coffman condition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Preemptible locks would break no-preemption, the opposite of mutual exclusion.

easy.prompt: Thread T holds Lock A and calls lock(B), which blocks. Which Coffman condition does T exhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No preemption: locks cannot be forcibly taken away.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Mutual exclusion: the lock cannot be shared.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hold-and-wait: it keeps Lock A while blocking for Lock B.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Circular wait: three threads form a cycle.

easy.hint: Focus on what it holds versus what it waits for at the same moment.
easy.explanation: Keeping one lock while blocking on another is exactly hold-and-wait.
easy.deepDive: Hold-and-wait means a thread retains allocated resources while requesting more. It matters because holding blocks others while the holder itself blocks. Atomic all-or-nothing lock acquisition breaks exactly this condition. Detecting it in code means spotting a blocking acquire while already holding a lock.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No-preemption is about whether the OS can steal the lock, not about holding while waiting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Mutual exclusion is just that locks are exclusive, already assumed here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Circular wait needs a cycle across threads; one thread alone cannot show it.

easy.prompt: A mutex can only be released by its holder calling unlock; the OS never steals it. Which Coffman condition is this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No-preemption: the holder only releases voluntarily via unlock.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hold-and-wait: the thread waits without holding anything.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Circular wait: two threads wait on each other.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mutual exclusion is absent because locks are sharable.

easy.hint: Who can release the lock: anyone, or only the holder?
easy.explanation: A mutex that only the holder can release is non-preemptible.
easy.deepDive: No-preemption means a resource can only be released by its holder. If the OS could revoke locks and roll the holder back, waiting threads could be unblocked. Databases do this by aborting transactions; thread mutexes normally do not. That is why lock deadlocks persist until a holder unlocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Waiting with nothing held is the opposite of hold-and-wait.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Circular wait describes a multi-thread cycle, not a property of one lock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mutexes are exclusive, so mutual exclusion is present, not absent.

easy.prompt: T1 holds A waits for B; T2 holds B waits for A. Both block forever. Which condition completes the deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mutual exclusion alone, because sharing always deadlocks.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hold-and-wait alone, because one thread waiting is deadlock.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No-preemption alone, because it blocks all progress.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Circular wait: T1 holds A waits B while T2 holds B waits A.

easy.hint: Draw arrows: holder -> lock -> waiter. Do the arrows loop back?
easy.explanation: Each thread holds what the other wants, forming a wait cycle.
easy.deepDive: Circular wait is a cycle of hold-and-wait edges: each thread holds something the next wants. All four Coffman conditions are necessary for deadlock, and the cycle is the one that ties threads together. Lock ordering breaks exactly this condition by forbidding cycles. A single waiting thread is just blocking, not deadlock.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Mutual exclusion alone never deadlocks; waiting plus holding is also needed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One thread blocking is normal waiting; deadlock needs a cycle.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No-preemption alone just means voluntary release; it needs a cycle to deadlock.

easy.prompt: Locks A and B have 1 instance each. T1 holds A waits B; T2 holds B waits A. Deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No deadlock, because a cycle never matters.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlock: single-instance cycle means each thread waits forever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No deadlock, because two threads can never deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Starvation, because one thread is prioritized.

easy.hint: Count copies of A and B: is there any free copy that could unblock a waiter?
easy.explanation: With one copy of each lock, a wait cycle leaves no free instance, so both block forever.
easy.deepDive: With one instance per lock, a resource-allocation-graph cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. Each edge means the exact instance wanted is held by the next waiter, so nobody can proceed. This is the special single-instance rule OSTEP stresses. With multiple instances the same cycle may be harmless because a free copy can satisfy a waiter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A single-instance cycle does matter; it guarantees deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Two threads with two locks is the classic minimal deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No priority or scheduler bias is described, so this is not starvation.

easy.prompt: Why does breaking just one Coffman condition prevent deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock is unavoidable once locks exist.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Detection finds deadlocks before they happen.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Breaking any one Coffman condition prevents deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Breaking one condition has no effect unless all four are broken.

easy.hint: If deadlock needs A and B and C and D, how many must you falsify to stop it?
easy.explanation: All four are necessary, so removing any one makes deadlock impossible.
easy.deepDive: Prevention works by negating necessity: all four conditions must hold for deadlock, so falsifying any one suffices. Each strategy maps to one condition: atomic acquisition, preemption, or ordering. The cost differs, which is why OSes choose per workload. Detection, by contrast, allows deadlock then recovers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Locks alone do not deadlock; the four conditions must coincide.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Finding deadlock beforehand is avoidance; detection finds it afterward.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: You need only one false condition, not all four, because necessity is conjunctive.

easy.prompt: Trace: T1 and T2 both block in lock() forever; CPU is idle; neither ever runs again. Which is it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock: all threads block forever with zero progress.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Livelock: threads spin and retry but make no progress.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Starvation: one thread is repeatedly denied while others progress.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Blocking: one thread waits briefly then proceeds.

easy.hint: Check progress: does anyone finish, or does everyone stay parked in lock()?
easy.explanation: Nobody moves and nobody can move: the hallmark of deadlock.
easy.deepDive: Deadlock means every deadlocked thread waits and the system makes no progress on those threads. Blocking is temporary waiting; starvation lets others progress. Livelock also makes no progress but threads are running, not blocked. The trace signature of deadlock is threads parked in lock() forever.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Livelock shows CPU busy with retries, not idle parked threads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Starvation needs some thread progressing while one is denied; here none progress.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Brief waiting that resolves is normal blocking, not forever.

easy.prompt: What does a Banker safe state mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A state where deadlock has already occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A state where one safe order exists but threads must use it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A state where Available covers every Need immediately.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A state where some order lets every process finish with Available plus releases.

easy.hint: Think future releases: can finishers free enough to unblock the rest?
easy.explanation: Safe means a finishing order exists, using releases to satisfy later needs.
easy.deepDive: Safety is existential: at least one sequence works using current Available plus what finishers release. It does not require immediate satisfiability or a forced order. Banker's algorithm searches for that witness sequence. Safe does not mean deadlock-free forever, only that deadlock can still be avoided with care.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Safe is the opposite: deadlock is still avoidable, not already present.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Threads need not follow the witness order; existence is enough.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Safety allows waiting for releases; immediate satisfiability is unnecessary.

easy.prompt: An OS periodically checks waits and kills a stuck process to unblock others. Detection or prevention?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Prevention: it stops deadlock before any wait occurs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Avoidance: it denies risky requests to stay safe.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Detection: it finds an existing deadlock so recovery can run.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ordering: it forbids lock cycles statically.

easy.hint: Did the OS deny a request, or did it notice threads already stuck?
easy.explanation: A detector reports deadlock after it forms; prevention would have stopped the wait.
easy.deepDive: Detection assumes deadlock may happen, periodically checks the allocation graph, and triggers recovery such as killing or preempting. It does not deny requests or enforce ordering up front. Confusing it with prevention or avoidance is the classic misconception. The cost is the detector plus the recovery policy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Nothing was stopped beforehand; stuck threads already existed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Avoidance runs Banker grant/deny per request, not periodic killing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No static lock order was enforced here.

easy.prompt: In UNIX, where does the filename '/home/user/doc.txt' actually live?

choices.label: A
choices.body: In the parent directory's data, as a (name → inode number) mapping

choices.label: B
choices.body: Inside the file's inode, alongside size and block pointers

choices.label: C
choices.body: In the superblock's filename table indexed by inode number

choices.label: D
choices.body: In the file's first data block as a header string

easy.hint: Ask: if two names can point at one file, can the name be stored inside that one file's inode?
easy.explanation: Names live in directory entries; the inode holds metadata and block pointers but no name.
easy.deepDive: This separation lets many names (hard links) point to one inode. Looking up a path means reading each directory's data to map a component name to an inode number. The inode itself only stores owner, size, times, and pointers to data blocks. Confusing the two makes hard links and renames impossible to explain.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Classic misconception: the inode holds no filename, which is why one inode can have many names.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: There is no global filename table; names are distributed across directory files.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Data blocks hold file content only; the name is directory metadata.

easy.prompt: What is a directory, at its simplest implementation level?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A file containing a list of (name, inode number) pairs

choices.label: B
choices.body: A kernel-only hash table that cannot be stored on disk

choices.label: C
choices.body: A copy of every file's data that it contains

choices.label: D
choices.body: A bitmap marking which inodes are allocated

easy.hint: Think: what minimal info lets you go from a human name to the metadata structure?
easy.explanation: A directory is a file of mappings from names to inode numbers.
easy.deepDive: That is why reading a directory shows names and ls -i shows the mapped inode numbers. Creating a file adds one mapping; unlinking removes one. The file's content and metadata live elsewhere, reached via the inode number.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Directories persist on disk as ordinary files with special interpretation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Directories do not duplicate file data; they only reference inodes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bitmaps track allocation; directories track naming.

easy.prompt: To open '/a/b/c', what must the FS do first?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Start at the root inode, read directory data to map 'a' → inode, then repeat for 'b' and 'c'

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hash the full string '/a/b/c' directly into a data block address

choices.label: C
choices.body: Scan all data blocks for one containing the string 'c'

choices.label: D
choices.body: Read inode 0 which always stores the target file's blocks

easy.hint: Path resolution is component-by-component — what lookup happens at each level?
easy.explanation: Each path component requires a directory lookup translating a name to the next inode.
easy.deepDive: The kernel starts from a known inode (root or cwd), reads its directory blocks, finds the next name, and loads that inode. Failure at any component fails the whole open. This is why deep paths cost multiple I/Os without caching.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No direct hash from pathname to block exists; resolution is iterative.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scanning data blocks would be O(filesystem size) and ignores structure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No single fixed inode holds arbitrary files.

easy.prompt: Which information does an inode hold?

choices.label: A
choices.body: File type, size, permissions, timestamps, and pointers to data blocks

choices.label: B
choices.body: The filename and its full directory path

choices.label: C
choices.body: The process file-descriptor table for open files

choices.label: D
choices.body: The disk's bitmap of all free blocks

easy.hint: Separate per-file metadata (needed to find blocks) from per-name and per-open state.
easy.explanation: The inode is per-file metadata: attributes plus addresses of data blocks.
easy.deepDive: Like a page table maps virtual pages to frames, the inode maps logical file offsets to disk blocks via direct and indirect pointers. Open-file offsets live in the kernel's open file table, not the inode. Names live in directories.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inode holds no name or path — that is the directory's job.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Descriptors and offsets are per-open state in memory, not on-disk inode state.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bitmaps are filesystem-wide allocation structures, not per-file.

easy.prompt: After 'ln fileA fileB' (hard link), what is true?

choices.label: A
choices.body: fileA and fileB share one inode; the inode link count becomes 2

choices.label: B
choices.body: A full duplicate copy of fileA's data blocks is created for fileB

choices.label: C
choices.body: fileB stores the text path 'fileA' and follows it on each open

choices.label: D
choices.body: fileA is deleted and replaced by a pointer to fileB

easy.hint: Hard link adds a second directory entry — does it allocate new data blocks?
easy.explanation: A hard link is a second name for the same inode; only the link count increments.
easy.deepDive: No data is copied, so writes via either name are visible via the other. The file's blocks are freed only when the last name is unlinked and no process holds it open. This is why hard links cannot be distinguished as 'original' vs 'copy'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Misconception: hard links duplicate no data; that would be a copy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Storing a path describes a symlink, not a hard link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Nothing is deleted; a new directory entry is added.

easy.prompt: After 'ln -s /data/real.txt link.txt', you delete /data/real.txt. What happens on opening link.txt?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Open fails: the symlink stores a path whose target no longer exists (dangling link)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Open succeeds because the symlink kept a private copy of the data

choices.label: C
choices.body: Open succeeds because deleting the target auto-updates the symlink

choices.label: D
choices.body: The symlink's inode is freed automatically when the target is deleted

easy.hint: A symlink's content is just a pathname — what if that pathname resolves to nothing?
easy.explanation: Symlinks reference by path, so removing the target leaves a dangling link.
easy.deepDive: The symlink has its own inode whose data is the target string. Each open re-resolves that path, so rename or removal breaks it. Hard links by contrast reference by inode and are immune to renames of sibling names.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Symlinks copy no data; they store only the target path.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Nothing updates symlinks on target deletion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Symlink and target inodes have independent lifetimes.

easy.prompt: A process opens a file, then calls read(fd, buf, 100) twice. What happens to the file offset?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each read starts where the previous left off; the offset advances by bytes read

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both reads return the first 100 bytes because the offset resets each call

choices.label: C
choices.body: The offset is stored in the inode and shared by all processes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Reads bypass the offset and always scan from block 0

easy.hint: The kernel remembers a cursor per open — how should sequential reads behave?
easy.explanation: The open file description holds an offset that advances with each read/write.
easy.deepDive: Descriptors index into per-process tables pointing at a shared open file description containing the offset. Sequential reads therefore stream through the file without explicit seeks. lseek or pread are needed to reposition or avoid moving it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Offset persists across calls; only lseek or reopen resets it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Offset is per-open state, not in the on-disk inode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: All normal reads/writes use the current offset.

easy.prompt: A process opens the same file twice (fd1, fd2), without dup/fork. How do their offsets relate?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Independent: reading via fd1 does not move fd2's offset

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shared: reading via fd1 advances fd2's offset equally

choices.label: C
choices.body: Aliased to the inode's offset field, so all opens move together

choices.label: D
choices.body: fd2 always starts at end-of-file regardless of fd1

easy.hint: Each open() creates a fresh open file description — what does that imply for cursors?
easy.explanation: Separate opens get separate descriptions and independent offsets.
easy.deepDive: This contrasts with dup() or fork(), which share one description and one offset. Independent offsets let two readers scan the same file at different positions. Writes through one are visible through the other only after repositioning, since file data is shared but cursors are not.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sharing happens only via dup/fork, not via a second open().
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: There is no offset field in the inode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both offsets start at 0 unless O_APPEND or lseek is used.

easy.prompt: In the Very Simple File System (VSFS), in what order do regions appear on disk?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Superblock, inode bitmap, data bitmap, inode table, data blocks

choices.label: B
choices.body: Data blocks, inode table, bitmaps, superblock at the end

choices.label: C
choices.body: Inode table interleaved one inode per data block

choices.label: D
choices.body: Superblock only; everything else is allocated dynamically with no fixed regions

easy.hint: Fixed metadata comes first so the FS can find allocation state before anything else.
easy.explanation: VSFS lays out superblock, then bitmaps, then inodes, then data for simple address math.
easy.deepDive: Fixed positions let the FS compute e.g. inode-block address as inodeTableStart + (inodeNum * inodeSize / blockSize). Bitmaps come early so allocators check them first. Data goes last because it is the largest and most variable region.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Metadata must be at known early offsets; data cannot precede it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inodes are packed densely in their table, not one per data block.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: VSFS uses static partitioning to keep the toy design simple.

easy.prompt: Why did FFS care about placing related data on nearby disk locations?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Seeks are slow; sequential/nearby placement turns many small I/Os into fast transfers

choices.label: B
choices.body: Nearby placement reduces the number of inodes needed per file

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disks can only address blocks within one cylinder group at a time

choices.label: D
choices.body: Locality eliminates the need for bitmaps

easy.hint: Compare seek time (~ms) to transfer time — which dominates for scattered small reads?
easy.explanation: Mechanical seeks dominate; locality minimizes seeks and maximizes bandwidth.
easy.deepDive: FFS groups each directory's inodes and files into the same cylinder group and allocates consecutive blocks together. On HDDs this avoids long seeks between related reads. Even on SSDs, contiguity helps prefetch and reduces metadata hops.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Placement does not change inode count; one inode per file regardless.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Any block is addressable; grouping is a performance policy, not a limit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Allocation tracking is still required regardless of placement.

easy.prompt: What is a block/inode bitmap used for?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One bit per block/inode recording free (0) vs allocated (1)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Counting how many hard links point to each inode

choices.label: C
choices.body: Storing file permission bits for fast access checks

choices.label: D
choices.body: Caching file data in memory to avoid disk reads

easy.hint: Allocation needs a fast 'is this slot free?' test — what compact structure gives that?
easy.explanation: Bitmaps give O(1) free/used tests and fast scans for a free slot.
easy.deepDive: Allocating a block sets its bit; freeing clears it. This differs from a reference count, which tracks how many names reference an inode. Bitmaps answer 'allocated?', link counts answer 'how many names?'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Link counts live in the inode, not in bitmaps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Permissions live in the inode mode field.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Caching is the buffer cache's job, not the bitmap's.

easy.prompt: A file is written but the machine crashes before fsync. What may happen?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Recently written data may be lost; writes were buffered and not yet durable

choices.label: B
choices.body: The file's permission bits are automatically reset to 000

choices.label: C
choices.body: All hard links to the file are converted to symlinks

choices.label: D
choices.body: The file's blocks are immediately returned to the bitmap on crash

easy.hint: write() copies into the page cache — when does data actually reach stable storage?
easy.explanation: write() is not durable; only fsync/fdatasync force data to disk.
easy.deepDive: OS buffers writes for performance and may reorder them. A crash discards unwritten buffers. Applications needing durability (databases, mail) must call fsync on the file — and fsync the directory after creates/renames.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Permissions change only via chmod, unrelated to crashes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Link type never changes spontaneously.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bitmap state on disk simply reflects the last flushed allocation, not an instant free.

easy.prompt: A CPU repeatedly reads a device status register in a loop until the keyboard reports a key ready. Which I/O method is this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Programmed I/O with polling

choices.label: B
choices.body: Interrupt-driven I/O

choices.label: C
choices.body: DMA transfer

choices.label: D
choices.body: Memory-mapped file write

easy.hint: Ask who waits: if the CPU itself spins checking status, what is that called?
easy.explanation: The CPU spins checking status, which is polling (programmed I/O) and wastes CPU cycles.
easy.deepDive: Polling keeps the CPU busy waiting instead of doing useful work or sleeping. It is simple with no interrupt machinery but burns cycles proportional to wait time. This waste motivates interrupts, where the device notifies the CPU only when ready.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Interrupts let the CPU sleep or run other work until the device signals; here the CPU spins.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA moves bulk data without CPU per-byte copies; here the CPU checks status byte by byte.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A file write goes through the file system; this is direct status-register spinning.

easy.prompt: A disk finishes a read and raises a signal so the CPU stops its current work and runs a handler to copy status. What changed versus polling?

choices.label: A
choices.body: CPU blocks or works until device interrupts; no spinning

choices.label: B
choices.body: CPU spins faster on the status register

choices.label: C
choices.body: DMA engine now runs application code

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disk seeks become free

easy.hint: Compare CPU use: what does the CPU do while the slow device works?
easy.explanation: With interrupts the CPU does other work or sleeps until signaled, avoiding spin waste.
easy.deepDive: An interrupt asynchronously transfers control to a handler, overlapping CPU work with device latency. It adds handler and context-switch cost but wins when devices are slow. Polling can still win for ultra-fast arrivals where interrupt cost exceeds spin cost.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Faster spinning is still polling and still wastes cycles; interrupts remove the spin.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA engines only move data between device and memory; they never run user code.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mechanical seek cost is unchanged; only CPU waiting behavior changed.

easy.prompt: Why is a random 4KB read on HDD much slower than the same read on SSD?

choices.label: A
choices.body: HDD pays mechanical seek plus rotation before transfer

choices.label: B
choices.body: HDD must erase a full block before every read

choices.label: C
choices.body: SSD spins its platter faster

choices.label: D
choices.body: HDD sectors wear out on read

easy.hint: Think about what moves physically on an HDD before any byte transfers.
easy.explanation: HDDs move the arm (seek) and wait for rotation, costing milliseconds before transfer.
easy.deepDive: Seek plus rotational delay dominate HDD random I/O, often 5-10ms versus microseconds of transfer. Sequential access amortizes one seek over many sectors. SSDs have no moving parts so random and sequential reads cost nearly the same.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Erase-before-write is an SSD/flash constraint, not an HDD read cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SSDs have no platters or motors; nothing spins.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reads do not wear HDDs; wear/erase limits apply to flash cells.

easy.prompt: Why can't an SSD simply overwrite one 4KB page in place like an HDD overwrites a sector?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Flash must erase a large block first and cells wear out

choices.label: B
choices.body: SSD heads must seek to the page first

choices.label: C
choices.body: SSD pages are encrypted and unreadable

choices.label: D
choices.body: SSDs have no controller to remap addresses

easy.hint: Recall the flash rule: program per page, erase per block, with limited cycles.
easy.explanation: Flash programs pages but erases whole blocks, and each cell tolerates limited erases.
easy.deepDive: The SSD controller therefore writes elsewhere and remaps via an FTL, garbage-collecting dead pages later. This causes write amplification where one logical write triggers extra internal moves. Wear leveling spreads erases so no block dies early.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: SSDs have no heads or seeks; that is HDD mechanics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Encryption is unrelated; the limit is erase granularity and wear.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SSDs do have a controller with an FTL that remaps precisely because of this limit.

easy.prompt: Disk queue has requests at tracks 10, 50, 90 with head at 0. Why does SCAN (elevator) beat FCFS here?

choices.label: A
choices.body: SCAN sweeps in one direction serving in track order, cutting seeks

choices.label: B
choices.body: SCAN encrypts requests to run faster

choices.label: C
choices.body: SCAN uses DMA to skip seeks

choices.label: D
choices.body: SCAN always serves newest request first

easy.hint: Trace head travel: what order does a one-way sweep visit 10, 50, 90 in?
easy.explanation: A directional sweep visits tracks in order, minimizing back-and-forth travel.
easy.deepDive: FCFS serves in arrival order even if that zigzags the arm across the disk. SCAN orders by position along the sweep, so total seek distance shrinks. This scheduling matters because seeks dominate HDD time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scheduling never encrypts; it only reorders the queue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA moves data after the head arrives; it does not move the arm.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Newest-first is LIFO, which SCAN does not do; SCAN is position-ordered.

easy.prompt: 4 disks of 1TB each in RAID-0. What is usable capacity and fault tolerance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 4TB usable, 0 disk failures tolerated

choices.label: B
choices.body: 3TB usable, 1 failure tolerated

choices.label: C
choices.body: 2TB usable, 2 failures tolerated

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1TB usable, 3 failures tolerated

easy.hint: RAID-0 stripes with no redundancy: add capacities, then ask what survives a loss.
easy.explanation: Striping sums capacities (4TB) but any disk loss destroys the stripe, so 0 faults tolerated.
easy.deepDive: RAID-0 maximizes capacity and parallelism since every disk holds unique chunks. The cost is reliability: failure probability is roughly the sum across disks. It is performance without protection.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 3TB with 1 fault is RAID-5 (parity), not striping without redundancy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 2TB with 2 faults resembles RAID-10/1+0 on 4 disks, not RAID-0.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1TB usable is RAID-1 mirroring of 4 disks, not striping.

easy.prompt: 2x1TB disks in RAID-1. What is usable capacity and fault tolerance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 1TB usable, 1 failure tolerated

choices.label: B
choices.body: 2TB usable, 0 failures tolerated

choices.label: C
choices.body: 2TB usable, 1 failure tolerated

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1TB usable, 2 failures tolerated

easy.hint: Mirroring keeps identical copies: how much unique data fits, and what if one copy dies?
easy.explanation: Mirrors store one copy's worth of unique data (1TB) and survive one disk loss.
easy.deepDive: RAID-1 pays 2x capacity for redundancy and can even speed reads by serving from either disk. Writes cost two disk writes. Losing both disks still loses data, so only one failure is tolerated.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 2TB with 0 faults is RAID-0 striping, not mirroring.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: You cannot get both full capacity and redundancy from two mirrored disks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Surviving 2 failures with 2 disks is impossible; both copies would be gone.

easy.prompt: Appending one data block without journaling needs 3 writes: data, inode, bitmap. Crash hits after 1 write. What is the risk?

choices.label: A
choices.body: File system left inconsistent, e.g. inode points to garbage or bitmap leaks

choices.label: B
choices.body: All 3 writes roll back atomically by hardware

choices.label: C
choices.body: Journal automatically replays the missing writes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Crash is impossible during a single append

easy.hint: Disks commit one sector at a time: what if only a subset of the 3 lands?
easy.explanation: Partial updates leave pointers and allocation state disagreeing, an inconsistency window.
easy.deepDive: Without atomicity across the three writes, any crash point yields a different corrupt state: dangling pointer, leaked block, or wrong size. The window spans from the first to the last write. Ordering alone cannot close it, which motivates journaling or CoW.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Disks provide no multi-block atomicity; each write lands independently.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No journal exists here, so nothing replays; that fix comes later.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Crashes and power loss can strike between any two disk writes.

easy.prompt: What does file-system journaling primarily guarantee after a crash?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Atomic all-or-nothing recovery of each committed update

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encryption of file data against theft

choices.label: C
choices.body: Zero disk seeks on every workload

choices.label: D
choices.body: Permanent immunity to disk media failure

easy.hint: Focus on crash atomicity: does the update appear fully or not at all?
easy.explanation: Journaling makes each transaction atomic: replay it fully or skip it cleanly.
easy.deepDive: The journal is a write-ahead log: intent is recorded before in-place update, so recovery can redo committed work and discard torn tails. It does not make disks faster or more reliable media. It only converts partial application into atomic recovery.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Journaling is not encryption; it adds redundancy for recovery, not secrecy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Journaling adds extra writes, so it usually costs seeks rather than removing them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Dead sectors still need RAID or backups; journaling handles crashes, not media death.

easy.prompt: How does LFS handle a small overwrite differently from a classic FFS update?

choices.label: A
choices.body: LFS appends the new version to the log end instead of overwriting in place

choices.label: B
choices.body: LFS encrypts the block in place

choices.label: C
choices.body: LFS seeks to the old block to minimize transfer

choices.label: D
choices.body: LFS deletes the whole segment on every write

easy.hint: Ask where the new bytes go: same address or next free log slot?
easy.explanation: LFS always writes to the log tail, turning random overwrites into sequential appends.
easy.deepDive: An inode map (imap) then points to the new location, so lookups indirect through imap. Old copies become garbage cleaned later. This batches many small writes into large sequential segments ideal for HDDs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: LFS does not encrypt; it relocates the write to the log tail.
