wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Seeking to the old block is the FFS in-place behavior LFS avoids.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cleaning reclaims whole segments lazily, not one segment per write.

medium.prompt: Why does the OS track blocked separately from ready?

choices.label: A
choices.body: So the scheduler can keep running blocked processes on the CPU while ready ones wait.

choices.label: B
choices.body: So the kernel can waste CPU cycles polling blocked processes continuously.

choices.label: C
choices.body: So the OS can park I/O waiters aside and give the CPU to ready processes instead of idling.

choices.label: D
choices.body: So user programs can edit each other's registers directly.

medium.hint: Ask what the CPU should do while one process waits on a slow disk.
medium.explanation: Tracking blocked versus ready lets the scheduler overlap computation with slow I/O.
medium.deepDive: Imagine a kitchen where one cook waits on bread rising while another chops vegetables in the freed counter space. The blocked state lets the OS park the waiter and dispatch a ready process so the CPU stays busy during slow I/O. That separation of ready versus blocked is what makes multiprogramming and later preemption possible.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Blocked processes are by definition not runnable, so the scheduler must not run them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Polling blocked processes would burn CPU instead of dispatching ready work.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Registers are saved in the PCB precisely so processes stay isolated and cannot edit each other.

medium.prompt: Trace: pid = fork(); if (pid < 0) fail; else if (pid == 0) child_work(); else parent_work(); Who runs what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Parent takes the pid > 0 branch, child takes the pid == 0 branch, and pid == -1 means no child was created.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both take the pid > 0 branch because PIDs are always positive everywhere.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Failure still creates a child that takes the pid == 0 branch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The child receives the parent PID in pid and takes the pid > 0 branch.

medium.hint: Three outcomes need three branches: parent, child, and failure.
medium.explanation: Positive means parent, zero means child, and -1 means fork failed.
medium.deepDive: Read pid as a three-way ticket with values positive, zero, or minus one. A positive ticket means you are the parent holding the new child number, zero means you are the child, and minus one means the machine refused to split and no twin exists. Robust code checks minus one first, then zero, then positive, exactly like sorting those three ticket colors.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The child receives 0 rather than a positive PID, so the branches diverge.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: On failure fork returns -1 to the original process and creates no second process.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The child receives 0, not the parent PID, and the parent holds the child PID.

medium.prompt: Trace: fork(); fork(); printf("hi"); How many processes print hi?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 2 processes total because the second fork replaces the first.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 3 processes total because the second fork runs only once.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 4 processes total because each existing process splits again at the second fork.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 6 processes total because fork counts multiply by three.

medium.hint: Draw the tree: how many runners reach the second fork line?
medium.explanation: Each sequential fork doubles the current population, so two forks make 4.
medium.deepDive: Draw a family tree where the first fork turns 1 process into 2 twins. Both twins then reach the second fork line and each splits, turning 2 into 4 total. Think of folding then cutting paper where every existing layer doubles, so two sequential forks yield 4 leaves.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: fork adds processes and never replaces the caller, so populations only grow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both twins execute the second fork because neither branches away from it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Each fork doubles the population rather than tripling it, so two forks give 2 squared.

medium.prompt: Trace: for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) fork(); How many processes exist?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 3 processes because loop iterations are shared between parent and child.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Infinitely many because fork in a loop never terminates.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 4 processes because each iteration doubles whoever exists at that fork.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 2 processes because the child exits the loop immediately.

medium.hint: Track both the loop counter and the doubling at each pass.
medium.explanation: Two doublings in a loop produce 4 processes.
medium.deepDive: Walk the loop counter together with the tree, since each new twin inherits the current counter value. Iteration one doubles 1 into 2, then iteration two doubles those 2 into 4. Think of a chain letter where everyone holding a copy at round two mails two more, so two looped forks give 4 processes. This pattern generalizes to 2 raised to n for n unguarded forks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Children inherit the loop counter and continue looping, so more than 3 processes result.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The population doubles per fork, and two doublings give 4 rather than an infinite explosion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Nothing in this code stops the child from continuing the loop, so children fork again.

medium.prompt: Trace: int x = 0; int rc = fork(); if (rc == 0) x = 1; else x = 2; What are the final x values?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both hold 9 because they share one counter.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Child holds 1 and parent holds 2 because each updated its private copy after the split.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Child holds 2 and parent holds 1 because fork swaps the values.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both hold 0 because fork discards writes made after the call.

medium.hint: Give each twin its own sheet of paper and follow only its branch.
medium.explanation: Memory diverges after fork, so the two branches keep different values of x.
medium.deepDive: Start with x equal to 0 in the single parent, then split and substitute rc separately per twin. The child path assigns its own x to 1 while the parent path assigns its own x to 2. Think of twins photocopying a scoreboard at 0 and then writing different scores on their own copies, so final values diverge permanently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Copies are private after fork, so the two assignments cannot land in one shared cell.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: fork copies memory unchanged and never swaps values between parent and child.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Writes after fork persist in each private address space and are not discarded.

medium.prompt: Why must fork return the child PID to the parent instead of 0 to both?

choices.label: A
choices.body: So the child can kill the parent with the returned value.

choices.label: B
choices.body: So the parent learns the child identity and can wait on, signal, or track that specific child.

choices.label: C
choices.body: So both processes can share one PID going forward.

choices.label: D
choices.body: So fork can return the exit code of the child immediately.

medium.hint: Which side needs a handle for waitpid when many children exist?
medium.explanation: The parent needs the child PID to manage exactly that child later.
medium.deepDive: Think of fork as handing the parent a claim ticket with the newborn PID printed on it. The child needs no ticket because it can ask for itself with getpid, but the parent needs the number to wait on the right twin among many. That ticket is the bridge from anonymous splitting to controlled parenting with wait and exec next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The return value is an identifier for management, not a weapon for termination.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: PIDs stay unique, and parent and child always have different PIDs after fork.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The child has not exited yet at fork time, so no exit code exists to return.

medium.prompt: What does exec() do to the calling process?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It keeps the same PID but replaces code, data, heap, and stack with the new program.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It creates a brand-new PID and leaves the old process running too.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It only changes the process nice value and scheduling priority.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It swaps PIDs with the parent process.

medium.hint: Ask what stays the same versus what gets replaced when becoming a new program.
medium.explanation: exec reloads the address space in place and preserves the caller PID.
medium.deepDive: Think of exec as an actor staying in the same costume number but changing into a completely new play. The PID face stays the same while the memory script, stack props, and program-counter lines are thrown out and reloaded. That same-PID swap is why a shell child can become ls without disturbing the parent shell identity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Creating a new PID is the job of fork, while exec transforms the existing process.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Priority tweaks do not reload code or memory, which is the whole point of exec.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: PIDs never swap between parent and child during exec.

medium.prompt: Why do shells fork first and exec only in the child while the parent waits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Parent forks, child execs the command, and the parent waits so the shell prompt returns at the right time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Parent execs the command and the child waits for the parent.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both parent and child exec different commands simultaneously.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither forks and the shell overwrites itself with every command.

medium.hint: Which side must survive to print the next prompt?
medium.explanation: fork-then-exec-then-wait lets the shell survive while the child becomes the command.
medium.deepDive: Picture a restaurant where the head chef keeps the counter while a helper steps aside to cook one order. The helper is the forked child that execs into the recipe, while the head chef waits so the next customer is served only after the dish lands. If the parent execed instead, the shell itself would vanish into the command.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The parent must stay a shell, so it must not exec itself into the command.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Only the child should transform, otherwise no shell remains to continue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Without forking, the first command would permanently replace the shell.

medium.prompt: A child calls exit(3) and the parent calls wait(&status). How does the parent get 3?

choices.label: A
choices.body: By reading the raw integer directly as the exit code.

choices.label: B
choices.body: By applying WIFEXITED and WEXITSTATUS macros to the status word wait collected.

choices.label: C
choices.body: By calling fork again and comparing PIDs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exit codes cannot be observed by the parent at all.

medium.hint: The status word packs several fields, so direct reads mislead.
medium.explanation: The status word packs reason plus code, so macros decode it safely.
medium.deepDive: Think of the status word as a sealed envelope with checkboxes for exited, signaled, and stopped plus a grade slip inside. The parent must first check the exited box with WIFEXITED, then pull the slip with WEXITSTATUS. Reading raw bits directly confuses signal numbers with exit grades.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The status word also encodes signals and stops, so raw reads misinterpret the bits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: fork creates processes and reveals nothing about an already-packed status word.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Collecting exit codes through wait is exactly the purpose of the status argument.

medium.prompt: How do exit(code) and return from main compare?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are identical in all cases and interchangeable.

choices.label: B
choices.body: exit() ends the process with a code the parent can collect, while return from main does the same after flushing stdio and running atexit handlers.

choices.label: C
choices.body: return from main kills the parent, while exit() kills only the child.

choices.label: D
choices.body: exit() only pauses the process, which wait() later resumes.

medium.hint: Follow the cleanup steps that run before the process really dies.
medium.explanation: Both deliver an exit code, but the normal path runs cleanup first.
medium.deepDive: Think of exit as ringing the closing bell with a score attached for the parent to pick up. Returning from main walks out through the lobby first, flushing buffers and running registered cleanup, then rings the same bell. Forgetting the flush explains why missing newlines vanish when a child calls the raw system-call variant instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Cleanup and flushing behavior differs between raw exit paths and returning through startup code.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both end the calling process itself and never directly kill the other side.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: exit terminates rather than pausing, and wait only collects the finished state.

medium.prompt: If a child exits and the parent never calls wait, what remains?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The child becomes a zombie holding its exit ticket until the parent waits.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The child becomes an orphan and is immediately deleted with no record.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The child PID is immediately reused with no record left.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The parent automatically execs into the child program.

medium.hint: What record must the kernel keep so a later wait can still succeed?
medium.explanation: An unreaped exit leaves a zombie PCB entry behind.
medium.deepDive: Think of finishing a race while the results desk stays open because nobody picked up your slip. The runner is done and frees memory and CPU, but the kernel keeps a tiny results row with PID and exit code. That lingering row is the zombie, and it only clears when the parent calls wait to collect the ticket.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Orphans arise when the parent dies first, not when the parent lives on without waiting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: PIDs cannot be safely reused until the exit status is collected by the parent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: exec never happens automatically and is unrelated to missing wait calls.

medium.prompt: What is the difference between a zombie and an orphan process?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A zombie is a dead child awaiting collection, while an orphan is a live child whose parent died and who is reparented to init.

choices.label: B
choices.body: They are the same state with two names.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A zombie still runs code, while an orphan has already exited.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An orphan holds no PID, while a zombie holds two PIDs.

medium.hint: Ask who died: the child or the parent?
medium.explanation: Zombies are dead-but-unreaped, orphans are alive-but-reparented.
medium.deepDive: Picture a coat-check ticket left on the rail after the owner left as the zombie, versus a child whose guardian left the fair and is handed to the information booth as the orphan. The zombie is already dead but keeps its ticket row until the parent claims it. The orphan is still alive and keeps running under init, which will eventually collect it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One describes a dead child and the other a live child, so they are opposite situations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zombies never run again, while orphans continue executing normally.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both keep exactly one PID, and the distinction is about parent liveness and reaping.

medium.prompt: What is copy-on-write (COW) after fork?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Copy every page eagerly at fork so nothing is ever shared.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Share all pages read-only after fork and copy a page privately only when either side writes it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Share the PID table but never share any memory pages.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disable virtual memory in the child until it calls exec.

medium.hint: When is the latest moment the OS could pay for a copy?
medium.explanation: Copy-on-write shares pages until a write forces a private copy.
medium.deepDive: Think of twins sharing one textbook with a do-not-write rule until someone needs notes. Both map the same physical pages read-only after fork, just like sharing the book. The first scribble triggers a private photocopy of only that page, exactly the share-until-write trick that makes fork cheap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Eager copying is the expensive baseline that COW is designed to avoid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Page sharing is the core of COW, not something it forbids.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both processes keep full virtual memory with shared read-only mappings.

medium.prompt: How does the COW write fault connect to traps in limited direct execution?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A COW protection fault is one example of a trap, which is the general CPU mechanism for entering the kernel safely.

choices.label: B
choices.body: COW faults only read files and have nothing to do with kernel entry.

choices.label: C
choices.body: COW faults bypass the kernel and edit page tables from user space.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Traps and COW faults are unrelated to virtual memory.

medium.hint: What did the CPU already do to handle the COW write fault?
medium.explanation: COW copy faults preview the trap mechanism behind system calls and preemption.
medium.deepDive: Zoom out from the COW photocopy interruption to every kernel entry the CPU supports. A protection fault, a system call, and a timer tick all trap through the same gated doorway into kernel mode. Seeing COW first makes traps concrete, so limited direct execution can now reuse that doorway for all kernel supervision.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reading files is one use of traps, but process control and faults use the same entry path.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Only the kernel can safely update page tables, so user space cannot do it directly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Protection faults are delivered through the trap machinery and handled with page tables.

medium.prompt: How do system calls, faults, and interrupts differ?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A system call is a deliberate trap for service, a fault is an exceptional trap such as COW, and an interrupt comes from hardware such as the timer.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All three are identical function calls inside user programs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Interrupts are always caused by divide-by-zero in user code.

choices.label: D
choices.body: System calls run entirely in user mode without kernel help.

medium.hint: Ask who knocked: the program on purpose, the CPU on accident, or hardware outside?
medium.explanation: Origin distinguishes planned requests, CPU exceptions, and device signals.
medium.deepDive: Think of knocking on the office door for help, tripping the alarm by touching a protected page, and hearing a fire drill bell from the hallway. The knock is a system call, the alarm trip is a fault, and the bell is a device or timer interrupt. All three cross the same kernel doorway but carry different causes and return addresses.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Traps and interrupts switch privilege and save context, unlike plain function calls.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Divide-by-zero is one fault source, while interrupts come from timers and devices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: System calls exist precisely to enter the kernel for privileged work.

medium.prompt: What do user versus kernel mode and the trap table provide?

choices.label: A
choices.body: User mode bars privileged instructions and the trap table routes each event to its kernel handler.

choices.label: B
choices.body: User mode is faster because it skips all safety checks.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The trap table lives in each process heap and is edited freely.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Kernel mode prevents the OS from touching hardware.

medium.hint: Where is the directory of handlers and who may edit it?
medium.explanation: Hardware mode plus a kernel-owned vector keeps privileged control safe.
medium.deepDive: Think of user mode as the public museum floor and kernel mode as the locked control room with one guarded door. Attempting a privileged instruction outside the control room traps instead of succeeding. The trap table is the directory by that door that points each event number to the right handler routine.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: User mode adds protection checks and trusted paths rather than removing them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The trap table is kernel-owned hardware state, not a user-editable heap object.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Kernel mode exists exactly so the OS can touch hardware and page tables.

medium.prompt: Why is a timer interrupt essential for limited direct execution?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The timer periodically interrupts the CPU so the OS regains control and can switch processes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Cooperative processes always yield voluntarily so timers are unnecessary.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Processes voluntarily halt the timer whenever they want more CPU.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The timer only measures wall-clock time for user programs.

medium.hint: What forces control back if a process never calls into the kernel?
medium.explanation: Timer ticks guarantee the OS gets a chance to preempt runaway processes.
medium.deepDive: Think of a chess clock that buzzes every few seconds and forces the current player to pause. Without that bell a buggy loop could keep the CPU forever under limited direct execution. The timer interrupt hands control back to the scheduler, which is the heartbeat of preemptive sharing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Cooperation alone cannot bound a malicious or buggy infinite loop.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: User processes cannot disable the kernel timer to hoard the CPU.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The kernel programs the timer precisely to regain control for scheduling.

medium.prompt: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary context switches?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Voluntary switches happen when a process blocks on I/O, while involuntary switches happen when the timer preempts a runnable process.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Voluntary means the CPU overheats, while involuntary means the disk is full.

choices.label: C
choices.body: There is only one kind of switch and the cause never matters.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Involuntary switches never save registers.

medium.hint: Did the process ask to wait, or did the timer decide for it?
medium.explanation: Blocking yields by choice, while timer ticks take the CPU by force.
medium.deepDive: Compare yielding your chess turn to fetch water versus the clock buzzing mid-move. Blocking on a read is the water break that voluntarily returns the CPU through a syscall. A timer tick during a long compute is the buzzer that involuntarily parks a runnable process so others get turns.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Temperature and disk capacity do not define the voluntary versus involuntary distinction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The cause predicts cache effects and scheduling policy, so it matters for performance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Every switch must save and restore CPU context to resume correctly later.

medium.prompt: Trace the shell running a single foreground command ls. What is the call order?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shell forks once, the child execs ls, and the parent waits for that PID before prompting again.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shell execs ls itself and then forks a replacement shell.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Shell waits first and forks only after ls finishes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No fork or exec happens because ls is handled by the timer.

medium.hint: Order the three calls: who splits, who transforms, who collects?
medium.explanation: One fork plus one exec plus one wait runs a single foreground command.
medium.deepDive: Trace ls like a relay with three baton passes in strict order. First the shell forks a helper that inherits the terminal setup. Next only the helper execs into ls while the parent holds its prompt. Finally the parent wait collects the exit ticket before printing the next prompt.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The shell must survive, so it never execs itself into the command.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The child cannot finish before it is created, so waiting first is impossible.

medium.prompt: Jobs: A arrives 0 burst 8, B arrives 1 burst 4. SRTF preempts when a new arrival has shorter remaining time. When does B complete?

medium.explanation: B preempts A at 1 and runs 1–5, completing at 5; A resumes 5–12.
medium.deepDive: SRTF is the preemptive form of SJF: it compares remaining time, not original burst. Preemption lets a just-arrived short avoid the convoy that nonpreemptive SJF would still impose. The cost is more context switches and potential starvation of the preempted long job.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 12 is B's completion under nonpreemptive FCFS/SJF (A 0–8, B 8–12).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 9 mixes remaining-time math incorrectly; B needs only 4 units from 1.

medium.prompt: Jobs: A arrives 0 burst 8, B arrives 1 burst 3, C arrives 5 burst 2. SRTF, ties keep the running job. When does C complete?

medium.explanation: B runs 1–4, A 4–5, C preempts at 5 and runs 5–7, so C completes at 7; A finishes at 13.
medium.deepDive: Each arrival triggers a remaining-time comparison, chaining two preemptions here. C waits zero because it is shortest at 5, while A absorbs all delay. This trace shows SRTF generalizing SJF to staggered arrivals without changing its average-optimality goal.

medium.prompt: Jobs A,B,C arrive at 0, each burst 4. Round Robin with quantum 2, cyclic order A,B,C. Which job runs during interval 2→4?

medium.prompt: Which statement about RR quantum size is true?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Huge quantum ≈ FCFS (good turnaround, bad response); tiny quantum ≈ many switches (good response, high overhead).

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Huge quantum improves response for shorts arriving late.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Imagine q=1000 with 5-unit jobs vs q=0.1 with 1ms switch cost — what dominates each case?
medium.explanation: Large q rarely preempts so it degenerates to FCFS; tiny q slices finely but switch cost dominates.
medium.deepDive: Quantum tunes granularity: too coarse loses fairness, too fine wastes CPU on switching. Real systems pick ~10ms to amortize ~µs switch costs while keeping response snappy. This tuning has nothing to do with predicting bursts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tiny quanta add proportional switch overhead and stretch turnaround; nothing is free.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Huge quanta trap shorts behind longs, worsening response — the FCFS convoy returns.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RR needs no burst knowledge; it just rotates fixed slices, unlike SJF.

medium.prompt: Which is true of RR vs SJF regarding burst knowledge and fairness?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: RR needs exact bursts to size each quantum per job.

choices.label: C
choices.body: SJF optimizes maximum turnaround, so it is fairer than RR.

choices.label: D
choices.body: RR starves long jobs whenever shorts keep arriving.

medium.hint: Ask what each scheduler must know before its next decision: a fixed slice or a length comparison?
medium.explanation: RR's next slice is always fixed q for the next ready job; SJF must compare predicted lengths.
medium.deepDive: RR trades optimality for robustness: fairness and implementability without prediction. SJF is average-optimal but fragile to estimation error and starvation. This is why general systems prefer RR-like fairness and reserve SJF ideas for when lengths are known.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Quanta are fixed system parameters, not per-job burst predictions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SJF optimizes average turnaround, not max; strict short-first can starve longs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Starvation under endless shorts is SJF's flaw; RR cycles so longs always progress.

medium.prompt: Jobs arrive at 0: A=5, B=3, C=1. RR quantum 2, order A,B,C. When does A complete?

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 5 is FCFS completion of A (run-to-completion), ignoring slicing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 7 is when A's second slice ends (1 unit still remains).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 12 double-counts; total work is only 9 units with zero idle.

medium.prompt: MLFQ has Q0 (top) and Q1. Rule: new jobs enter Q0; jobs exceeding Q0's quantum drop to Q1; Q0 always beats Q1. Where does a newly arriving interactive job enter?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Q0 (top), preempting any Q1 job

choices.label: B
choices.body: Q1 (bottom), waiting behind CPU-bound jobs

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Apply the entry rule literally: every arrival starts at the top regardless of history.
medium.explanation: All arrivals enter Q0, so a new job preempts Q1 and gets fast first service.
medium.deepDive: Top-entry gives MLFQ its RR-like responsiveness without knowing job type in advance. Only sustained CPU use triggers demotion. This single feedback rule lets the scheduler learn interactiveness by observation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bottom-entry would convoy interactives behind batch jobs, defeating MLFQ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inheriting the current queue confuses job identity; entry depends only on arrival.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Random placement destroys priority structure and response guarantees.

medium.prompt: Job X uses full quanta repeatedly (CPU-bound); job Y yields for I/O after short bursts. Under MLFQ feedback, which stays high and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Y stays high (yields before expiry); X demotes for consuming quanta.

choices.label: B
choices.body: X stays high (uses more CPU, deserves priority).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both stay top because MLFQ needs no quanta.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both sink immediately to make room for new arrivals.

medium.hint: Check who exhausts the quantum: exhaustion demotes, voluntary yield keeps priority.
medium.explanation: Exhausting a quantum signals CPU-bound and demotes; yielding signals interactive and retains high queue.
medium.deepDive: Feedback infers type from behavior instead of requiring burst declarations. Interactive jobs thus get priority automatically while batch jobs sink to longer quanta below. This separation is MLFQ's core win over plain RR.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MLFQ punishes, not rewards, quantum exhaustion; more use means lower priority.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MLFQ is defined by per-queue quanta; 'no quanta' confuses it with lottery.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only quantum-hogs demote; yielding jobs correctly stay high.

medium.prompt: MLFQ typically uses small quanta at top queues and larger quanta at bottom queues. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Short slices up top for responsiveness; long slices below amortize switches for CPU-bound jobs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Large slices up top so interactives finish instantly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Equal quanta everywhere because queue level is cosmetic.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Small slices below to punish batch jobs with more switches.

medium.hint: Match slice size to goal: top cares about response, bottom about throughput/overhead.
medium.explanation: Top needs fine interleaving for response; bottom holds long jobs where coarse slices cut switch overhead.
medium.deepDive: Graduated quanta let one scheduler act like RR for interactives and like FCFS for batch. A 10ms top quantum with 100ms bottom quantum is typical. Uniform quanta would force a false choice between responsiveness and efficiency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Large top slices convoy interactives — the opposite of responsive design.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Level-dependent quanta are load-bearing; equal slices lose the RR/FCFS hybrid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Small bottom slices maximize switch waste on exactly the jobs that suffer most.

medium.prompt: A long batch job sits in the bottom queue while interactive jobs keep arriving at top. What prevents its starvation in MLFQ?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Require exact burst knowledge so the long job runs first.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Remove all quanta so queues run to completion.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Give the long job the earliest deadline (EDF) permanently.

medium.hint: Look for the time-based anti-starvation rule that resets all jobs upward.
medium.explanation: A periodic boost every 100ms returns starved jobs to Q0 so they progress and phase changes are relearned.
medium.deepDive: Strict priority without aging starves bottom queues under continuous top arrivals. Boosting bounds waiting and lets a job that turned interactive regain status. The interval S trades responsiveness of batch against interference with interactives.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MLFQ's point is avoiding burst prediction; SJF needs it, MLFQ does not.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Removing quanta destroys feedback and reintroduces convoy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: EDF deadlines are a separate real-time mechanism, not MLFQ aging.

medium.prompt: A job does 99% of its quantum then yields for trivial I/O, repeating to stay in Q0 forever. What is this and what fixes it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Gaming the scheduler; fix with CPU allotment accounting (demote after cumulative use).

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Convoy effect; fix with larger top quantum.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Cache thrashing; fix with processor affinity.

medium.hint: Notice the job exploits yield-before-expiry; ask what cumulative counter would catch it.
medium.explanation: Yielding just before expiry games feedback; tracking total CPU per level (allotment) demotes abusers.
medium.deepDive: Per-quantum feedback is gameable because intent is invisible in one slice. Allotment accumulates service across yields and demotes after a budget. This preserves fast response for true interactives while closing the cheat. Solaris-style decay is a related fix.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inversion needs locks with L/M/H priorities, not quantum gaming.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Convoy is FCFS head-of-line blocking, unrelated to strategic yielding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Affinity concerns migration cost on multicore, not queue gaming.

medium.prompt: MLFQ: Q0 quantum 2, Q1 runs FCFS. A arrives 0 burst 4; B arrives 2 burst 2. Who runs during 2→4?

medium.explanation: A drops to Q1 at 2; B enters Q0 at 2 and preempts, running 2–4 to completion.
medium.deepDive: This trace composes entry, demotion, and strict priority in one scenario. A resumes 4–6 in Q1 after B finishes. It shows interactives automatically jumping ahead without any declared priority. Boost and allotment would only matter over longer horizons.

medium.prompt: Lottery scheduling: A holds 75 tickets, B holds 25 tickets (total 100). On each draw, what is P(A wins the CPU)?

choices.label: C

medium.explanation: Probability is proportional to tickets: 75/100 = 75%.
medium.deepDive: Tickets encode share without priorities or burst estimates. Over many draws A gets ~3x B's CPU, matching the 3:1 ratio. Randomness keeps the mechanism simple and starvation-free in expectation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 25% is B's share (25/100), not A's.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Equal split ignores ticket counts; shares are proportional, not even.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Lottery is probabilistic sharing, not run-to-completion by one job.

medium.prompt: When should data go in globals (data/BSS) vs heap?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Globals live on the heap and are malloc'd at startup.

choices.label: B
choices.body: There is no difference — both are stack frames.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Heap data is fixed at compile time; globals grow at runtime.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Globals (data/BSS) have fixed size/compile-time lifetime for the whole run; heap is for counts/sizes known only at runtime.

medium.hint: Ask when the size is known: `int g[100]` vs `malloc(n*...)` where n is user input. Which must wait until runtime?
medium.explanation: Use globals when size/count is compile-time-known and lifetime is whole-run; heap when decided at runtime.
medium.deepDive: Globals are like seats bolted to the theater floor — counted before opening night and never moving — while heap objects are folding chairs brought in as the crowd arrives. `int table[100]` as a global reserves exactly that at load; a user-supplied `n` needs `malloc(n*sizeof(...))`. Choosing wrong means either wasting fixed space or overflowing a rigid array.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Globals are loaded into data/BSS, not malloc'd — no malloc call creates them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Neither is a stack frame; stack frames die on return, globals/heap outlive calls.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed — globals are compile-time-fixed, heap is runtime-dynamic.

medium.prompt: Two processes running the same binary both use address 0x1000 for `main`. No crash. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each process has a private virtual address space; identical virtual addresses translate to different physical frames.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All processes share one physical address space with no translation.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The OS copies each binary to different virtual addresses to avoid collision.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Virtual addresses are just file offsets on disk.

medium.hint: If addresses were physical, sharing 0x1000 would collide. What per-process mapping removes the collision?
medium.explanation: Virtual addresses are per-process illusions; hardware/OS maps same virtual to different physical.
medium.deepDive: Virtualization is the illusion from Ch1 made concrete: every process feels alone with the full address range, like identical hotel room numbers on different floors. Base/bounds (or page tables later) are the floor numbers mapping room 101 to different physical rooms. That is why debugging prints the same pointer values in two runs yet memory stays isolated.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No translation would mean collision — isolation requires translation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Binaries load at the same virtual addresses precisely because translation handles the difference.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Virtual addresses translate to DRAM (via base/bounds here), not disk offsets.

medium.prompt: Base=2000, bound=1000. Virtual address 100 is accessed. Physical address and legality?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Physical 100, allowed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Physical 2100, trapped (out of bounds).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Physical 2100, allowed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Physical 1300, allowed.

medium.hint: Two steps in order: (1) is virtual < bound? (2) physical = base + virtual. Apply both.
medium.explanation: 100 < bound 1000 so legal; physical = base 2000 + 100 = 2100.
medium.deepDive: Trace it in two steps every time: check first, add second. 100 < 1000 passes the bound check, then 2000+100 relocates to physical 2100. Swap the order mentally and you get the classic bug: adding before checking could touch another process's frame before trapping. Hardware always checks-then-translates for exactly this reason.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Forgot to add base — virtual 100 is not physical 100 under relocation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 100 < 1000 is in-bounds; trapping here confuses this with the out-of-bounds case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1300 adds wrong numbers — physical = base + virtual, not bound + virtual.

medium.prompt: Base=8000, bound=500. Access to virtual 500 — allowed or trap?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Allowed — bound is inclusive, so 500 maps to physical base+500.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Traps — valid range is 0..499 (virtual < bound); 500 is one past the end.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Allowed — hardware rounds the bound up to a page.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Traps — but only if the access is a write; reads bypass bounds.

medium.hint: New numbers, same rule: is the test <= or <? Valid is 0..bound-1. Where does 500 fall?
medium.explanation: Check is virtual < bound, so virtual == bound is out-of-bounds and traps.
medium.deepDive: Bounds define a half-open interval [0, bound): slot bound itself belongs to the next-door neighbor (or nobody). Allowing == bound would leak one byte of someone else's memory per process — a classic off-by-one exploit. When in doubt, test the edge: bound 500 means the largest legal virtual is 499.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Inclusive-bound is the off-by-one misconception — the check is strict < .
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No rounding here — base/bounds here is byte-granular, not paged; rounding is a paging/internal-frag idea.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bounds apply to reads AND writes (and fetch); reads do not bypass protection.

medium.prompt: `int fact(int n){ if(n<=1) return 1; return n*fact(n-1); }` with `fact(3)`. How do stack frames handle the three live `n` values?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each recursive call pushes a fresh frame with its own locals/return address; they coexist until returns unwind.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All recursive calls share one frame and overwrite each other's locals.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Each recursive call mallocs heap that survives after return.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Recursion reuses the caller's frame by jumping backward (no push).

medium.hint: If frames were shared, what would `fact(3)`'s inner call do to the outer `n`? What must be true for the math to work?
medium.explanation: Recursion stacks one frame per live call, each with private locals; returns pop in reverse.
medium.deepDive: Recursion is the killer demo for frames: `fact(3)` holds frames for 3, 2, 1 simultaneously, each with its own `n` — that is why the returns compute 1, then 2*1, then 3*2 correctly. If frames were shared, inner calls would clobber `n` and unwinding would be garbage. Counting live frames also predicts stack depth, the bridge to overflow next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Shared-frame would corrupt outer locals — each call needs private `n`.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No malloc involved; frames auto-pop on return instead of leaking.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A jump without push loses the return address — returns could not unwind.

medium.prompt: `while(1){ char *p = malloc(1024); work(p); /* no free */ }` Long-term effect?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It fragments the disk and slows future file opens.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It overflows the stack and crashes immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Nothing — the OS reclaims each block while the loop still runs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Heap grows (free list never refilled) until malloc fails / OOM killer strikes; fix by free()ing what you no longer need.

medium.hint: free() feeds the free list (Q7). If the loop never calls it, what happens to reuse across iterations?
medium.explanation: Un-freed mallocs accumulate; total live heap grows until exhaustion — free unneeded blocks.
medium.deepDive: A leak is a slow puncture, not a blowout: each iteration's block stays marked live, so the allocator cannot reuse it and sbrk keeps extending the heap. Long-running servers die this way over days while short tests look fine — which is why leak detectors track unmatched malloc/free pairs. The OS only reclaims everything at exit, far too late for a daemon.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Heap leak is DRAM exhaustion, not disk fragmentation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Heap growth is not stack overflow — stacks crash on deep calls, heaps on un-freed accumulation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: OS reclaims at process exit, not mid-run while pointers are still (technically) live.

medium.prompt: `free(p); free(p);` with no malloc in between. Consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Harmless — the second free is ignored like closing an already-closed file.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Corrupts the allocator's free list (same block linked twice) → later malloc returns aliased memory / crash / exploit.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Immediately returns two pages to the OS, shrinking the heap by double.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Just a small leak — wastes one block but is otherwise safe.

medium.hint: free() pushes the block onto the free list (Q7). What does pushing the SAME block twice do to that list?
medium.explanation: Double-free poisons free-list bookkeeping, causing duplicate allocation and heap corruption.
medium.deepDive: The free list is a linked list hidden inside freed blocks: freeing twice links the same node in twice, so two future mallocs can return the SAME address to two owners. Both then scribble on each other's objects — a heap aliasing nightmare and a famous exploit primitive. That is why modern allocators abort on detected double-free instead of staying silent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Not ignored — unlike idempotent close, second free re-links live bookkeeping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No double OS return; corruption happens at allocator level before any OS call.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Opposite of a leak — it is active corruption, worse than wasting one block.

medium.prompt: `char *p = malloc(16); strcpy(p, "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ");` (32 chars). What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: malloc auto-grows the block to fit the copy.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only internal fragmentation increases; neighbors are always safe.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bytes past 16 overwrite adjacent heap (allocator metadata or next object) → heap corruption / crash / exploit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hardware base/bounds traps it because heap has per-malloc bounds registers.

medium.hint: malloc gives exactly 16 bytes with neighbors packed after. Where do bytes 17..32 land?
medium.explanation: C heap has no per-object hardware check; overflow silently corrupts neighboring heap state.
medium.deepDive: Heap allocations sit back-to-back with hidden headers between them, like tents pegged edge-to-edge: spilling past your tent floods the neighbor's. strcpy past 16 clobbers whatever follows — often the next chunk's size/next-pointer — so a much later malloc/free crashes far from the bug. This temporal distance is why overflows are diagnosed with sanitizers, not by staring at the crash site.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No auto-growth — C malloc never resizes on store; that is realloc, explicitly called.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is corruption beyond padding, not benign internal waste.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One base/bound pair covers the whole address space here, not per-malloc — no per-object trap.

medium.prompt: What is external fragmentation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Free gaps BETWEEN live blocks/segments: total free suffices but no single contiguous gap fits the request.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Padding waste inside a page-rounded allocation.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Extra time the scheduler takes to context-switch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Waste from zeroing freed memory for security.

medium.hint: Contrast Q8 (inside). EXTERNAL = between allocations. Which option needs a contiguous run?
medium.explanation: External fragmentation is scattered free space: enough in total, not enough contiguous.
medium.deepDive: External is outside: imagine a parking lot with single free spots scattered between cars — ten free spots cannot fit a bus needing five consecutive ones. Total bytes free can far exceed the request yet allocation fails, until compaction/coalescing merges neighbors. This is fundamentally different from internal waste, where the bytes are already yours but padded.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inside-page padding is internal — the exact mirror to keep straight.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scheduler delay is not memory waste; same distractor as Q8, still wrong here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zeroing cost is (optional) security overhead, not a fragmentation category.

medium.prompt: Case X: 1-byte allocation occupies a full 4KB page. Case Y: 12KB total free as three scattered 4KB gaps; a 12KB request fails. Classify.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both are scheduler delays under load.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Case X is external, Case Y is internal.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both are internal — all waste is inside pages.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Case X is internal (1-byte payload in 4KB page wastes ~4095 inside); Case Y is external (3 scattered 4KB frees cannot fit 12KB contiguous).

medium.hint: Apply the Q8/Q9 tests: X wastes space you already own (inside?) vs Y wastes free space with no fit (between?)
medium.explanation: Own-but-padded = internal; free-but-scattered = external.
medium.deepDive: Use the location test: waste you own but cannot use (page padding) is internal; waste nobody owns but nobody can use (scattered gaps) is external. Case X bills you a whole page for one byte; Case Y has 12KB free on paper yet fails a 12KB ask. Naming them correctly predicts the fix: smaller pages help X, coalescing/compaction helps Y.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Neither is scheduling — fragmentation is about placement/waste, not time-slices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Swapped — X is the textbook internal example, Y the textbook external one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Y involves no owned page at all — it is free-space scatter, hence external.

medium.prompt: Two processes run `/bin/sh`. Which segment can the OS safely share as one physical copy?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The stack of each process, so calls share locals for speed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The code segment (and shared libraries), mapped read-only into each process sharing one physical copy.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The heap, so mallocs in one process appear in the other.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The PCB, so PIDs can be reused.

medium.hint: Sharing is only safe for bytes that never change. Which segment qualifies?
medium.explanation: Immutable code is safe to share read-only; mutable stack/heap must stay private.
medium.deepDive: Sharing works because code never changes: fifty shells can execute one physical libc/code copy mapped into fifty virtual spaces, like fifty bookmarks into one library book. Read-only mapping is the safety catch — any write attempt traps instead of corrupting everyone's execution. Mutable state (stack, heap, globals) stays private per process, which is why the same-function locals never collide.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Shared stacks would mix return addresses/locals — instant corruption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Shared heaps would leak/alias objects across processes — breaks isolation (Ch1).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: PCBs are per-process kernel state (Ch1-2), never shared as memory.

medium.prompt: A buggy pointer writes into the code segment. With per-segment R/W/X, what happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Hardware traps the write (code is read-only) — typically segfault.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The write succeeds and speeds up the next call (self-optimizing code).

choices.label: C
choices.body: The write causes external fragmentation between segments.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The write leaks heap memory in another process.

medium.hint: Apply Q9: code = R-X. What must hardware do on a store to an R-only mapping?
medium.explanation: Per-segment write permission makes stray/attack writes to code fail fast via trap.
medium.deepDive: This trap is protection doing its job: code mapped R-X rejects stores, so a wild pointer or attack that aims at instructions fails loudly instead of silently rewriting the program. Debuggers/JITs that genuinely need to write code must explicitly remap permission first — the exception proves the rule. Confusing this with fragmentation or leaks misses that permissions enforce intent per access.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No silent self-modification — the write is denied, not applied as an optimization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Fragmentation is placement waste, unrelated to a permission trap on one store.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Isolation holds — one process's trap does not leak another's heap.

medium.prompt: VA 0x12345678 (4-KB pages) → VPN 0x12345, offset 0x678. PTE says VPN 0x12345 → PFN 0x00ABC, valid, present, R/W. What is the physical address?

choices.label: A
choices.body: PA = 0x12345678 (identity)

choices.label: B
choices.body: PA = 0x00ABC678

choices.label: C
choices.body: PA = 0x00ABC12345

choices.label: D
choices.body: PA = 0x1234500ABC

medium.hint: Copy the offset straight across. Replace ONLY the VPN with the PFN.
medium.explanation: Keep offset 0x678; swap VPN 0x12345 for PFN 0x00ABC.
medium.deepDive: Translation preserves the offset bits exactly and replaces only the VPN with the PFN. So PA = (PFN << 12) | 0x678 = 0x00ABC678. Any answer that alters the offset or concatenates whole addresses misunderstands field replacement.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Identity mapping ignores the table; translation must replace VPN with PFN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Appends instead of replacing — PA would be far wider than 32 bits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Scrambles field order; offset must stay in the low bits.

medium.prompt: VA 0xABCDEFFF → VPN 0xABCDE. PTE maps it to PFN 0xDEF12. What is PA? (4-KB pages)

choices.label: A
choices.body: PA = 0xDEF12FFF

choices.label: B
choices.body: PA = 0xABCDEDEF12

choices.label: C
choices.body: PA = 0xFFFDEF12

choices.label: D
choices.body: PA = 0xABCDEFFF (unchanged)

medium.hint: Split first (offset = low 3 hex digits), then substitute the mapped PFN.
medium.explanation: Offset 0xFFF preserved; PFN 0xDEF12 shifted 12 → 0xDEF12FFF.
medium.deepDive: Same operation on a fresh VA: offset 0xFFF survives, VPN 0xABCDE becomes PFN 0xDEF12. Getting two addresses right in a row confirms the rule is field substitution, not arithmetic. Next the page size changes, forcing recomputation of the split point.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Concatenates VPN and PFN; the VPN must disappear from the PA.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Puts offset in high bits; offset is always low.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Forgets translation entirely; VA ≠ PA when mapped elsewhere.

medium.prompt: VA = 0x12345678 with 8-KB pages. What are VPN and offset?

choices.label: A
choices.body: VPN = 0x1234, offset = 0x5678

choices.label: B
choices.body: VPN = 0x123456, offset = 0x78

choices.label: C
choices.body: VPN = 0x91A2B, offset = 0x1678

choices.label: D
choices.body: VPN = 0x91A2B1C78, offset = 0x0

medium.hint: 2^13 = 8192. Mask the low 13 bits (0x1FFF), don't just cut hex digits.
medium.explanation: 13-bit offset: VPN = VA >> 13 = 0x91A2B, offset = VA & 0x1FFF = 0x1678.
medium.deepDive: 8-KB pages mean 13 offset bits, so split on bits not hex digits: offset = VA & 0x1FFF = 0x1678, VPN = VA >> 13 = 0x91A2B. Because 13 is not a multiple of 4, no clean hex-digit cut exists. This proves the split point is log2(page size), forcing binary masking for non-4KB pages.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Uses a 16-bit (64-KB) split — wrong page size.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Uses an 8-bit split (256-B pages).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Claims page-aligned with zero offset; low bits of 0x5678 are nonzero.

medium.prompt: PTE: valid = 1, present = 1, RW = 0 (read-only). A store hits this page. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Page fault to disk; fetch the page and resume

choices.label: B
choices.body: TLB miss only; walk succeeds silently

choices.label: C
choices.body: Dirty-bit write-back, then allow

choices.label: D
choices.body: Protection fault (segfault); read-only page cannot be written

medium.hint: Two checks in order: is it valid/present? Then: is this ACCESS kind allowed?
medium.explanation: Valid + present but RW = 0 on a store → protection violation, not disk I/O.
medium.deepDive: Validity passed but permission failed: RW = 0 denies stores while allowing loads. Hardware raises a protection fault, not a paging I/O, and the OS typically kills the process or delivers SIGSEGV. Distinguishing permission faults from present-bit page faults is the core debugging skill here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Disk fetch is for present = 0; this page is already resident.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A TLB miss still completes via the walk; a permission violation traps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dirty bit is set BY a successful write, not a precondition for one.

medium.prompt: Distinguish: PTE valid = 1, present = 0 on access. What does the OS do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Valid = 1, present = 0 → legal address swapped out; fault, fetch from disk, resume

choices.label: B
choices.body: Valid = 0, present = 1 → fetch from disk

choices.label: C
choices.body: Valid = 0, present = 0 → fetch from disk and resume

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bigger page tables would avoid this fault

medium.hint: Separate legality (valid) from residency (present). Which combo means swapped?
medium.explanation: Valid says legal; present says resident. Legal + nonresident = page fault with I/O.
medium.deepDive: Valid means the OS promised this VPN to the process; present means it is currently in DRAM. Valid-but-not-present is the classic demand-paging case: block, read from swap/file, set present, retry. Valid = 0 can never be fixed by I/O — it is a program bug.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Impossible combo treated as invalid; present cannot rescue valid = 0.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Valid = 0 means illegal address — no disk read makes it legal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: table size does not affect residency; more entries ≠ more RAM.

medium.prompt: What are the accessed and dirty bits for?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Valid bit, to kill the process faster

choices.label: B
choices.body: Accessed for clock/LRU replacement; dirty to skip write-back of clean pages

choices.label: C
choices.body: Present bit, to index the inode

choices.label: D
choices.body: RW bit, to count internal fragmentation

medium.hint: Which bits let the OS learn recency and avoid useless disk writes?
medium.explanation: Accessed ≈ recency for replacement; dirty ≈ needs write-back on evict.
medium.deepDive: Hardware sets accessed on any touch and dirty on any write; the OS clears them to sample recency. The clock algorithm sweeps checking accessed, and eviction writes back only dirty victims. Without these bits every eviction would need a disk write and replacement would be blind.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Valid decides legality, not replacement policy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real misconception: inodes are file metadata; present tracks DRAM residency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RW controls permission; fragmentation is a sizing issue, not a bit.

medium.prompt: Contrast a segfault vs a page fault in PTE-bit terms.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both resume after disk I/O

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both kill the process immediately

choices.label: C
choices.body: Invalid VPN (valid = 0) → segfault/kill; swapped page (valid = 1, present = 0) → page fault, fetch, resume

choices.label: D
choices.body: The TLB decides which fault it is

medium.hint: Can the OS fix it with a disk read? If yes, which bit pattern allows that?
medium.explanation: Valid = 0 is a bug (segfault); valid + swapped is an I/O event (page fault).
medium.deepDive: The valid bit is the fork: 0 means the program touched an unmapped VPN — unrecoverable, signal or kill. Valid-but-not-present means the OS overcommitted or demand-paged — recoverable via I/O and retry. Confusing them leads to either crashing good programs or endlessly faulting on bad addresses.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Invalid addresses have nothing on disk to fetch; I/O cannot fix a bug.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Swapped pages must not kill — the data exists, just not in RAM.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The TLB caches translations; fault type comes from PTE bits in the walk.

medium.prompt: 32-bit VA, 4-KB pages, 4-byte PTEs. How big is a single-level linear page table?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ~4 KB

choices.label: B
choices.body: ~4 MB

choices.label: C
choices.body: ~4 GB

choices.label: D
choices.body: ~4 TB

medium.hint: First count entries (address space / page size), then multiply by entry size.
medium.explanation: 2^20 entries × 4 B = 4 MiB per address space.
medium.deepDive: Count virtual pages: 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 ≈ 1M, times 4 bytes = 4 MB per process. That exceeds a typical small process's data and is paid even when mostly sparse. This number is the canonical motivation for two-level tables.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is one page, not 1M entries; you forgot to multiply.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the whole address space size, not the table.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Off by 1000×; check powers: 2^20 × 2^2 = 2^22.

medium.prompt: Same 32-bit VA but 16-KB pages, 4-B PTEs. Table size?

choices.label: B
choices.body: ~4 MB — page size never matters

choices.label: C
choices.body: ~16 KB

medium.hint: Recompute entry count with 16-KB (2^14) pages. What shrinks and what grows?
medium.explanation: Fewer, bigger pages → fewer entries → smaller table but more frag.
medium.deepDive: Larger pages mean fewer VPNs: 2^32/2^14 = 2^18 = 256K entries × 4 B = 1 MB. Table size shrinks, but each last-page waste grows — the classic table-size vs internal-fragmentation trade. This tension explains why systems use multiple page sizes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Page size directly sets entry count; it always matters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Confuses one page-table page with the whole table.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Multiplies instead of dividing by page size.

medium.prompt: A heap grows sparsely with holes (mmap gaps). Which scheme handles it with least relocation pain?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Segmentation, for fixed-size placement

choices.label: B
choices.body: Linear paging, for tiny tables on sparse spaces

choices.label: C
choices.body: Paging, for sparse heap growth via valid bits without moving other regions

choices.label: D
choices.body: No translation, for speed

medium.hint: Which scheme can punch invalid holes at 4-KB granularity with no relocation?
medium.explanation: Per-page valid bits express sparsity while frames scatter freely.
medium.deepDive: A sparse heap has valid pages scattered among invalid ones; paging marks holes invalid at page granularity with no data movement. Segmentation would need many tiny segments or suffer external gaps. The remaining pain is table cost for holes, fixed by multilevel tables next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Segments are variable-sized — that is the source of placement pain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Linear tables are biggest exactly when sparse; multilevel fixes that.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No translation removes protection and sparse allocation entirely.

medium.prompt: Two processes share libc code but keep data private. Which fits naturally?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Paging, sharing at 4-KB granularity with per-PTE protections

choices.label: B
choices.body: Segmentation, because segments cannot be shared

choices.label: C
choices.body: Paging via shared inodes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Segmentation, because fixed pages cannot be shared

medium.hint: Do you need whole-region or per-page control to share code but not data?
medium.explanation: Alias shared code PFNs read-only into each table; keep data private.
medium.deepDive: Libraries need some pages shared read-only/executable and others private writable. Paging aliases individual PFNs into each process with different RW bits, impossible at whole-segment granularity without carving many segments. This fine-grained sharing is why modern systems page shared libraries.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Segments can be shared, just coarsely — the granularity is the issue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real misconception: inodes do not alias memory; PTEs alias PFNs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pages are the shared unit here; the statement inverts both schemes.

medium.prompt: What sparsity benefit does per-segment page tables (hybrid) give over one linear table?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It removes page faults

choices.label: B
choices.body: It makes pages variable-sized

choices.label: C
choices.body: It stores the PID in the VA

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unused segments need no page table; sparse regions cost nothing

medium.hint: If each segment has its own table, what do you pay for an empty segment?
medium.explanation: Pay tables only for live segments; holes between segments are free.
medium.deepDive: Each segment owns a table sized to that segment only, so a tiny stack gets a tiny table and an unused segment gets none. Bounds checks catch cross-segment bugs before the page lookup. The price is a segment check plus a page walk on every access.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Real misconception: no table design removes faults; residency still matters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Pages stay fixed-size; segments stay variable — hybrid combines, not blends.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real misconception: PID stays in OS registers, not VA bits.

medium.prompt: 4-KB pages. A segment holds 9000 bytes. How much internal fragmentation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 0 bytes — 9000 is a page multiple

choices.label: C
choices.body: 9000 bytes

choices.label: D
choices.body: 4096 bytes always

medium.hint: How many 4-KB pages cover 9000 bytes? Subtract.
medium.deepDive: Round 9000 up to 3 × 4096 = 12288; waste = 3288 in the tail page. Only the last page wastes — full pages are fully used. This single-segment example generalizes to per-segment waste summed across code/stack/heap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 9000 / 4096 ≈ 2.2, so 3 pages — not exact.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the data size, not the waste; waste is allocated-minus-used.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Waste varies with size mod page; it is not one fixed page.

medium.prompt: 4-KB pages. Code = 5000 B, heap = 7000 B, stack = 3000 B. Total internal waste?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 4096 bytes

choices.label: B
choices.body: 12288 bytes

choices.label: C
choices.body: ~5.4 KB (5480 B: 3192 + 1192 + 1096 across three segments)

choices.label: D
choices.body: 0 bytes with paging

medium.hint: Compute each segment's last-page tail separately, then add.
medium.explanation: Sum per-segment tails: 3192 + 1192 + 1096 = 5480 B (≈5.4 KB).
medium.deepDive: Code: ceil(5000/4096)=2 pages waste 3192. Heap: ceil(7000/4096)=2 waste 1192. Stack: ceil(3000/4096)=1 waste 1096... total ≈ 3192+1192+1096 = 5480? Recompute: 8192−5000=3192; 8192−7000=1192; 4096−3000=1096; sum=5480 bytes ≈ 5.35 KB. Rounded choice ~5.6 KB captures method; exact sum 5480 B. Waste scales with segment count, averaging half a page each.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is one page, not three tails summed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is 3 pages allocated for one segment — wrong aggregation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Paging always has last-page waste unless every segment is page-aligned.

medium.prompt: Set up PTEs so parent + child share code but not data.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shared code: same PFN, RW = 0 in both; private data: different PFNs, RW = 1

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shared code: same VPN in both tables; data likewise

choices.label: C
choices.body: Shared code via shared PTE entry; data via inode

choices.label: D
choices.body: All pages same PFN for efficiency

medium.hint: Which number must match for sharing — VPN or PFN? Which bits differ?
medium.explanation: Alias PFN for code (R/O both), split PFNs for data (R/W private).
medium.deepDive: Each process keeps its own VPN numbering; aliasing happens at the PFN value. Code entries point at one frame read-only so neither writer can corrupt the other. Data entries point at distinct frames writable. Fork with copy-on-write starts shared then splits on write, using dirty/RW tricks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: VPNs are per-process indexes; sharing means equal PFN, not equal VPN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: PTEs are never shared across tables; inodes don't map memory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sharing data PFNs would corrupt both processes on write.

medium.prompt: 48-bit VA, 4-KB pages, 8-byte PTEs. Linear table size?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 4 KB

choices.label: B
choices.body: 4 MB

choices.label: C
choices.body: 4 GB

choices.label: D
choices.body: 512 GB (2^36 entries × 8 B)

medium.hint: Entries = 2^(48−12). Multiply by 8. Sanity-check vs RAM size.
medium.explanation: 2^(48−12) = 2^36 entries × 8 B ≈ 512 GiB — impossible as one array.
medium.deepDive: 48-bit VA with 4-KB pages gives 36 VPN bits = 68B virtual pages. At 8 bytes each the linear table is ~512 GB per process — orders beyond DRAM. This impossibility proof is why x86-64 uses 4-level trees where unallocated subtrees need no memory. Sizing is the bridge from mechanism to multilevel design.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Off by ~10^8; that is a couple pages of table.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the 32-bit answer; 16 more VA bits multiply by 65536.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Confuses address-space size slice with table size.

medium.prompt: TLB miss, but PTE present=1. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Walk the page table in memory, install the translation in the TLB, retry

choices.label: B
choices.body: Read the page from disk and kill the TLB entry

choices.label: C
choices.body: Flush the entire address space and restart the process

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ask the disk controller for the VPN mapping

medium.hint: Check the present bit in the PTE found by the walk: what does present=1 imply?
medium.explanation: A TLB miss on a present page just walks the table and refills the TLB; no disk is involved.
medium.deepDive: A TLB miss with present=1 is the common case: translation exists in the table but was not cached. Hardware (x86) or OS walks the table, refills the TLB entry, and retries without disk I/O. Only present=0 escalates to a fault. Confusing miss with fault overestimates disk traffic by orders of magnitude.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Disk is only for present=0; here the page is already in RAM.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Restarting is absurd; a single refill fixes a miss in nanoseconds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Disks know nothing of VPNs; the page table is the authority.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

medium.prompt: Why flush the TLB on context switch, and how do ASIDs change that?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TLB entries are never flushed; stale mappings are harmless

choices.label: B
choices.body: ASIDs make every access go to disk

choices.label: C
choices.body: ASIDs remove the need for page tables

choices.label: D
choices.body: Without ASIDs the OS must flush the TLB on context switch to avoid using another process's mappings

medium.hint: If two processes both use VPN 5, what stops process B from using A's cached translation?
medium.explanation: ASIDs tag TLB entries per process so switches skip the flush; without them a flush is mandatory.
medium.deepDive: VPN 10 means different PFNs in different processes, so untagged TLB entries are ambiguous across switches. Without an address-space tag the OS flushes all entries on switch, paying cold misses. ASIDs tag each entry with a process ID so entries can coexist; only same-ASID or global (kernel) entries match. Flushes are still needed on munmap/mprotect via shootdown.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Stale mappings corrupt memory; that is exactly why the flush exists.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ASIDs only add a tag compare; they never touch disk.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tables remain authoritative; ASIDs only disambiguate the cache.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

medium.prompt: TLB=2ns, mem=100ns, two-level tables, hit 90%. EAT?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 112 ns

choices.label: B
choices.body: 122 ns

choices.label: C
choices.body: 302 ns

choices.label: D
choices.body: 102 ns

medium.hint: How many memory reads does one miss add when there are two table levels?
medium.explanation: Two-level miss costs two reads, so EAT is 122 ns.
medium.deepDive: A two-level miss pays two table reads instead of one. Base cost is TLB plus data, and the 10 percent miss rate adds about 20 on average. Total is 122, showing deeper tables scale the miss penalty linearly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 112 counts only one table read on a miss, forgetting the second level.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 302 is the miss-only cost, not the weighted average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 102 is the hit-only cost with no miss penalty.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

medium.prompt: Base EAT 111ns plus 0.01% faults x 8ms disk. Approx EAT?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 100 ns

choices.label: B
choices.body: ~911 ns (111 base + ~800 disk expectation)

choices.label: C
choices.body: 8 ms for every access

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1 ns

medium.hint: Weight the disk cost by its tiny probability, then compare to the ns-scale base.
medium.explanation: Even rare faults dominate: about 800 ns of disk expectation plus 111 ns base gives about 911 ns.
medium.deepDive: Weight the 8 ms disk by its tiny probability, adding about 800 ns of expected cost. Add the 111 ns memory base for about 911 ns total. The lesson is leverage: a one-in-ten-thousand fault dominates EAT when disk is far slower than RAM.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 100ns ignores both TLB and the disk expectation entirely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 8ms charges disk to every access instead of 1 in 10,000.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1ns is just the TLB lookup, dropping data, walks, and disk.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

medium.prompt: 4GB space but program uses 2MB code + 1MB heap + 8KB stack. How many second-level tables?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only 2 second-level tables (for code and stack/heap ends), rest invalid in directory

choices.label: B
choices.body: All 1024 second-level tables fully allocated

choices.label: C
choices.body: No page tables at all

choices.label: D
choices.body: One PTE per byte of address space

medium.hint: Map code/heap/stack to 4MB chunks: how many chunks actually contain valid pages?
medium.explanation: A sparse program touches few 4MB chunks, so only those second-level tables exist.
medium.deepDive: Code at the bottom plus heap growing up and stack at the top touch perhaps two 4MB chunks. The directory marks the middle ~1022 entries invalid, so no frames back them. Cost is 2 tables (8KB) plus directory, versus 4MB for a flat table. Sparsity converts directly to saved frames.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Full allocation is the flat-table cost multilevels avoid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Valid pages still need PTEs somewhere; tables cannot vanish.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: PTEs cover pages (4KB), not bytes; per-byte would be astronomically larger.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

medium.prompt: What do 2MB huge pages change vs 4KB pages?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Huge pages eliminate page tables and the TLB

choices.label: B
choices.body: Huge pages increase TLB misses

choices.label: C
choices.body: Huge pages make internal fragmentation impossible

choices.label: D
choices.body: One 2MB huge page covers 512x 4KB pages with one TLB entry, shrinking tables and TLB pressure

medium.hint: Compare coverage per entry: how many 4KB PTEs fit in 2MB?
medium.explanation: Huge pages collapse 512 small mappings into one entry, cutting table size and TLB misses at the cost of fragmentation.
medium.deepDive: A 2MB page uses one directory entry pointing directly to data, replacing 512 PTEs and covering with one TLB slot what needed 512 slots. Tables still exist (directory plus huge PTEs) and faults still occur. The price is internal waste: a 10KB segment in a 2MB page wastes ~2MB. Use huge pages for large dense regions, small pages for the rest.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Tables and TLB remain; huge pages just use fewer, larger entries -- they remove nothing entirely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fewer, larger entries reduce TLB pressure, not increase it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Larger pages worsen internal fragmentation for small segments.

medium.prompt: OPT policy, 3 frames, refs 1,2,3,4,1,2,5. Which victim when 4 faults?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Evict the page that will be used farthest in the future

choices.label: B
choices.body: Evict a random page

choices.label: C
choices.body: Evict the most recently used page

choices.label: D
choices.body: Evict the least recently used page

medium.hint: If you could see the future trace, which resident page could you afford to lose longest?
medium.explanation: OPT (MIN) evicts the page reused farthest in the future; it is optimal but needs future knowledge.
medium.deepDive: OPT looks into the known future of the trace and evicts the page whose next use is latest (or never). On 1,2,3,4,1,2,5 with 3 frames it keeps 1,2 and evicts 3 for 4, giving the provable minimum faults. It is unimplementable online but sets the bar every real policy is measured against. Do not confuse optimal with practical.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Random is a baseline that ignores both past and future.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Evicting MRU is pathological here; it discards 1,2 just before reuse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: LRU uses the past as a proxy; OPT uses the actual future -- different victims on this trace.

medium.prompt: How do FIFO and LRU differ on refs 1,2,3,1,4 with 3 frames?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Identical victims on every trace

choices.label: B
choices.body: FIFO evicts the oldest arrival, LRU evicts the least-recently-touched; they diverge when a page is old but recently reused

choices.label: C
choices.body: FIFO tracks reuse, LRU tracks arrival

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither ever faults after warmup

medium.hint: Replay 1,2,3,1,4: what does the hit to 1 change under each policy?
medium.explanation: FIFO ignores hits; LRU reorders on hits, so an old-but-reused page survives under LRU but not FIFO.
medium.deepDive: Take 1,2,3,1,4 with 3 frames: at 4, FIFO evicts 1 (oldest) despite its reuse, LRU evicts 2 (untouched since start). Hits update LRU order but never move FIFO. That single difference -- hits matter for LRU, not FIFO -- explains Belady and the performance gap. When hand-running, move entries on hits only for LRU.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: They agree on sequential scans but split as soon as reuse appears.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: This swaps the definitions; FIFO=arrival order, LRU=recency order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Any cold or capacity miss still faults under both.
