medium.prompt: Which is a concrete Belady demonstration?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 3 frames: 9 faults, 4 frames: 10 faults on 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5

choices.label: B
choices.body: 4 frames always beats 3 frames for FIFO

choices.label: C
choices.body: FIFO is a stack algorithm

choices.label: D
choices.body: LRU shows the anomaly on this trace

medium.hint: Hand-run both frame counts: where does the 4-frame run keep the wrong pages?
medium.explanation: This classic string makes FIFO worse with 4 frames than 3, proving more frames can hurt FIFO.
medium.deepDive: The textbook Belady string makes FIFO fault 9 times with 3 frames but 10 with 4: the extra frame pins pages 1,2 early, shifting the eviction wave so later 3,4 miss where they had hit. More capacity changes timing, not just capacity. LRU on the same string improves monotonically. Memorize this string as the canonical counterexample.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is exactly what Belady disproves for FIFO.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: FIFO is not stack; LRU/OPT are -- stack means more frames never hurts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: LRU never exhibits Belady; only FIFO/Random do.

medium.prompt: Clock with 3 frames, ref bits [1,1,0], hand at frame 0, fault on page 4. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Evict the page the hand points to regardless of ref bit

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sort all pages by exact last-use timestamp

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always evict the most recently used page

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sweep: clear ref=1 to 0 and advance; evict the first ref=0 page found

medium.hint: What should the hand do when it sees a page that was recently used (ref=1)?
medium.explanation: Clock gives ref=1 pages a second chance and evicts the first ref=0 page the hand finds.
medium.deepDive: Clock keeps a circular hand over frames. On a fault it clears each ref=1 entry to 0 and advances, then evicts the first ref=0 entry it finds. Hardware sets ref on access while software only clears it. Simulating hand position plus bits across faults is the exam skill.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Ignoring ref bits reduces Clock to FIFO, losing its LRU approximation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Exact timestamps are LRU, not Clock; Clock uses one bit per page.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Evicting MRU is the opposite of any recency policy.

medium.prompt: What is a working set and how does it predict thrashing?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The number of TLB entries

choices.label: C
choices.body: Total swap space on disk

choices.label: D
choices.body: The set of pages in the last W references; if it exceeds frames, faulting spikes

choices.label: B
choices.body: All pages ever touched by the process

medium.hint: Over what horizon should recency be measured: one access, all history, or a recent window?
medium.explanation: Working set = distinct pages in recent window W; overflow means thrashing.
medium.deepDive: Denning's working set W(t,W) is the distinct pages referenced in the last W accesses. Sum across runnable processes: if it fits, fault rate stays low; overflow it and you thrash. The window W is the knob: too small underestimates locality, too large over-admits. Fault-frequency schemes track this implicitly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TLB size is unrelated; working sets are about resident data pages.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: All-history grows forever and never captures current locality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Swap size bounds capacity, not the locality that predicts faults.

medium.prompt: How do you recognize thrashing from system counters?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Disk I/O falls and CPU rises

choices.label: B
choices.body: Paging I/O spikes while CPU utilization collapses

choices.label: C
choices.body: TLB hit rate hits 100%

choices.label: D
choices.body: Page tables shrink to zero

medium.hint: If every process blocks on page-ins, what happens to ready-queue CPU usage?
medium.explanation: Thrashing shows high paging with low CPU: processes queue on disk instead of running.
medium.deepDive: The thrashing signature on a monitor is unmistakable: page-in/out storms plus idle CPU, because every timeslice blocks on disk. New students expect high CPU; the opposite happens. The OS response is to suspend a process (reduce multiprogramming) until working sets fit again. Adding RAM helps only if it covers the overflow.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This describes a healthy warm cache, the inverse of thrashing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TLB hits cannot fix missing resident pages; faulting bypasses the TLB.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tables persist regardless; thrashing is about data residency.

medium.prompt: Why does the dirty bit matter when evicting to swap?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Evicting a dirty page needs a disk writeback; a clean page can be dropped and re-read later

choices.label: B
choices.body: Clean pages need writeback, dirty pages do not

choices.label: C
choices.body: Dirty and clean cost the same

choices.label: D
choices.body: Present bit decides dirtiness

medium.hint: Which page's frame contents exist nowhere else on disk?
medium.explanation: Dirty evictions pay a write plus later read; clean evictions skip the write.
medium.deepDive: The dirty bit records stores since page-in. Clean eviction just overwrites the frame since the data exists on disk already. Dirty eviction must first write the frame to swap, which is why replacement prefers clean victims.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This inverts reality; dirty means modified and must be saved.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Equal cost ignores the extra writeback I/O for dirty pages.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Present tracks residency; dirty tracks modification -- separate PTE bits.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

medium.prompt: What is the full PTE/TLB dance on a swap fault?

choices.label: A
choices.body: PTE present=1 means on disk

choices.label: B
choices.body: Faults never update the TLB

choices.label: C
choices.body: Swap slot is allocated after the page is freed

choices.label: D
choices.body: On fault: trap, allocate/victimize frame (write back if dirty), read from swap/file, set PTE present with new PFN, flush stale TLB, retry

medium.hint: Sequence the PTE transitions: what must be true before the retrying instruction can succeed?
medium.explanation: Fault handling = trap, make a frame, page in, install present PTE, invalidate TLB, retry.
medium.deepDive: Follow the PTE lifecycle: present=0 with a swap/disk locator traps; the pager frees a frame (writing back only if dirty), issues the disk read, then flips present=1 with the new PFN and clears the stale TLB entry. Retry then hits. Present=1 versus 0 is the resident question; dirty is the writeback question. Keep the two bits orthogonal.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Present=1 means resident in RAM; present=0 means consult swap/disk info.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Refilled TLB entries are the whole point of retry; otherwise you walk every time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The swap home must exist before eviction so dirty victims have somewhere to go.

medium.prompt: What happens on a COW write fault?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Copy the whole address space at fork

choices.label: C
choices.body: Trap on write to a shared read-only page: alloc frame, copy contents, remap private writable, resume

choices.label: D
choices.body: Merge parent and child page tables permanently

choices.label: B
choices.body: Send the faulting page to swap

medium.hint: Which single page needs duplicating, and what PTE change makes the retry succeed?
medium.explanation: A COW write fault privately duplicates just the faulted page and remaps it writable.
medium.deepDive: The write fault path: MMU faults on store to a COW (read-only, refcount>1) page. The OS allocates a frame, memcpy's 4KB, decrements the shared count, installs a private RW PTE for the faulter, and flushes that TLB entry. Other sharers keep the original. Cost is one page, not the address space, which is why fork is fast.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Whole-copy is the eager cost COW exists to avoid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tables stay per-process; only the shared frames overlap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Swap is for eviction, not for a RAM-resident shared page.

medium.prompt: How does an inverted page table differ from a forward table?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One PTE per virtual page of every process (size ~ address space)

choices.label: B
choices.body: One entry per disk block

choices.label: C
choices.body: One entry per physical frame, found by hashing (PID,VPN)

choices.label: D
choices.body: No page tables at all, only a TLB

medium.hint: What scales better when virtual space dwarfs physical RAM: indexing by VPN or by frame?
medium.explanation: An inverted table has one entry per frame, located by hashing the (process,VPN) pair.
medium.deepDive: Inverted tables flip the index: instead of per-process VPN-indexed tables, one system table has one entry per frame storing (pid,vpn) plus chain pointer. Lookup hashes (pid,vpn) and walks the collision chain. Size scales with RAM, not virtual space -- ideal for huge 64-bit spaces. Sharing and hashing collisions are the complications forward tables avoid.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes forward per-process tables, the opposite of inverted.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Disk blocks are tracked by swap maps, not page tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The TLB still needs its backing authority; inverted tables are that authority.

medium.prompt: One thread of a 4-thread process overflows its stack and faults. What happens to the other threads?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the overflowing thread crashes; others continue normally

choices.label: B
choices.body: The overflow is silently ignored because stacks are virtual

choices.label: C
choices.body: The whole process crashes, killing all its threads at once

choices.label: D
choices.body: The kernel moves the overflowing stack into a new address space

medium.hint: Ask what protection boundary exists: between processes or between threads of one process?
medium.explanation: Threads share one address space with no isolation, so a fatal stack fault tears down the entire process.
medium.deepDive: All threads live in one address space with no isolation between them. A stack overflow corrupts adjacent memory or hits an unmapped guard and faults the process. The OS cannot kill just one thread because protection is per-process. This is the cost of sharing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: There is no per-thread isolation to contain the fault; that isolation exists only between processes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Overflows are faults, not ignorable; stacks are bounded virtual regions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The kernel never migrates a stack to a new address space; threads stay in one space.

medium.prompt: Why do multithreaded processes give each thread a fixed-size stack instead of one freely growing stack?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each stack is a fixed-size region; unbounded growth would collide with another thread's stack or heap

choices.label: B
choices.body: Thread stacks grow into separate address spaces on demand

choices.label: C
choices.body: The kernel merges all thread stacks into one growable stack

choices.label: D
choices.body: Stacks need no bounds because virtual memory is infinite

medium.hint: Picture one stack growing freely versus four stacks in one room: what stops them colliding?
medium.explanation: Multiple stacks share one address space, so each must be bounded to avoid colliding with a neighbor.
medium.deepDive: A single-threaded process can let its one stack grow toward the heap freely. With many threads, each stack needs its own bounded region carved from the address space. Letting one grow without limit would overwrite a neighbor. Hence pthreads default to fixed sizes like 8 MB.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Threads never get separate address spaces; all stacks live in the one process space.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Merging stacks would mix call frames; each thread must keep its own call chain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Virtual memory is finite and shared; unbounded growth guarantees collision.

medium.prompt: In the M:1 (many user threads to one kernel thread) model, one user thread calls blocking read(). What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the calling thread blocks; others keep running in parallel

choices.label: B
choices.body: The block is retried automatically on another CPU

choices.label: C
choices.body: The kernel converts the block into a yield that never sleeps

choices.label: D
choices.body: The single kernel thread blocks, so every user thread of the process stalls

medium.hint: Count kernel-visible entities: if there is exactly one and it BLOCKs, what can the kernel run from this process?
medium.explanation: With only one kernel thread, a blocking syscall deschedules the entire process and all its user threads.
medium.deepDive: M:1 multiplexes all user threads onto one kernel entity. The kernel sees only that one entity, so when it blocks on I/O the whole process leaves the run queue. No other user thread can be scheduled until the I/O completes. This is why M:1 cannot overlap blocking I/O.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is 1:1 behavior; M:1 has no other kernel thread to keep running.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The kernel cannot migrate a blocked entity to another CPU; BLOCKED means not runnable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Blocking still sleeps; M:1 has no mechanism to keep user threads running through it.

medium.prompt: In the 1:1 model with 4 threads, one thread blocks on read(). What do the other three do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the calling thread BLOCKs; the kernel schedules the other kernel threads on remaining CPUs

choices.label: B
choices.body: All threads BLOCK because they share one program counter

choices.label: C
choices.body: The whole address space is swapped out until the I/O completes

choices.label: D
choices.body: The kernel never switches; the blocking thread spins until I/O finishes

medium.hint: Ask how many kernel threads can be RUNNABLE while one is BLOCKED in a 1:1 process with 4 threads.
medium.explanation: 1:1 gives each thread its own kernel schedulable state, so BLOCKED applies per-thread, not per-process.
medium.deepDive: In 1:1 each user thread is independently schedulable by the kernel. Blocking affects only the thread that issued the syscall. Other threads stay RUNNABLE and run on other cores or after a switch. This isolation is exactly what M:1 lacks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Threads have separate PCs; sharing an address space does not merge control flow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Blocking one thread never swaps the whole address space; others keep running.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The kernel does switch away from BLOCKED threads; spinning would waste the CPU.

medium.prompt: main creates a worker thread, does not join it, and returns immediately. What can go wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The child threads keep running as orphans after main returns

choices.label: B
choices.body: main returning exits the process, which can kill peer threads before they finish

choices.label: C
choices.body: main returning automatically joins all threads and saves their results

choices.label: D
choices.body: Threads are unaffected because each has its own address space

medium.hint: Recall wait() for processes: what happens to needed results if the parent never waits? Map that to threads.
medium.explanation: Process exit destroys all threads, so main must pthread_join (or pthread_exit) instead of returning early.
medium.deepDive: Returning from main ends the process unless pthread_exit is used or threads are joined. Peer threads share that process and vanish with it. So missing join plus early main return is a classic lost-work bug. The fix is to join every thread whose result or side effect you need.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Threads are not orphaned like processes; they die with their process.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Return from main never auto-joins; only explicit join collects results.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Threads share the address space, so process exit takes them all down.

medium.prompt: A loop does for(i=0;i<5;i++) pthread_create(&t[i],NULL,fn,&i); where fn prints *(int*)arg. What output is likely?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each thread safely gets its own copy of i because integers are copied on create

choices.label: B
choices.body: The program always prints 0 1 2 3 4 in order

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threads can all read the same final i (e.g., all print 5) because they share the loop variable's address

choices.label: D
choices.body: The compiler rejects passing &i since stacks are private

medium.hint: Ask when each thread dereferences the pointer versus when the loop increments i: who is ordered?
medium.explanation: All threads share the same &i, so by the time they run the loop has usually advanced i to its final value.
medium.deepDive: Passing &i shares one mutable location with every thread and no ordering. The loop advances i while threads dereference the pointer whenever scheduled. Most threads then observe the final value. The fix is one private value per thread, such as a heap slot or cast integer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Integers are not copied; only the pointer value is copied, still pointing at shared i.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No ordering exists between loop and threads, so in-order output is not guaranteed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Passing a stack address compiles fine; the bug is sharing it, not the type.

medium.prompt: Two threads each block on a 10-ms disk read on a single core. Run concurrently, roughly how long for both to finish?

choices.label: A
choices.body: About 10 ms, because the two 10-ms waits overlap

choices.label: B
choices.body: About 20 ms, because threads cannot overlap waits on one core

choices.label: C
choices.body: About 5 ms, because two threads halve each I/O latency

choices.label: D
choices.body: About 0 ms, because blocking I/O becomes nonblocking with threads

medium.hint: Draw two 10-ms waits: serial stacks them end to end, overlapped stacks them side by side. Which length counts?
medium.explanation: Concurrent BLOCKED waits overlap in time, so elapsed time is near the max (10 ms), not the sum.
medium.deepDive: Serial code pays 10 plus 10 ms of idle waiting. With two threads one waits while the other waits, so elapsed time is roughly max, not sum. CPU work still serializes on one core but I/O waits overlap. That max-versus-sum distinction is the whole overlap calculation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Overlap works on one core because the core is idle during BLOCKED waits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Latency of each I/O stays 10 ms; overlap hides waiting but never shortens one I/O.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Threads do not make blocking nonblocking; each thread still sleeps 10 ms.

medium.prompt: A single-core CPU runs a CPU-bound loop. Will 4 threads finish it faster than 1 thread?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes: N threads make a CPU-bound loop N times faster on one core

choices.label: B
choices.body: Yes, because context switches add extra compute power

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes, because each thread gets its own CPU cache that adds up

choices.label: D
choices.body: No: one CPU does the same total compute; threads only add switch overhead

medium.hint: Ask what the CPU does during a pure compute loop: does it ever idle for a peer thread to steal?
medium.explanation: Single-core compute throughput is fixed; threading a CPU-bound loop cannot create more cycles.
medium.deepDive: Threads help when the CPU would otherwise idle during I/O. A CPU-bound loop never idles, so there is no idle time to reclaim. Splitting it across threads on one core just adds context-switch cost. Speedup for CPU-bound work needs more cores, not more threads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: More threads do not speed CPU-bound work on one core; total instructions are unchanged.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Switches cost cycles; they never create compute power.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Caches do not add CPUs; sharing one core still serializes execution.

medium.prompt: Two threads run counter++ on shared int counter = 0 with no locks. Why can the final value be 1 instead of 2?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One C increment is atomic, so no interleaving is possible

choices.label: B
choices.body: counter++ compiles to load, add, store, so two threads can interleave and lose an update

choices.label: C
choices.body: The compiler serializes thread accesses to globals automatically

choices.label: D
choices.body: Interleaving is impossible because the kernel never preempts threads

medium.hint: Expand counter++ into assembly: what three steps must happen, and where could a switch slip in?
medium.explanation: Increment is three steps; a thread switch between load and store lets both threads write back the same value.
medium.deepDive: At the machine level increment reads memory, modifies a register, and writes back. A preemption between load and store lets another thread load the same old value. Both then store old plus one, losing one increment. This load-add-store window is the classic race to picture.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: C increments are not atomic; they are load-add-store sequences.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The compiler adds no synchronization unless you use atomics or locks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The kernel does preempt threads via timer interrupts; switches can land anywhere.

medium.prompt: Two threads each do counter++ 1000 times on shared counter starting at 0, no locks. What final values are possible?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always 2000, because increments never interfere

choices.label: B
choices.body: At most 2000 but possibly less, because paired load-add-store sequences can overwrite each other

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exactly 1000, because threads take turns perfectly

choices.label: D
choices.body: More than 2000, because threads duplicate increments

medium.hint: If two increments overlap so both store old+1, how many net increments appear? Extend to 1000 pairs.
medium.explanation: Overlapping increments can collapse, so the result is between 1000 and 2000, often below 2000.
medium.deepDive: Each lost interleaving collapses two increments into one visible update. With 1000 per thread the result ranges from 1000 up to 2000 depending on overlap. It can never exceed 2000 since no update is duplicated. This range is the signature of a lost-update race.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 2000 occurs only with no overlap; any overlapping pair loses one update.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Turn-taking is not enforced; the scheduler interleaves arbitrarily.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Increments are never duplicated; the error only loses updates.

medium.prompt: Each of 2 requests needs a 20-ms blocking read. Compare serial versus 2-threaded total time on one core.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Serial: 40 ms; overlapped: ~20 ms, because waits coincide

choices.label: B
choices.body: Serial: 20 ms; overlapped: 40 ms, because threads slow I/O

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both take 40 ms because the kernel never switches during I/O

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both take 10 ms because threads divide each wait by 2

medium.hint: Sketch time left to right: serial waits sit end to end; threaded waits stack vertically. Compare lengths.
medium.explanation: Serial waits add (20+20) while overlapped waits coincide, costing roughly one wait.
medium.deepDive: Two 20-ms blocking reads in sequence cost 40 ms of mostly idle time. Two threads let both devices wait simultaneously, so elapsed time tracks one wait. The CPU does almost nothing in either case. This timeline picture generalizes to servers hiding hundreds of concurrent waits.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Threads never slow I/O; serial math is 40 and overlap can only shrink it toward 20.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The kernel does switch away from BLOCKED threads; that switch is the whole win.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Each wait stays 20 ms; threads overlap waits rather than splitting one wait.

medium.prompt: What is the goal of the M:N (hybrid) threading model?

choices.label: A
choices.body: M:N is identical to M:1 and cannot use multiple CPUs

choices.label: B
choices.body: M:N forbids blocking syscalls entirely

choices.label: C
choices.body: M:N gives each user thread its own process

choices.label: D
choices.body: M:N maps M user threads onto N kernel threads to balance parallelism with low switch cost

medium.hint: Ask what each extreme gives: M:1 cheap switches but no parallelism, 1:1 parallelism but costly. What would combine them?
medium.explanation: M:N multiplexes many user threads over a smaller pool of kernel threads to get parallelism with cheaper switches.
medium.deepDive: M:N wants 1:1 style parallelism using fewer kernel entities plus M:1 style cheap user-level switches. The runtime multiplexes user threads over a pool of kernel threads sized near core count. Blocking handling and scheduling get complex, which is why most systems settled on 1:1. It remains the conceptual bridge between the two extremes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: M:N targets multiprocessor parallelism, unlike M:1 which is stuck on one kernel thread.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: M:N must handle blocking specially, not forbid it; that handling is its hard part.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: User threads still share one address space; separate processes would abandon threads.

medium.prompt: Profiling shows a mutex held across counter increment + disk log serializes 32 threads. What is the principled fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Move the file write inside the lock to make the region bigger and safer.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shrink the lock to cover only the shared counter increment; keep I/O outside.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Duplicate the counter so each thread has its own lock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Remove the lock and use a sleep to avoid the race.

medium.hint: Which lines actually need mutual exclusion, and which just ride along holding the lock?
medium.explanation: Keep only the shared-state update inside; bigger critical sections directly reduce parallel throughput.
medium.deepDive: Throughput under a lock is bounded by the length of the critical section: every extra instruction inside serializes all contenders. Shrinking to the minimal shared update restores overlap of slow I/O while preserving the invariant. Duplicating state or sleeping neither protects the shared update nor removes the serialization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Bigger regions serialize more, hurting throughput.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Separate counters change semantics unless merged properly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sleep does not make the update atomic.

medium.prompt: After shrinking a critical section, throughput doubles. What can you conclude?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It guarantees the program uses all cores equally.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It proves the code has no races.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It means contention dropped but correctness still needs lock-discipline review.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It means the lock can now be removed.

medium.hint: Does speed prove every path holds the lock, or only that holders wait less?
medium.explanation: Faster only means less serialization; correctness still requires verifying every shared access is locked.
medium.deepDive: Shorter hold times reduce queueing, so throughput rises — but performance tells nothing about whether every shared access is covered. Correctness requires checking that all paths touching the invariant hold the right lock. Removing the lock on performance grounds reintroduces the original race.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Core balance depends on work partitioning, not just lock length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Only a discipline audit proves absence of races.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The lock is still what makes it correct.

medium.prompt: On multicore, a lock is held for ~50ns with low contention. Spin (TAS) or block?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spin with TAS when the wait is short and contenders stay scheduled on other cores.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always block in the kernel, even for a 10-instruction hold time.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Spin whenever single-core, because preemption helps spinning.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Spin while holding another spinlock indefinitely.

medium.hint: Compare the expected wait (nanoseconds vs milliseconds) against the cost of a context switch.
medium.explanation: Spin only for short waits with the holder running elsewhere; otherwise the context-switch cost of blocking is cheaper.
medium.deepDive: Spinning avoids context-switch cost (microseconds) when the holder runs concurrently on another core and releases within nanoseconds. Blocking wins when the wait exceeds a switch or the holder is preempted, since spinning then burns a whole quantum. Single-core spinning is pure waste because the holder cannot run until the spinner is descheduled.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A kernel switch costs far more than a 50ns wait.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: On one core the spinner prevents the holder from running.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Nested indefinite spinning risks deadlock and wastes cycles.

medium.prompt: A thread holding a TAS spinlock is preempted on a loaded machine. What happens to spinners?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spinning becomes faster because the preempted holder gets priority.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Nothing changes; TAS spinning is immune to scheduling.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The lock becomes fair automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The spinner burns its whole quantum while the holder cannot run — use blocking or yield on contention.

medium.hint: If the lock holder is descheduled, what does each spinning cycle accomplish?
medium.explanation: Preempted holder + spinners = wasted quanta; blocking lets the holder run again.
medium.deepDive: TAS spinlocks assume the holder is making progress on another core. If the holder is descheduled, every spinner wastes its quantum waiting for a thread that cannot run — the classic preemption-while-holding pathology. Blocking locks (or at minimum yield/backoff) return the CPU so the holder can be rescheduled, trading a switch for useful progress.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Preemption makes spinning strictly worse, not faster.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Spinlock performance is highly schedule-sensitive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TAS is unfair; arrival order is not honored.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

medium.prompt: To raise list concurrency, you move from one global lock to per-node locks for sorted insert. What is the safe pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lock the whole traversal plus update with one global lock — required for correctness.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hand-over-hand: hold predecessor and current locks, release predecessor after securing current; keep a global acquisition order.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Lock only the head node; the rest cannot change concurrently.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Lock nodes in whatever order the traversal encounters them, varying per thread.

medium.hint: How can a thread advance without ever leaving the node it is about to modify unprotected?
medium.explanation: Couple two locks while stepping forward under a fixed order: parallel yet safe from races and AB-BA deadlock.
medium.deepDive: Hand-over-hand (lock coupling) holds at most two adjacent locks while advancing, so distant updates proceed in parallel yet no unlinked node is edited without its lock. A consistent address or key order prevents the AB-BA deadlock of ad-hoc ordering. Locking only the head leaves the tail fully racy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the old coarse scheme, not the fine-grained upgrade.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tail nodes are still shared and mutable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Inconsistent order causes AB-BA deadlock.

medium.prompt: A stats counter is incremented millions of times/sec but read once/sec. What does a per-CPU approximate counter guarantee?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Exact at every instant with zero extra cost.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Correct only if updates use floating point.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Approximate between merges but exact after a final barrier/merge; updates stay cheap and local.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exact only on single-core machines.

medium.hint: Who pays for synchronization — every updater on a global lock, or only the occasional reader doing a merge?
medium.explanation: Per-CPU locals plus periodic merge scale updates; reads are stale until the next merge.
medium.deepDive: Sloppy/approximate counters give each CPU a local counter updated lock-free and merge them only when a reader demands a total, trading read freshness for update scalability. The global lock bottleneck disappears because increments rarely contend. A final barrier before the last read restores exactness when the use case (e.g., total requests served) tolerates staleness in between.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Staleness between merges is the explicit tradeoff.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Core count does not determine exactness; the merge does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Representation is irrelevant to the staleness tradeoff.

medium.prompt: Bounded-buffer consumer (Mesa CVs): which wait pattern is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.body: `if (count==0) wait(); consume();` — signal guarantees the predicate still holds.

choices.label: B
choices.body: `while (count==0) wait(); consume();` — re-check after every wakeup (Mesa semantics).

choices.label: C
choices.body: `wait(); if (count>0) consume();` with no loop and no predicate test before waiting.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unlock, then `if (count==0) wait();` without holding the mutex.

medium.hint: After signal, who runs first — and can a second consumer slip in before the woken one re-acquires the mutex?
medium.explanation: Mesa wakeups only hint; another thread may consume first, so the waiter must re-test in a while loop.
medium.deepDive: Mesa semantics leave the woken thread to compete for the mutex, so another consumer can steal the item first — the predicate may be false again by the time the waiter runs. The while loop converts a spurious or stolen wakeup into another sleep instead of an underflow. This bounded-buffer consumer is the canonical anchor: signal is a hint, the predicate plus loop is the guarantee.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Signal guarantees nothing about who runs next; the item may be gone — the key misconception.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Waiting without testing the predicate first can miss or spuriously consume.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Wait must hold the mutex to be atomic with the test.

medium.prompt: What is the core difference between Hoare and Mesa condition-variable semantics?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are identical; the woken thread always runs next in both.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Mesa is always faster and therefore always preferred.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mesa: woken thread competes for the mutex (must re-check); Hoare: lock passes directly to the woken thread.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hoare requires while loops but Mesa forbids them.

medium.hint: After signal, does the woken thread run immediately with the lock, or rejoin the queue for it?
medium.explanation: Hoare hands off the lock so the predicate survives; Mesa forces re-competition so it may not.
medium.deepDive: Hoare semantics hand the monitor lock immediately to the signaled thread, so the predicate the signaler established still holds and no re-check is logically needed. Mesa wakes the waiter into the ready set where it must re-acquire the lock and therefore re-check. Real systems (pthreads, Java) are Mesa-like, so while-loops are mandatory in practice.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Only Hoare gives immediate handoff; Mesa re-competes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed depends on contention; semantics differ regardless.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mesa is the one that mandates while loops.

medium.prompt: Bounded buffer with many consumers: when should you use signal vs broadcast?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wake one waiter when exactly one slot/item state changed; broadcast when many waiters may all be able to proceed (e.g., multiple consumers after bulk produce).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always broadcast; signal is deprecated and incorrect.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always signal; broadcast can cause deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Signal the producer when the buffer is full.

medium.hint: If one item arrives but five consumers wait, how many should usefully wake?
medium.explanation: Signal for one satisfiable waiter, broadcast when an event may satisfy many different predicates.
medium.deepDive: Signal wakes one waiter and is efficient when exactly one thread can make progress, while broadcast wakes all so each can re-check its own predicate. With multiple consumers and one item, broadcast causes a thundering herd where all but one re-sleep — correct but wasteful. Choosing correctly preserves both liveness and the blocking-cost savings from Scheduling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Signal is correct and cheaper when one waiter suffices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Broadcast never deadlocks by itself; it just wakes more threads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A full buffer means producers wait; signal consumers when items appear.

medium.prompt: Single-consumer bounded buffer with mutex + empty/full semaphores. What is the correct consumer order?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Consume first, then wait on full, then wait on mutex.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Wait on full, then post to empty before acquiring the mutex.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hold the mutex while waiting on the full semaphore.

choices.label: D
choices.body: sem_wait(full); lock(mutex); dequeue; unlock(mutex); sem_post(empty).

medium.hint: What happens to the producer if the consumer blocks while still holding the mutex?
medium.explanation: Count first outside the lock, then briefly lock only for dequeue, then release the slot count.
medium.deepDive: Ordering matters on both sides: counting waits happen outside the mutex so a blocked consumer does not hold the lock the producer needs, and posts happen after unlock so no woken thread immediately blocks on the mutex. Reversing the order either deadlocks (wait-while-holding) or breaks flow control. This is the standard mutex + empty/full semaphore solution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Waiting must precede consuming; you cannot consume what is not there.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Posting empty before removing corrupts the slot count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Blocking while holding the mutex deadlocks the producer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

medium.prompt: Multiple producers and consumers share one bounded buffer. What wait structure avoids waking the wrong side?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The mutex alone, because parities never interleave.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two CVs (or semaphores): one for non-full, one for non-empty, plus a mutex for indices — each waiter tests its own predicate in a loop.

choices.label: C
choices.body: One CV shared with no predicate, signaled on every operation.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No mutex, just yield() in a retry loop.

medium.hint: Can a producer's signal usefully wake another producer when the buffer is still full?
medium.explanation: Separate wait conditions for not-full and not-empty prevent waking the wrong side; the mutex guards indices.
medium.deepDive: Producers wait on not-full and consumers on not-empty: distinct predicates need distinct wait channels or counts, otherwise a signal can wake the wrong side and stall progress. Each side loops on its own predicate under Mesa semantics. A single predicateless CV degenerates into lost-wakeup roulette.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Indices are shared and interleave freely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Without predicates, wakeups routinely hit threads that cannot proceed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Yield loops waste CPU and do not enforce counts.

medium.prompt: Give the correct condition-variable shape for producer/consumer on a bounded buffer.

choices.label: A
choices.body: It is impossible with CVs; only semaphores work.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Use one CV and have producers signal producers.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Producer waits while full, appends, then signals non-empty; consumer waits while empty, removes, then signals non-full — all predicate tests in while loops under the mutex.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Signal before modifying the buffer to reduce latency.

medium.hint: Should the waiter be woken before or after the buffer state it depends on has changed?
medium.explanation: Test-then-wait in a loop, mutate under lock, then signal the opposite side's predicate.
medium.deepDive: The CV solution mirrors the semaphore counts with explicit predicates: not-full and not-empty tested in while loops. Mutation happens under the mutex, and signaling after the state change ensures a woken thread observes the new state once it re-acquires the lock. Signaling before the change lets the waiter wake, re-check, and sleep again — a lost-wakeup-shaped performance bug.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CVs with two predicates solve it cleanly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Producers must wake consumers and vice versa.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Early signal wakes a waiter that still sees the old predicate.

medium.prompt: 8-connection pool with a counting semaphore (init 8) plus an idle list. What is the correct discipline?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Wait on the pool semaphore to take a connection, post when returning it; the count enforces at most 8 holders.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Use the pool semaphore as an owned mutex: only the thread that waited may post.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Initialize the pool semaphore to 1 regardless of pool size.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Skip the mutex on the idle list because the semaphore already excludes.

medium.hint: Does the count tell you *which* connection you got, or only *that* one is available?
medium.explanation: Counting semaphore limits concurrent holders to pool size; a separate short mutex still guards the idle-list pick.
medium.deepDive: The counting semaphore is admission control: it blocks the 9th acquirer until someone returns a connection. Picking which idle entry to take still mutates a shared list and needs its own brief mutex. Treating the semaphore as an owned lock is the classic error — any thread can post, so ownership discipline must come from the code, not the primitive.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Semaphores have no owner; any thread may post — unlike a mutex.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Init must equal pool size, not 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The count admits holders; the list pick is still a critical section.

medium.prompt: A read-mostly config uses reader-preference reader-writer lock. What is its key behavior and risk?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Readers never need any lock because reads commute.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Give writers priority by blocking new readers once a writer waits — always optimal.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Alternate strictly one reader then one writer regardless of load.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reader-preference: readers share the lock, first reader blocks writers; risk is writer starvation under continuous readers.

medium.hint: If readers keep arriving before the last one leaves, when does a waiting writer enter?
medium.explanation: Sharing among readers boosts concurrency but continuous readers can starve writers.
medium.deepDive: Reader-preference lets concurrent readers overlap since they do not mutate, admitting the first reader and releasing on the last. Writers exclude everyone. Under a steady reader stream the writer waits indefinitely — starvation, the Scheduling fairness problem in miniature. The fix lineage leads to writer-preference and fair turnstiles next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Concurrent reads still need to coordinate against writers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Writer-preference can starve readers instead; neither is always optimal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Strict alternation wastes read parallelism.

medium.prompt: How do you build a reusable barrier for N threads from a mutex + semaphore?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A single mutex with no counter, unlocked by the last arriver.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A mutex-protected arrival count plus a turnstile semaphore (init 0); last arriver posts N times (or broadcasts a gate).

choices.label: C
choices.body: N independent spinloops on a shared flag with no count.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A binary semaphore initialized to N used directly as the barrier.

medium.hint: What two pieces are needed: tracking how many arrived, and holding early arrivals where?
medium.explanation: Count arrivals under a mutex; block the rest on a closed gate the last arriver opens.
medium.deepDive: The count must itself be a critical section, and arrivals must block on a gate until the Nth arrival opens it. Posting N times (or flipping a generation epoch for reuse) releases exactly the waiting set. Bare spinloops or a raw counting semaphore cannot distinguish generations and break on reuse.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Without a count and gate, arrivals cannot be detected or held.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No count means no way to know all arrived.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A bare count of N does not gate early arrivals correctly across generations.

medium.prompt: What is the standard lock-free stack push with compare-and-swap (CAS)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: CAS is slower than a mutex, so it is never useful.

choices.label: B
choices.body: CAS avoids all ABA problems by definition.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A lock-free push loops `do { old=top; new->next=old; } while(!CAS(&top,old,new));` retrying on concurrent interference.

choices.label: D
choices.body: One CAS without a loop is enough because hardware retries automatically.

medium.hint: What should a failed CAS do — give up, or re-read the new top and try again?
medium.explanation: CAS makes each push attempt atomic; the loop retries only when another thread interfered.
medium.deepDive: Compare-and-swap installs the new top only if it still equals the observed old, making each attempt atomic; the retry loop turns concurrent interference into a harmless retry instead of a lost update. This is the lock-free pushing bridge: mutual exclusion is replaced by optimistic retry. Pop is where ABA bites, taken up in stretch.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CAS is the basis of many fast lock-free structures.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CAS suffers the classic ABA false-positive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Software must loop; hardware reports failure once.

medium.prompt: Code does lock(A); lock(B) blocking. Which change breaks hold-and-wait?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Use try-lock and keep Lock A while retrying B.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Release Lock A before waiting, or request A+B atomically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Allow the OS to steal locks but keep holding while waiting.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Keep hold-and-wait but add more threads.

medium.hint: Which fix ensures the thread never parks while holding A?
medium.explanation: Not holding while blocking removes hold-and-wait.
medium.deepDive: Code that does lock(A); lock(B) with blocking exhibits hold-and-wait. Wrapping the pair in an atomic multi-acquire or dropping held locks before the next request removes it. Try-lock loops that retain A while spinning still hold-and-wait. The fix must ensure no thread blocks while holding.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Keeping A while retrying B still holds while waiting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: This mixes ideas; holding while waiting preserves hold-and-wait even with preemption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More threads only add more waiters; the pattern remains.

medium.prompt: Pool R has 3 buffers, 1 free. P1 holds 1 waits for 1; P2 holds 1 waits for 1. Deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No deadlock: 1 free buffer lets a waiter finish and release.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlock: any wait edges mean deadlock regardless of free copies.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deadlock: unlimited instances still always deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Starvation because buffers are identical.

medium.hint: Count free copies: can one waiter be satisfied right now?
medium.explanation: A free copy breaks the cycle: one thread proceeds, then releases.
medium.deepDive: With multiple instances, a wait cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock. A free instance can satisfy one waiter, whose completion releases more and cascades. This is why the single-instance cycle rule does not generalize. Always check Available before declaring deadlock from a graph cycle.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This states the cycle-always-deadlocks misconception; free copies refute it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: More instances make deadlock less likely, not inevitable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Identical instances do not imply priority denial.

medium.prompt: Pool R has 2 buffers, 0 free. P1 holds 1 waits for 1; P2 holds 1 waits for 1. Deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock, because two waiters always deadlock.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No deadlock, because two instances can never deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Livelock, because buffers are preemptible.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlock: 0 free copies and each waits for a held copy.

medium.hint: Same shape as before, but now count free: is there any escape?
medium.explanation: No free copy exists to break the wait, so both block forever.
medium.deepDive: When every copy is held and every holder waits for another copy, no waiter can be satisfied and the cycle is real deadlock. Instance counting is the decider: zero free plus full demand equals stuck. Adding just one free instance would dissolve it. That is why RAG analysis must label counts, not just arrows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The count matters, not just waiter number; with 0 free the cycle is real, but this option states it as a blanket rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Two instances can deadlock when all are held and wanted, as here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No spinning or retry is described; threads are blocked, so this is deadlock, not livelock.

medium.prompt: Tape pool has 4 instances, 2 free. P1 holds 1 waits 1; P2 holds 1 waits 1. Deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The cycle proves deadlock without checking counts.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Four instances guarantee deadlock.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No deadlock: 2 free tapes satisfy a waiter, cascading releases.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Prevention by ordering, because tapes are numbered.

medium.hint: Simulate one grant from the free pool: what does the finisher return?
medium.explanation: Free copies let a waiter complete; releases then unblock the rest.
medium.deepDive: Free instances are escape hatches: one grant lets a holder finish and return all its copies, raising Available further. With 2 free out of 4, at least one of the two waiters proceeds immediately. Students who memorize cycle-equals-deadlock miss this cascade. Banker safety exploits exactly this release cascade.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Counts must be checked; this is the key multi-instance correction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: More total copies with free copies reduce danger, not guarantee it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No lock order was imposed; the rescue is free instances, not numbering.

medium.prompt: Which prevention breaks hold-and-wait for lock(A); lock(B)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Require holding A while requesting B to keep throughput.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Acquire A+B atomically (all-or-nothing) so no one holds while waiting.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Add a detector that kills after deadlock forms.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Increase instances of B so deadlock is rarer.

medium.hint: Which option makes waiting and holding mutually exclusive?
medium.explanation: All-or-nothing acquisition means waiting happens with empty hands.
medium.deepDive: Atomic acquisition falsifies hold-and-wait: a thread either gets everything or holds nothing while waiting. It can waste concurrency by holding unneeded locks early. But it is simple and needs no global order. OSTEP pairs it against ordering and preemption as the three prevention levers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This preserves hold-and-wait; it is the problem, not the fix.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Killing after the fact is detection/recovery, not prevention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More copies reduce probability but keep all four conditions true.

medium.prompt: Which prevention breaks no-preemption?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Let the OS revoke a lock, roll back the holder, and grant it to a waiter.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Request all locks in one atomic step.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Enforce a global lock order A before B.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Run a periodic cycle detector.

medium.hint: Which fix lets someone other than the holder take the resource?
medium.explanation: Forcible revocation with rollback is exactly breaking no-preemption.
medium.deepDive: Preemption breaks no-preemption by allowing forced revocation plus rollback to a consistent state. It works for CPU or DB records with logged state but is hard for mutexes guarding arbitrary critical sections. Atomic request and ordering target different conditions. Detection also revokes but only after deadlock, so timing distinguishes them.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Atomic acquisition breaks hold-and-wait, not no-preemption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Global order breaks circular wait, not preemption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Periodic detection is recovery, allowed only after deadlock forms.

medium.prompt: T1 does A-then-B, T2 does B-then-A. Which prevention fixes the cycle?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Atomic acquisition of all locks.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Preempting held locks with rollback.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Detecting cycles and killing a holder.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Global order: every thread acquires A before B.

medium.hint: Which rule makes T2's B-then-A request illegal?
medium.explanation: Ordered acquisition forbids the A-after-B edge that would close the cycle.
medium.deepDive: A total order on locks makes cycles impossible: a thread holding B never requests a lower-ranked A, so wait edges always point upward. It preserves concurrency better than atomic acquisition but requires discipline and known lock sets. Violations reintroduce cycles silently. That is why large codebases lint lock order.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Atomicity would also work but ordering is the direct cycle-breaker here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Preemption breaks a different condition and needs rollback support.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Killing is post-hoc recovery, not static prevention.

medium.prompt: Single resource Total 10. Alloc [P0 2,P1 3,P2 2], Max [7,6,5], Avail 3. Safe?

choices.label: A
choices.body: P0, P1, P2 because allocation order is the safe order.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Unsafe: no order can finish.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Safe with witness P1, P0, P2.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Safe because Available covers all Needs at once.

medium.hint: Compute Need=Max-Alloc, then find who fits in Available 3 first.
medium.explanation: Only P1 fits in Available 3; its release cascades to unblock P0 then P2.
medium.deepDive: Check Needs: P0 needs 5, P1 needs 3, P2 needs 3 with Available 3. Only P1 is satisfiable, so it must go first. After P1 releases 3, Available becomes 6, unblocking P0, whose release then covers P2. Finding this cascade is the Banker safety test. Allocation order is irrelevant.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Allocation order is not the safety order; Need decides.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A finishing cascade exists, so it is safe.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Available 3 covers only P1, not all; safety uses sequential releases.

medium.prompt: Same system Avail 3, Needs [5,3,3]. P0 requests 2. Grant or deny?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deny: granting leaves Avail 1 satisfying nobody, an unsafe state.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Grant: requests should always be granted when Avail allows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Grant because the state stays safe via P0 first.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Deny because P0 already holds too much.

medium.hint: Simulate the grant: recompute Avail and Needs, then look for any fittable Need.
medium.explanation: Immediate grant is possible but the residue satisfies no Need, so deny to stay safe.
medium.deepDive: Banker grant rule: grant only if the resulting state is still safe. P0 requesting 2 from Avail 3 leaves Avail 1 with Needs [3,3,3] after updated Alloc, so nobody can proceed. Immediate satisfiability does not imply safety. Denial keeps the prior safe state instead of risking deadlock.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Avail-satisfiable is insufficient; the residue must keep a safe sequence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P0 would need 3 with Avail 1, so P0-first fails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Holding much is fine; the reason is loss of a safe sequence.

medium.prompt: Same system Avail 3, Needs [5,3,3]. P1 requests 1 instead. Grant or deny?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Grant because Avail covers the request.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Grant because P2 can always go first.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deny because all Banker requests must be denied.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Grant: residue Avail 2 still leaves witness P1,P0,P2.

medium.hint: Apply the grant to P1 only, then re-run the safety search from Avail 2.
medium.explanation: P1 still fits after its own grant, so a safe sequence survives.
medium.deepDive: After P1 requests 1, Allocs become [2,4,2] and Avail drops 3 to 2. Needs become [5,2,3], and P1 with Need 2 still fits Avail 2, preserving the cascade. This contrasts with the prior P0 request that destroyed safety. Same Avail, different requester: safety depends on who requests.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Covering the request is not the test; surviving safety is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: P2 cannot go first with Need 3 over Avail 2; P1 goes first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Banker grants safe requests; blanket denial wastes concurrency.

medium.prompt: Detector sees Avail 3, P1 Need 3, others Need 5. P1 holds 3. Deadlocked?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock has occurred because a thread is waiting.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No action: P1 can finish with Avail, then cascade; no cycle of unmet demand.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deadlock because Available is less than total Need.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Must kill P0 immediately as prevention.

medium.hint: Run one reduction step: does anyone fit in Available?
medium.explanation: Reduction eliminates P1 first, proving no deadlock.
medium.deepDive: Detection reduces the graph: repeatedly grant satisfiable waits from Available plus releases. Here P1 fits, so it is removed and its holdings recycled, which then satisfies others. If reduction consumes all processes, no deadlock exists. Available below total Need is normal; only irreducible residue indicates deadlock.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Single waiting is blocking, not deadlock; reduction decides.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Available is almost always below total Need; safety uses sequencing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Killing is recovery for real deadlock, not for a reducible state.

medium.prompt: Trace: both threads loop { try-lock; on fail backoff; retry } for 10s, CPU busy, neither enters. Which?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock: threads are blocked in lock().

choices.label: C
choices.body: Starvation: one thread finishes repeatedly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlock because CPU is idle.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Safe state because retries preserve correctness.

medium.hint: Are they parked in lock() or spinning and retrying?
medium.explanation: Both run and retry yet never enter: classic livelock, not parked deadlock.
medium.deepDive: Livelock threads run but retry the same failing step, consuming CPU with zero progress. Here both loop lock-try plus backoff and collide forever. Unlike deadlock they are not parked, and unlike starvation both fail equally. Randomized backoff usually breaks the symmetry. Tracing CPU-busy plus zero commits signals livelock.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Blocked-in-lock would show idle CPU and parked stacks, not retries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Idle CPU contradicts the busy retry loop described.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Safety is a Banker property, not a spin-loop outcome.

medium.prompt: 'ls -i' shows a.txt and b.txt with the same inode number 4521. What does this mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are hard links to one inode; edits via one appear via the other

choices.label: B
choices.body: They are independent files that happen to share cached data

choices.label: C
choices.body: One is a symlink whose target path resolved to the other

choices.label: D
choices.body: The filesystem is corrupted: inode numbers must be unique per name

medium.hint: Same inode number in two directory entries — how many data-block sets exist?
medium.explanation: One inode, two names: a single file with link count 2.
medium.deepDive: stat confirms: same inode, nlink=2, same size and blocks. Symlinks would show different inode numbers and file type 'l'. This is the observable proof that names live in directories, not inodes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sharing an inode number means sharing identity, not just cache.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A symlink has its own inode; numbers would differ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sharing is legal and expected for hard links.

medium.prompt: stat() reports size=5000 bytes on 4KB blocks. How many data blocks must the inode point to (at least)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 2 blocks (8192 bytes), with 3192 bytes of internal fragmentation in the last block

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exactly 5000/512 = 9 blocks with no waste

choices.label: C
choices.body: 1 block, because inodes store up to 4KB inline

choices.label: D
choices.body: 5000 blocks, one per byte

medium.hint: Divide size by block size and round up — what fills the tail of the last block?
medium.explanation: File I/O is in whole blocks; the tail of the last block is wasted slack space.
medium.deepDive: ceil(5000/4096)=2 blocks. The inode's size field records the exact byte count so reads stop mid-block. The wasted tail is internal fragmentation, the price of block-granular allocation carried over from paging.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Allocation is in filesystem blocks (4KB here), not 512-byte sectors.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: VSFS/FFS inodes store pointers, not 4KB of inline data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Blocks hold many bytes; allocation is not byte-granular.

medium.prompt: A file has link count 2. A process calls unlink() on one name while another process holds the file open. When are blocks freed?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only after the second name is unlinked AND the open descriptor is closed

choices.label: B
choices.body: Immediately at the first unlink, and the open reader gets an error

choices.label: C
choices.body: Immediately when the file is closed, even if both names still exist

choices.label: D
choices.body: Never; unlinked-while-open files leak permanently

medium.hint: Two lifetimes guard the blocks: directory references and open references — when is each dropped?
medium.explanation: Blocks free only when link count hits 0 and the in-memory reference count hits 0.
medium.deepDive: This refutes 'unlink always frees immediately'.POSIX deletion is two-stage: unlink removes a name and decrements nlink; the inode and blocks persist while open. Temp files exploit this: create, unlink, keep using the descriptor invisibly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Misconception: unlink removes a name, not necessarily the data; open holders keep access.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Closing alone frees nothing while names still reference the inode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The last close reclaims the anonymous inode; no leak.

medium.prompt: Which operation will fail with 'Invalid cross-device link'?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Hard-linking /diskA/file to a name on /diskB (different filesystems)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Symlinking /diskA/file from a name on /diskB

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hard-linking two names within the same filesystem

choices.label: D
choices.body: Renaming a file within the same directory

medium.hint: Hard links embed an inode number — is that number meaningful on another filesystem?
medium.explanation: Inode numbers are filesystem-local, so hard links cannot span filesystems.
medium.deepDive: Each filesystem has its own inode table; number 100 on diskA is unrelated to number 100 on diskB. Symlinks store paths (strings) so they cross freely. Same-filesystem hard links and renames stay within one inode namespace and succeed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Symlinks cross filesystems precisely because they store paths.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Same-FS hard links are the supported case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Same-directory rename only edits one directory file.

medium.prompt: fd = open('f', O_RDWR); dup2(fd, 5); lseek(fd, 10, SEEK_SET); What offset does a write via fd 5 use?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 10 — dup shares the open file description and its single offset

choices.label: B
choices.body: 0 — dup snapshots the offset at dup time and diverges after

choices.label: C
choices.body: End-of-file, because dup implies O_APPEND

choices.label: D
choices.body: Undefined; dup descriptors cannot be used for I/O

medium.hint: dup creates a second descriptor to the same description — how many cursors is that?
medium.explanation: One shared description means one shared offset; seeks via either are visible via both.
medium.deepDive: Contrast with a second open(), which creates a second description with its own offset. Shell redirection relies on dup-sharing so that a child and parent append coherently. For independent cursors, open twice or use pread/pwrite.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No snapshot: the offset is shared state, not copied.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: O_APPEND is a separate flag; dup does not set it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both descriptors are fully usable for I/O.

medium.prompt: Parent opens a log file, then fork()s. Parent and child each write 100 bytes without seeking. What is the likely result?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Interleaved/overwritten data from a shared offset updated by both (unless O_APPEND)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two clean 100-byte appends, because fork duplicates the offset independently

choices.label: C
choices.body: Child writes fail; descriptors are closed across fork

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each write goes to offset 0 and both succeed without interference

medium.hint: fork inherits descriptors pointing at the same description — who moves the shared cursor?
medium.explanation: Fork shares offsets, so concurrent writes race on one cursor and can overwrite each other.
medium.deepDive: Each write advances the shared offset, but two processes can read the same offset before either advances it, causing overlap. O_APPEND forces each write to seek to EOF atomically, fixing this pattern. Separate opens would give independent cursors instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fork does not copy the offset; it shares it like dup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Descriptors survive fork by design.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Writes use the current shared offset, not 0.

medium.prompt: VSFS: 4KB blocks, 256-byte inodes, inode table starts at block 5. Where is inode 32?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Block 7 (inodes 0-15 in block 5, 16-31 in block 6, 32+ in block 7)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Block 32, because inode N always lives in block N

choices.label: C
choices.body: Block 5 + 32*256 bytes counted in blocks from byte 0 of disk

choices.label: D
choices.body: In the data region; inode position is allocated dynamically

medium.hint: How many inodes fit per 4KB block? Divide the inode number by that.
medium.explanation: 16 inodes/block, so inode 32 is the first entry of the third table block.
medium.deepDive: Formula: block = tableStart + (ino * inodeSize / blockSize); offset = (ino * inodeSize) % blockSize = 4096/256=16 per block. Fixed math is the payoff of static layout: no search needed to find an inode.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inodes are densely packed; block number ≠ inode number.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Must divide by block size and add table start; raw byte offset alone is not a block number.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Inode table position is static in VSFS.

medium.prompt: An inode has 12 direct pointers plus 1 single-indirect pointer (4KB blocks, 4-byte block numbers). Max blocks addressable?

choices.label: C
choices.body: 13 blocks total

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1024 blocks; direct pointers are ignored once indirect exists

medium.hint: One 4KB indirect block holds how many 4-byte addresses? Add the directs.
medium.explanation: The indirect block holds 1024 pointers; plus 12 direct gives 1036.
medium.deepDive: Directs handle small files with zero extra I/O; the indirect adds one extra read for larger files. This tiered scheme (like multi-level page tables) keeps small files cheap while scaling up. Double-indirect extends this quadratically.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Directs add, they do not multiply the indirect fan-out.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Counts the pointer slot, not the blocks each pointer addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Directs remain usable alongside indirects.

medium.prompt: Same geometry (4KB blocks, 4-byte pointers). How many data blocks does one double-indirect pointer address?

choices.label: C
choices.body: 1024 + 1024 = 2048 bytes worth of blocks

choices.label: D
choices.body: 12 blocks, same as direct coverage

medium.hint: Double-indirect is a block of pointers to blocks of pointers — multiply the fan-outs.
medium.explanation: 1024 single-indirect blocks each holding 1024 data pointers gives ~1M blocks.
medium.deepDive: At 4KB each that is ~4GB from one double-indirect pointer, at the cost of 3 disk reads to reach data. Triple-indirect would cube the fan-out. Exam trap: 2048 confuses additive (direct+indirect) with multiplicative (indirect²) growth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Adds instead of multiplying the two levels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mixes byte and block units and adds levels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Direct coverage is unrelated to indirect fan-out.

medium.prompt: FFS divides the disk into cylinder groups, each with its own inodes + bitmaps + data. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To keep a directory's inodes near its files' data, minimizing seeks

choices.label: B
choices.body: To allow hard links to cross filesystems

choices.label: C
choices.body: To store filenames inside inodes more compactly

choices.label: D
choices.body: To eliminate the need for fsync on crash recovery

medium.hint: If metadata for /a is on the opposite side of the disk from /a's data, what does ls + cat cost?
medium.explanation: Co-locating related inodes and data in one group keeps related I/Os nearby.
medium.deepDive: FFS allocates a new file's inode in its directory's group and its blocks in the same group when space allows. Pure VSFS scatters inodes far from data. Grouping replicates the superblock sparingly so one group failure need not kill the FS.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Grouping does not change cross-FS inode-number scoping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Names still live in directories, unchanged by grouping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Crash durability still needs fsync/journaling.

medium.prompt: FFS allocation policy: new file 'dir/foo' and its first blocks go where for best locality?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Inode in dir's cylinder group; data blocks contiguous in the same group if possible

choices.label: B
choices.body: Inode in group 0 always; data striped randomly across all groups

choices.label: C
choices.body: Inode and data in whichever group has the most free space globally

choices.label: D
choices.body: Data in dir's group but inode in a remote dedicated inode group

medium.hint: Two locality goals: same-group-as-directory, then contiguous — which option gives both?
medium.explanation: Same-group placement plus contiguous allocation gives one short seek then streaming transfer.
medium.deepDive: FFS first tries the directory's group, then a nearby group for large files that overflow. Random or global-best-fit placement would scatter related files. Separating all inodes remotely reintroduces the VSFS seek penalty.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Centralizing inodes and randomizing data maximizes seeks — the VSFS problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Global best-fit ignores relatedness and fragments locality over time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Splitting inode from data guarantees a long seek per file open.

medium.prompt: Creating a new empty file requires which persistent updates?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Set inode-bitmap bit, initialize the inode, add directory entry (and data bitmap only when blocks later allocated)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Set data-bitmap bit only; inodes are created implicitly on first write

choices.label: C
choices.body: Increment the file's link count and copy its data blocks

choices.label: D
choices.body: Rewrite the superblock and zero all bitmaps

medium.hint: Empty file needs an inode but no data blocks — which structures record that?
medium.explanation: Inode allocation + inode init + directory link; data allocation is deferred.
medium.deepDive: Missing any step leaks or corrupts: bitmap set without init exposes garbage; init without bitmap risks double-alloc; entry without inode dangles. Crash between steps is why ordering and journaling matter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inode allocation is mandatory; data blocks are not needed for empty files.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No data exists to copy; link count starts at 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Superblock and full bitmap rewrite are unnecessary and destructive.

medium.prompt: What is the difference between an inode bitmap bit and an inode link count?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bitmap: is the inode allocated? Link count: how many directory names point to it?

choices.label: B
choices.body: They are identical; either can be used to free the inode

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bitmap counts names; link count marks free vs used blocks

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bitmap lives in the inode; link count lives in the superblock

medium.hint: One answers allocation, the other answers name-sharing — which frees the inode requires which values?
medium.explanation: Freeing needs bitmap=allocated cleared only when link count reaches 0 (and no open refs).
medium.deepDive: Bitmap lifecycle is alloc/free; refcount lifecycle is link/unlink. Confusing them causes premature free (clearing bitmap while names remain) or leaks (dropping last name without clearing bitmap). Both must agree to reclaim safely.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: They track different things; both conditions must hold to free.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Swaps their roles exactly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Swaps their locations: bitmap in FS metadata, count in inode.

medium.prompt: File mode 0640 (rw-r-----). Which access is allowed?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Owner read/write, group read, others nothing

choices.label: B
choices.body: Everyone read/write, no execute anywhere

choices.label: C
choices.body: Owner execute only, group write only

choices.label: D
choices.body: Owner nothing; group and others full access

medium.hint: Split octal 6-4-0 into rwx triples — what does each digit expand to?
medium.explanation: 6=rw-, 4=r--, 0=--- mapping to owner/group/other.
medium.deepDive: Mode bits stored in the inode are checked at open() against the caller's uid/gid. They do not encrypt data and root bypasses them. Directories need +x to permit lookup traversal, a common companion trap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 640 grants nothing to others; 666 would grant all rw.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Misreads octal positions and bit values.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reverses the owner/other order.

medium.prompt: What is the correct ordered trace for creat('dir/f') in a VSFS-like FS?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Read dir → alloc inode (bitmap+init) → add dir entry → flush dir + inode

choices.label: B
choices.body: Allocate data block → write data → invent an inode number without bitmap → return

choices.label: C
choices.body: Add dir entry first → pick any inode number → init inode whenever convenient

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zero the entire disk → write superblock → create the file

medium.hint: You must verify the name is free, claim metadata, then publish the name — what order is crash-safe-ish?
medium.explanation: Check-then-allocate-then-link keeps the new name from ever pointing at garbage.
medium.deepDive: Reading the directory first prevents duplicates. Setting the bitmap before init prevents double-alloc; linking last prevents a visible name resolving to an uninitialized inode. Write-back order to disk refines this further for crash consistency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Skips bitmap and directory linkage — file would be unreachable and racy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Publishing the name before the inode is ready exposes garbage on crash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Gratuitous full-disk work; unrelated to create.

medium.prompt: Resolving open('a/b/c') when cwd inode is known requires:

choices.label: A
choices.body: For each component: load current dir inode → read its blocks → find next name → load next inode; fail if any missing or not a directory

choices.label: B
choices.body: One read of the root bitmap followed by direct data access to 'c'

choices.label: C
choices.body: Scanning the inode table for an inode whose stored path equals 'a/b/c'

choices.label: D
choices.body: Following double-indirect pointers named 'a', 'b', 'c' inside one inode

medium.hint: Each non-final component must be a directory — what check + lookup repeats?
medium.explanation: Lookup is iterative per-component directory search with type checks.
medium.deepDive: Permissions (+x) are checked per directory, symlinks redirect resolution, and mount points switch filesystems mid-path. Caching (dcache) skips disk reads but the logical walk is identical. Inodes store no paths, so C is impossible.
