wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bitmaps do not resolve names; one read cannot walk three levels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inodes store no path strings to scan for.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Block pointers address file data, not namespace components.

medium.prompt: A database does random 4KB writes. Why does it tune differently on HDD vs SSD regarding elevator scheduling?

choices.label: A
choices.body: HDD needs SCAN-style merging to avoid seeks; SSD ignores seeks, fears erase/write-amplification

choices.label: B
choices.body: SSD needs longer seeks than HDD

choices.label: C
choices.body: HDD wears out on writes so must batch erases

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both need identical elevator tuning

medium.hint: Match the scarce resource: what dominates cost on each device?
medium.explanation: HDD cost is arm movement, so order by position; SSD cost is erase cycles and GC.
medium.deepDive: Elevator schedulers exist to minimize HDD seeks, giving large wins on random I/O. On SSDs seeks are zero, so deep reordering adds latency without benefit and can fight internal parallelism. SSD tuning instead batches erases and leaves spare over-provisioned space.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: SSDs have no seeks at all; HDDs are the ones with millisecond seeks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Wear/erase limits belong to flash, not spinning disks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Identical tuning wastes SSD queue depth and under-optimizes HDD seeks.

medium.prompt: 5 disks of 2TB in RAID-5. What are usable capacity and fault tolerance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 8TB usable, 1 failure tolerated

choices.label: B
choices.body: 10TB usable, 0 failures tolerated

choices.label: C
choices.body: 2TB usable, 4 failures tolerated

choices.label: D
choices.body: 8TB usable, 2 failures tolerated

medium.hint: RAID-5 reserves one disk worth of rotating parity: subtract it, then count survivable losses.
medium.explanation: One parity equivalent is lost: (5-1)*2TB=8TB, and parity reconstructs any single loss.
medium.deepDive: Rotating parity avoids the RAID-4 dedicated parity bottleneck while keeping single-fault tolerance. Capacity efficiency is (N-1)/N, improving with more disks. Two concurrent failures still destroy data; that needs RAID-6.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 10TB with 0 faults is RAID-0; parity always costs one disk equivalent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 2TB usable is full mirroring, not parity striping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 2-fault tolerance with this capacity is RAID-6, which costs two parities.

medium.prompt: A 1MB disk-to-memory copy uses programmed I/O vs DMA. What does DMA change?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Controller moves data directly; CPU only sets up and gets one interrupt

choices.label: B
choices.body: CPU copies each byte faster by polling harder

choices.label: C
choices.body: DMA engine executes the user program during transfer

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disk transfer rate doubles automatically

medium.hint: Count CPU involvement per byte: who moves the bytes in each design?
medium.explanation: DMA offloads per-byte movement; the CPU handles one setup plus completion interrupt.
medium.deepDive: Programmed I/O costs a CPU copy per word plus polling, saturating the CPU on bulk I/O. DMA lets controller and memory interact while the CPU runs other threads. The OS driver still programs addresses and handles the completion interrupt.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Polling harder increases CPU waste; DMA removes per-byte CPU work instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA is a dumb data mover; it never fetches or executes instructions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Media rate is unchanged; only CPU overhead drops.

medium.prompt: Where does the device driver fit between app, OS, and DMA/interrupt hardware?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Driver translates OS requests into device commands, programs DMA, handles interrupts

choices.label: B
choices.body: Driver replaces the file system and bypasses the kernel

choices.label: C
choices.body: Driver runs as unprivileged user code moving each byte

choices.label: D
choices.body: Driver physically spins the disk platter

medium.hint: Think layers: app calls OS, OS calls what to speak device registers?
medium.explanation: The driver is the OS layer that programs registers/DMA and services device interrupts.
medium.deepDive: Apps issue abstract read/write; the kernel routes to the driver, which knows register layouts and timing. The driver starts DMA, sleeps the caller, and wakes it on interrupt. This isolation lets one kernel support many devices.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Drivers sit under the file system inside the kernel; they do not replace it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Drivers are privileged kernel code; user code cannot safely touch registers or IRQs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The motor spins the platter; software only issues commands.

medium.prompt: Head at 20 moving up. Queue: 10, 30, 60, 25. What SCAN service order and total travel to finish at 60?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 25, 30, 60 then 10; travel 40 up + 50 down = 90

choices.label: C
choices.body: 60, 30, 25, 10; travel 40 only

medium.hint: Sweep up first serving everything above 20 in order, then reverse for 10.
medium.explanation: SCAN continues up (25,30,60 = 40 travel) then reverses down to 10 (+50 = 90).
medium.deepDive: SCAN never reverses mid-sweep, so requests behind the head wait one full sweep. Total travel is up-distance plus down-distance to the lowest pending request. FCFS order 10,30,60,25 would travel far more by zigzagging.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That visits 10 first by jumping backward, which is FCFS-like, not upward SCAN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Jumping straight to 60 skips 25 and 30 that lie on the way up.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 30 then 25 goes backward while moving up; SCAN serves ascending on the up-sweep.

medium.prompt: How does C-SCAN differ from SCAN in head movement and fairness?

choices.label: A
choices.body: C-SCAN wraps to start without serving on return, giving uniform wait

choices.label: B
choices.body: C-SCAN serves both directions to minimize all travel

choices.label: C
choices.body: C-SCAN always picks the closest request (SSTF)

choices.label: D
choices.body: C-SCAN disables interrupts during seeks

medium.hint: Picture a circular sweep: serve one way, jump back idle — who waits how long?
medium.explanation: C-SCAN serves only upward then jumps back, so wait time is uniform along the disk.
medium.deepDive: SCAN favors middle tracks (served in both directions) and starves edge tracks relatively. C-SCAN treats the disk as circular, equalizing worst-case wait at the cost of extra empty return travel. Use C-SCAN when variance matters more than average.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Serving both directions is plain SCAN; C-SCAN idles on the return.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Closest-first is SSTF, which risks starvation unlike circular SCAN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Interrupts stay enabled; C-SCAN is only a queue ordering policy.

medium.prompt: Appending a block writes data (D), inode (I), bitmap (B). Crash shows I points to D but B still marks D free. What happened?

choices.label: A
choices.body: I and D landed but B did not; later allocator may reuse D causing double-allocation

choices.label: B
choices.body: Journal replayed and checkpointed cleanly

choices.label: C
choices.body: DMA encrypted the bitmap

choices.label: D
choices.body: No inconsistency; bitmap always lags safely

medium.hint: Check agreement: inode claims the block but free-map disagrees — who else may claim it?
medium.explanation: The bitmap missed its update, so the block looks both used and free.
medium.deepDive: Ordering I before B opens this window; ordering B before I opens the leak window instead. No single order closes both windows because crashes split any sequence. Recovery must detect or prevent partial states via journaling, fsck, or CoW.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No journal exists in this scenario, so no replay occurred.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA never encrypts; this is a torn multi-write update.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Disagreement is the definition of inconsistency and can corrupt two files.

medium.prompt: After a crash, fsck finds an allocated inode with a refcount mismatch and a block marked free but referenced. What does fsck do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Scans all inodes/blocks and rebuilds bitmaps and counts to consistent state

choices.label: B
choices.body: Re-executes the interrupted user program from the start

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decrypts the journal to recover passwords

choices.label: D
choices.body: Physically repairs bad sectors

medium.hint: fsck cannot undo the crash; what global check can it recompute from surviving metadata?
medium.explanation: fsck cross-checks every pointer and rebuilds allocation structures by full scan.
medium.deepDive: fsck phases check superblock, inodes, directory connectivity, and reference counts, fixing leaks and double-allocs by rewriting bitmaps. It is correct but slow, scanning the whole disk after every crash. Journaling was added largely to avoid this full scan.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: fsck repairs metadata only; it never reruns application logic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The journal holds block images, not passwords, and needs no decryption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bad-sector remapping is drive firmware work, not fsck.

medium.prompt: Creating file /a/b needs inode, directory entry, and bitmap updates. Crash leaves the inode allocated but no directory entry. What is this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Orphan inode leak from torn multi-structure update

choices.label: B
choices.body: Successful atomic commit

choices.label: C
choices.body: DMA overrun error

choices.label: D
choices.body: Elevator misordering

medium.hint: Can you reach the inode by pathname? If not, what resource was wasted?
medium.explanation: The inode update landed but the directory update did not, leaking an unreachable inode.
medium.deepDive: File creation spans independent structures with no hardware atomicity, so any interleaving plus crash orphans or dangles state. fsck finds such inodes with link-count zero and frees or moves them to lost+found. Journaling groups the three writes into one atomic transaction instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Atomic commit would make all or none visible; here half is visible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA moves bytes; it does not create directory entries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Elevator orders disk queue, not file-system structural atomicity.

medium.prompt: Journaling a transaction writes TxBegin (TB), journal data+metadata (J), commit (C), then in-place (P). What is the correct crash-safe order?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TB -> J -> C -> P, with C only after J is durable

choices.label: B
choices.body: P -> C -> J -> TB

choices.label: C
choices.body: C -> TB -> J -> P

choices.label: D
choices.body: J -> P -> TB -> C encrypted

medium.hint: Write-ahead means intent hits disk before the commit word and before home locations.
medium.explanation: Log contents first, then commit marker, then overwrite home; commit never precedes its log.
medium.deepDive: If crash precedes C, recovery discards the partial journal entry. If crash follows C, recovery replays J to home locations. Writing P before C would expose torn in-place state with no redo source. Barriers ensure the device does not reorder these steps.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Updating home before logging destroys the redo source; recovery becomes impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Committing before logging lets recovery replay garbage or nothing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Order is wrong and journaling is not encryption; C must follow durable J.

medium.prompt: After a crash the journal holds T1 with commit and T2 without commit. What does replay do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Redo T1 to home locations, discard T2

choices.label: B
choices.body: Redo both T1 and T2 fully

choices.label: C
choices.body: Discard both and run full fsck always

choices.label: D
choices.body: Decrypt T2 then apply it

medium.hint: The commit block is the atomic switch: what does its presence tell recovery?
medium.explanation: Commit means all-or-nothing succeeded, so only T1 is safe to redo.
medium.deepDive: The commit record makes the transaction atomic despite multiple journal blocks. A missing or torn commit implies the logger crashed mid-write, so those blocks may be garbage. Redoing T1 is idempotent, so replaying twice after another crash stays safe.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: T2 may be partial garbage; applying it would corrupt home locations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The point of the journal is to avoid full fsck when a commit record decides fate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No decryption exists; T2 is discarded because it lacks commit, not because it is locked.

medium.prompt: When can journal space for a committed transaction be freed (checkpointed)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: After its blocks are durably written to home locations

choices.label: B
choices.body: Immediately after the commit block is written

choices.label: C
choices.body: Before the transaction even starts

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only after full disk reformat

medium.hint: The journal is the backup copy: when is the home copy safe enough to stand alone?
medium.explanation: Checkpoint copies journaled blocks home, then the log tail may advance.
medium.deepDive: Freeing at commit time would lose the only durable copy if the home write later crashed. Journals are circular, so checkpointing bounds recovery work and reclaims space. Slow checkpointing stalls new transactions when the log fills.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Commit only guarantees the log copy; home still holds stale data until checkpoint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Freeing before start discards data that was never logged.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reformat is unnecessary; steady-state checkpointing reuses the circular log.

medium.prompt: LFS writes 100 small files, then deletes 90 in one segment. How does cleaning reclaim space?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Read live blocks, compact them to new segment, free old segment

choices.label: B
choices.body: Overwrite deleted blocks in place with zeros

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decrypt the segment to recover blocks

choices.label: D
choices.body: Run elevator SCAN to defragment heads

medium.hint: Segments are append-only: how do you empty a mostly-dead one without in-place edits?
medium.explanation: Cleaner migrates survivors forward, then frees the whole segment for reuse.
medium.deepDive: Segment summary blocks identify live versus dead data via imap checks. Cleaning cost is proportional to live fraction, so nearly-empty segments are cheapest to clean. This background work is LFS's price for turning all writes sequential.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: In-place zeroing violates append-only design and would cost seeks LFS avoids.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No encryption is involved; liveness comes from imap reachability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Elevator schedules HDD seeks; it does not reclaim log segments.

medium.prompt: A CoW file system takes a snapshot, then the user overwrites block X. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: New data goes to a new block; snapshot root still points to old X

choices.label: B
choices.body: Old block X is overwritten in place for both views

choices.label: C
choices.body: Entire disk is copied to a new disk

choices.label: D
choices.body: Snapshot is deleted automatically

medium.hint: Copy-on-write shares until a write arrives: which copy moves?
medium.explanation: Writes redirect to fresh blocks, preserving the snapshot's old roots and pointers.
medium.deepDive: Snapshots share the tree root cheaply at creation (O(1) root copy). Only overwritten blocks diverge, so snapshot cost is proportional to churn. Reference counts track sharing so deletion frees only unshared blocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: In-place overwrite would corrupt the snapshot; CoW never overwrites shared blocks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Full copying defeats the purpose; sharing plus redirect makes snapshots cheap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Snapshots persist until explicitly deleted; writes do not remove them.

hard.prompt: A photo-sharing server handles 1000 clients at once and stores their uploads. How do the three pieces each show up here?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Virtualization shares the CPU across clients, concurrency coordinates their overlapping requests, and persistence stores the uploads durably

choices.label: B
choices.body: All three pieces are just different names for the file system

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only persistence matters because serving is just disk reads

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only virtualization matters because one server means one client

hard.hint: Walk the life of one uploaded photo: sharing the CPU, not colliding with other uploads, surviving a crash. How many pieces does that touch?
hard.explanation: A busy server exercises every piece at once: sharing hardware, coordinating overlapping work, and storing results durably.
hard.deepDive: Trace one upload: the scheduler time-slices the CPU so a thousand connections each feel served, a lock guards the shared session table while two requests arrive together, and the file system commits the bytes to disk before replying success. Drop any one piece and the story breaks: no sharing means one slow client blocks everyone, no coordination corrupts the table, and no durability loses the file on crash. Why it matters: real systems always blend all three pieces, so this mapping habit is how you read any production design.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The file system is the persistence piece only; it does not schedule the CPU or synchronize requests.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Serving involves scheduling, shared buffers, and sockets long before any disk read happens.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A server multiplexes many clients onto few CPUs, so sharing is the whole ballgame.

hard.prompt: When does the virtualization illusion visibly crack?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Everything slows down or isolation visibly breaks, revealing the shared reality underneath

choices.label: B
choices.body: Programs run faster because sharing doubles the hardware

choices.label: C
choices.body: Nothing observable ever changes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each program gains extra private RAM

hard.hint: If ten programs each believe they own the CPU, what happens when all ten compute furiously at once?
hard.explanation: The illusion is leaky under contention: overload exposes sharing through slowdowns, which is why scheduling and memory management exist.
hard.deepDive: Consider a hotel where every guest was promised a private pool, until everyone jumps in at noon and the water turns crowded and cold. Overload the CPU or memory and response times spike, exactly like that overbooked pool exposing the sharing. Why it matters: performance isolation is never perfect, so OS designers add scheduling fairness and memory pressure signals to keep the illusion convincing under load.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sharing divides finite hardware; it never multiplies it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Contention is directly observable as latency and throughput loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overload shrinks each program's effective share instead of granting more.

hard.prompt: Two programs print counting numbers at the same time and their outputs appear interleaved line by line. What best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The OS rapidly switched the CPU between them, so their outputs interleaved

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each program owned a separate physical CPU

choices.label: C
choices.body: One program finished entirely before the other started

choices.label: D
choices.body: The printer merged two files at random

hard.hint: Two programs print at once and their lines mix together like shuffled cards. What kind of rapid sharing produces a shuffle?
hard.explanation: Interleaved output from two simultaneously running programs is the visible fingerprint of CPU time-sharing via context switches.
hard.deepDive: Mini-trace it: program A prints 1, the timer fires, the OS saves A and restores B which prints X, then control returns and A prints 2, yielding 1 X 2. Neither program knows it was paused, since its registers and memory were frozen and revived intact. Why it matters: interleaved output you can see with your own eyes is the cheapest proof that time-sharing is real.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A single-CPU machine shows the same interleaving, so duplicate hardware is not required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Strict serial execution would print all of one program's lines before the other's.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No printer is involved; the terminal simply displays whatever each running program emits.

hard.prompt: Which trace correctly shows the mode-bit journey during one timer-driven preemption?

choices.label: A
choices.body: User → timer interrupt → kernel handler → scheduler → restore next program → user

choices.label: C
choices.body: User → user edits mode bit → keeps running uninterrupted

choices.label: B
choices.body: Kernel → asks program permission → waits for approval

choices.label: D
choices.body: User → reboot → kernel → user

hard.hint: Start with a program running restricted, add a timer firing, then a scheduler choosing. Which sequence visits both modes in that order?
hard.explanation: Timer-driven preemption is a repeating mode loop: user execution, hardware trap to the kernel handler, scheduling decision, restore to user mode.
hard.deepDive: Mini-trace a 10 ms quantum: your program runs in user mode, the timer fires and the hardware flips to kernel mode at the handler, the scheduler picks the next program, and the OS restores it into user mode. The mode bit therefore flickers on every slice, thousands of times per second, without any program noticing. Why it matters: seeing the full loop proves the kernel stays in charge even though user programs do most of the visible work.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The kernel never needs a program's permission; the hardware hands control to the kernel by design.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: User code cannot touch the mode bit, so self-promotion traces are impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No reboot occurs; preemption is a lightweight trap-and-return cycle.

hard.prompt: Trace what happens when a program calls printf("hi") and the output finally reaches the terminal.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Library printf buffers text in user mode, write traps into the kernel, the kernel stores bytes, and control returns to the program

choices.label: B
choices.body: printf drives the disk hardware directly

choices.label: C
choices.body: write runs entirely in user mode with no kernel entry

choices.label: D
choices.body: The kernel calls printf on the program's behalf

hard.hint: Follow the letters from your code to the screen: who buffers, who crosses the wall, who touches hardware? Which order tells that story?
hard.explanation: The full path crosses layers once: user library buffering, then one guarded kernel crossing that performs the privileged device work.
hard.deepDive: Mini-trace printf("hi"): the library appends two letters to its user-mode buffer and returns instantly, then a later flush issues write, the trap flips to kernel mode, the file system and driver commit the bytes, and the kernel returns a count to the program. Counting the single crossing shows where the milliseconds really go. Why it matters: this trace is the template for every I/O path you will optimize or debug for the rest of the course.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: User libraries can never touch device hardware directly; only the kernel holds that privilege.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: write is defined by its kernel crossing; without the trap it would just be another library function.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Control flows upward from program to kernel, never downward from kernel into library formatting.

hard.prompt: Why do C libraries wrap raw system calls instead of having every program call the kernel directly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Convenience, buffering for performance, and portability across different kernels

choices.label: B
choices.body: To slow programs down deliberately

choices.label: C
choices.body: To grant programs kernel privileges permanently

choices.label: D
choices.body: To replace the kernel entirely

hard.hint: If every print crossed into the kernel one character at a time, what would batching save? And who hides Linux-versus-macOS differences?
hard.explanation: Wrappers exist to simplify interfaces, batch crossings through buffering, and shield programs from kernel differences.
hard.deepDive: Raw system calls are like talking to the vault in legal jargon one coin at a time: correct but exhausting. Library wrappers translate friendly calls into batched, well-formed kernel requests and hide OS differences behind one stable face. Why it matters: nearly all the I/O performance wins and portability you enjoy come from this thin user-mode layer, not from new hardware.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Wrappers speed programs up by batching crossings; slowness is the problem they solve.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Wrappers hold no privilege themselves and return to user mode after each kernel request.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Libraries depend on the kernel for every privileged act and could never replace it.

hard.prompt: A multilevel feedback scheduler is retuned for a new workload. Which change respects the policy/mechanism split?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Tuning time-slice lengths and priority boosts while the context-switch code stays untouched

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rewriting the register save/restore assembly for each new goal

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deleting the timer interrupt handler

choices.label: D
choices.body: Merging the scheduler into device drivers

hard.hint: A guitar is retuned, not rebuilt, for each song. Which choice adjusts knobs while the machinery stands still?
hard.explanation: MLFQ knobs (quanta, priorities, boost interval) are policy parameters; the underlying save/restore machinery is reused unchanged.
hard.deepDive: Picture tuning a guitar without rebuilding it: the strings and frets stay put while you adjust tension until the chord rings true. Multilevel feedback queues work the same way, with slice sizes and boost intervals as the tuning knobs over a fixed switching engine. Why it matters: this is the everyday workflow of systems tuning, where experiments stay cheap because the dangerous machinery never moves.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rewriting save/restore assembly for a tuning goal violates the split and risks breaking everything.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Removing timer interrupts destroys preemption, the very machinery policies rely on.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Folding scheduling into drivers tangles unrelated machinery instead of separating concerns.

hard.prompt: Your department buys a shared server and demands fairness across student jobs above raw speed. Following OSTEP's design advice, what do you change?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Change only the scheduling policy to favor the new goal, reusing the existing switching mechanism

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rewrite the trap handler and device drivers from scratch

choices.label: C
choices.body: Remove user-kernel modes to save crossing costs

choices.label: D
choices.body: Give every program direct hardware access

hard.hint: The streets stay, the traffic rules change. Which choice repaves nothing while serving the new goal?
hard.explanation: New goals should be expressed as new policies layered over proven mechanisms, minimizing risk and rework.
hard.deepDive: Treat it like a city changing bus priority lanes without repaving streets: the roads and signals remain while the routing rules shift toward the new goal. A fairness-first campus server therefore gets a new queuing rule, tested quickly because the context switcher and trap paths never changed. Why it matters: this is how real OS evolution happens, with bold policy experiments riding on boring stable machinery.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rewriting trap and driver machinery for a scheduling goal is maximum risk for minimum relevance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropping protection to save cycles trades away security for a scheduling concern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Direct hardware access abandons every protection lesson for no scheduling benefit.

hard.prompt: Why does stronger isolation typically reduce raw performance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Extra crossings and checks for isolation consume CPU time that could run programs

choices.label: B
choices.body: Virtualization creates additional physical CPUs

choices.label: C
choices.body: Isolation removes all need for scheduling

choices.label: D
choices.body: Protection checks make programs compute faster

hard.hint: Airport lines keep flights safe but nobody flies faster because of them. What does the OS security line cost?
hard.explanation: Protection is not free: each guarded crossing and validation burns cycles, which is the core performance-versus-protection trade-off.
hard.deepDive: Airport security keeps flights safe precisely by making every traveler wait in line: the screening is pure overhead on the journey. Mode crossings, permission checks, and page-table work are the OS security line, taxing each operation to keep neighbors isolated. Why it matters: quantifying this tax tells you when to batch crossings, and when the safety is worth every microsecond.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No new hardware appears; the same CPU now spends slices on guarding as well as running.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sharing still needs scheduling; isolation adds checks on top rather than removing the scheduler.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Checks add instructions to each path, so they slow the journey while making it safer.

hard.prompt: Two products share one OS: a medical monitor and a game console cache. How should their storage settings differ?

choices.label: A
choices.body: An always-flushed journal for a medical device versus batched writes for a video-game cache

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deleting the file system on both devices

choices.label: C
choices.body: Using identical settings because all systems want the same thing

choices.label: D
choices.body: Turning off all crash protection everywhere

hard.hint: A heart monitor and a game cache fear data loss very differently. Should their durability knobs match or differ?
hard.explanation: Different deployments weight goals differently: life-critical storage pays for maximum durability while caches trade it for speed.
hard.deepDive: Prescribe like a doctor: the heart monitor gets the strongest, slowest medicine because a lost heartbeat is unacceptable, while the game cache gets the fast, lossy syrup because a dropped texture is trivial. Same file-system machinery, opposite policy doses, each matched to what failure costs. Why it matters: great OS design is contextual, tuning identical mechanisms until each deployment's dominant goal wins.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Deleting storage dodges the design question instead of answering it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Identical settings ignore the chapter's lesson that goal weights differ by context.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Disabling protection everywhere serves neither the monitor's safety nor the cache's tuned speed.

hard.prompt: How can a program avoid accumulating zombies?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Call wait or waitpid in a loop, handle SIGCHLD, or double-fork so init adopts the worker.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Call exec in the parent so PIDs change automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Call fork more times to overwrite the zombie.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zombies cannot be avoided and must be ignored forever.

hard.hint: How can the ticket get claimed if the direct parent is busy?
hard.explanation: Reaping promptly or handing children to init prevents zombie buildup.
hard.deepDive: Think of zombies as unclaimed coat tickets that vanish once someone claims them or the booth changes hands. A wait loop claims each ticket promptly, SIGCHLD handling automates the pickup bell, and double-fork hands the worker directly to init. That is why servers loop on waitpid with no hang and daemons fork twice before starting work.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: exec transforms one process image and does nothing to reap terminated children.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: More forks create more children to reap rather than clearing existing zombies.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Standard reaping and adoption patterns reliably clear zombies.

hard.prompt: After fork with COW, the parent writes to a shared page. What happens?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The write traps, the kernel copies the page to a new frame, and remaps the writer privately with write permission.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both processes crash immediately with a segmentation fault.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The write goes through to the shared frame so both see it.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The kernel copies the entire address space on every single write.

hard.hint: Trace the fault: trap, copy one page, remap, resume.
hard.explanation: A protection fault upgrades one shared page into a private writable copy.
hard.deepDive: Follow one pencil stroke to the shared textbook page step by step. The read-only mark causes a protection trap into the kernel instead of corrupting the twin copy. The kernel photocopies just that page, updates the writer mapping to the fresh frame, and resumes the store, so only the writer sees the change.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: COW faults are handled transparently and are not fatal errors.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Allowing shared mutation would break process isolation after fork.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only the faulting page is copied, not the whole address space.

hard.prompt: Why is fork followed by exec much cheaper with COW?

choices.label: A
choices.body: COW is always slower because sharing adds overhead to every instruction.

choices.label: B
choices.body: fork plus exec is cheap with COW because most shared pages are discarded by exec without ever being copied.

choices.label: C
choices.body: COW removes the need for fork entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Page tables are not needed when COW is enabled.

hard.hint: How many pages does a forked child use before it execs?
hard.explanation: COW defers copies that exec usually makes unnecessary.
hard.deepDive: Think of photocopying a whole library just to glance at one new book title. Without COW, fork pays for every page up front even when the child immediately execs and throws them away. With COW the child shares pages briefly and exec drops them, paying only for page tables plus pages written before exec.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sharing avoids copies and wins whenever writes are few, which fork-plus-exec guarantees.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: fork still creates the child context, while COW only optimizes its memory cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: COW depends on page tables with read-only shared entries plus fault handling.

hard.prompt: Why can frequent context switches hurt performance beyond the switch code itself?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the few cycles that copy registers matter and caches are unaffected.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Switches are free because the CPU runs both processes simultaneously on one core.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Direct save-restore cycles plus indirect cache, TLB, and pipeline disruption after the switch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only disk seek time matters for context switches.

hard.hint: Ask what runs slower right after a new address space loads.
hard.explanation: Both the switch path and the polluted caches that follow cost performance.
hard.deepDive: Think of changing rally drivers plus driving the first miles with cold tires. The crew stopwatch time is the direct cost of saving registers and switching page tables. The cold-cache misses, TLB refills, and branch mispredictions afterward are the indirect tax that makes rapid switching painful.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: New address spaces typically miss in caches and TLBs, adding large indirect costs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One core runs one process at a time, so switches serialize rather than overlap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Switches are a CPU and memory-locality cost, not a disk-arm cost.

hard.prompt: Trace the shell pipeline ls | wc. Which steps are required?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Create one pipe, fork twice, dup each end onto stdin or stdout in the right child, close unused ends, exec each program, and wait for both.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Run both programs in the shell process with no pipe or fork.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Fork once and let both programs share the same stdout file description.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exec both programs in the same child process one after another.

hard.hint: Which ends must each child keep, and when does the reader see EOF?
hard.explanation: A pipe plus two redirected children plus two waits forms a pipeline.
hard.deepDive: Think of a restaurant pass window connecting the grill cook to the plating cook. The pipe call builds the window, two forks hire the cooks, and dup moves each window end onto stdin or stdout like relabeling doors. Closing spare ends matters because the reader sees end-of-file only after every write end closes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Separate programs need separate processes plus a kernel pipe between them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One fork gives one child, but a pipeline needs two children sharing one pipe.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One process image holds one program, so two programs need two execed children.

hard.prompt: How do output redirection ls > out and background jobs sleep & work?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Redirection dups a file onto stdin or stdout in the child before exec, and & forks without waiting so the shell prompts immediately.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Redirection edits the binary on disk and & disables fork entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Redirection only works for pipelines and & always waits for exit codes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Background jobs share the shell PID and need no fork.

hard.hint: Which call rewires descriptors, and which skipped call returns the prompt early?
hard.explanation: dup wires files into place and skipping wait makes a job run in background.
hard.deepDive: Think of rerouting a kitchen hose to a bucket before cooking and starting a slow stew you do not watch. Redirection dups the bucket file onto descriptor 0 or 1 in the child, then exec keeps that wiring. The ampersand skips the wait pickup, so the prompt returns at once while the job ticket stays listed for a later wait.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Redirection rewires descriptors at runtime rather than editing binaries, and background jobs still fork.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Redirection works for single commands too, and background means the shell does not wait yet.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Background jobs are separate processes with their own PIDs that the shell tracks.

hard.prompt: Stride: A stride 10 pass 0, B stride 20 pass 0. Rule: run lowest pass (ties → A), then pass += stride. What is the first-three run sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A, B, A

choices.label: B
choices.body: B, B, A

choices.label: C
choices.body: A, A, A (B starves)

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random each time like lottery

hard.hint: Step it: A0 vs B0 →A (A10); A10 vs B0 →B (B20); A10 vs B20 →A.
hard.explanation: Dispatch 1 A, 2 B, 3 A, giving exact 2:1 pacing over three slots.
hard.deepDive: Deterministic passes remove lottery variance while preserving proportions. B is guaranteed a slot by step 2, unlike a probabilistic draw. This predictability is stride's edge for tight share enforcement. Longer traces repeat the A,B,A pattern periodically.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: B cannot run twice first; after B's pass jumps to 20, A's 10 is lower.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: B never starves; its pass stays lowest every other round by construction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Randomness is lottery's property; stride is fully deterministic.

hard.prompt: Which best compares lottery/stride to SJF regarding knowledge and starvation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Proportional share needs no burst estimates and guarantees every holder nonzero share; SJF needs estimates and can starve longs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Lottery needs exact bursts to assign tickets.

choices.label: C
choices.body: SJF optimizes maximum turnaround so it never starves.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Stride requires a per-level quantum hierarchy like MLFQ.

hard.hint: Ask what each needs to decide: ticket counts vs length ranking, and who can wait forever.
hard.explanation: Tickets are administrative shares, not predictions; every ticket wins eventually, unlike SJF longs under endless shorts.
hard.deepDive: Proportional share trades average-optimality for controllability and fairness. Operators set importance via tickets without predicting service. Dynamic changes (ticket transfer, inflation) adjust shares at runtime. That flexibility is why lottery/stride suit shared servers over pure SJF.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tickets encode priority/share administratively, not measured bursts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SJF minimizes average, not max, and starvation is its classic flaw.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Quanta hierarchies belong to MLFQ; stride uses passes and strides only.

hard.prompt: Two CPUs. Design 1: single global ready queue with locking. Design 2: one queue per CPU with work stealing. What is the core tradeoff?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Global balances load automatically but lock contention + migration hurt affinity; per-CPU scales and preserves affinity but risks imbalance without stealing.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Global needs burst estimates; per-CPU needs no quanta.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Per-CPU always balances perfectly with zero migration cost.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Global eliminates cache effects so affinity is irrelevant.

hard.hint: Compare where the next idle CPU finds work vs what locking and moving jobs costs.
hard.explanation: A global queue self-balances but serializes on its lock and bounces jobs; per-CPU avoids locks and keeps cache warm but needs stealing to fix skew.
hard.deepDive: Scalability pushes toward per-CPU queues as core counts grow, since a single lock becomes a bottleneck. Affinity then becomes exploitable because jobs tend to rerun where their data is cached. Work stealing recovers balance by moving jobs only when a CPU idles.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Neither design needs burst predictions or abandons quanta; the issue is locking vs balance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Per-CPU alone imbalances freely; stealing is required and migration has cache cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Caches are per-core physical state; queue design cannot eliminate affinity effects.

hard.prompt: A job's working set is cached on CPU0. The scheduler considers moving it to idle CPU1. Why might it stay on CPU0 despite the idle core?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cache affinity: warm cache hits on CPU0 outweigh waiting; migration pays cold-miss + coherence costs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Affinity lets the job skip its burst (burst prediction improves).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Migration removes the need for quanta on CPU1.

choices.label: D
choices.body: EDF deadlines are always met by staying put.

hard.hint: Weigh a short wait for a warm cache against immediate run with cold misses.
hard.explanation: Rerunning where data is cached avoids refetching lines; moving trades queue delay for miss latency.
hard.deepDive: Affinity-aware schedulers briefly prefer the home CPU, migrating only when imbalance exceeds the miss penalty. Last-level cache and TLB warmth can be worth microseconds to milliseconds. Blind migration optimizes queue length while pessimizing memory latency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Affinity does not change service time estimates; it changes memory latency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Quanta are orthogonal; migration never removes time-slicing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: EDF guarantees are unrelated to cache placement under overload.

hard.prompt: CPU0 queue: three 10ms jobs (30ms). CPU1 idle. Migration cost ~2ms of cold misses. What should a work-stealing scheduler do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Steal one job to CPU1 (≈12ms vs 30ms makespan despite 2ms cost).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Keep all on CPU0 to preserve affinity at any imbalance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Require burst estimates before any steal (SJF first).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Round-robin quanta of 0.01ms to hide the imbalance.

hard.hint: Compare makespan 30 vs balanced ~15+2; steal only because surplus exceeds cost.
hard.explanation: Moving one 10ms job lets CPUs finish in ~20 and ~12ms; 2ms penalty is far below the 18ms idle saving.
hard.deepDive: Stealing thresholds weigh queue surplus against migration cost to avoid thrashing. Small imbalances stay put for affinity; large ones migrate. Periodic balancing (not per-tick) amortizes the decision overhead. This cost-benefit framing generalizes beyond the numbers here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Absolute affinity wastes a whole core; affinity is a preference, not a veto.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stealing balances queue length, not burst order; no prediction is needed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tiny quanta add switch overhead without moving work across cores.

hard.prompt: Four CPUs each with local queues; brief imbalance is common but affinity matters. Which balancing policy fits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Periodic rebalance + steal only when a CPU idles; otherwise keep jobs home.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Migrate a random job on every timer tick to equalize counts exactly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Single global queue with a giant lock for perfect balance.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Pin every job forever; never migrate regardless of idleness.

hard.hint: Prefer the option that migrates rarely (idle-triggered) over always-migrate or never-migrate.
hard.explanation: Idle-triggered stealing plus infrequent rebalance fixes real skew while preserving warm caches in the common case.
hard.deepDive: Continuous migration churns caches for negligible balance gains. Linux-style schedulers therefore balance on wake/idle paths and periodic ticks with decaying domains. Strict pinning wastes cores and strict global locking bottlenecks. Lazy balancing is the engineered middle.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Per-tick random migration maximizes coherence traffic for transient skew.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A giant global lock serializes all scheduling decisions as cores scale.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Never migrating strands capacity idle while others queue deeply.

hard.prompt: Low-priority L holds a lock, high-priority H blocks on it, medium-priority M (runnable, no lock) preempts L. What is this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Priority inversion: H waits indirectly on M via L's delayed critical section.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Convoy effect from FCFS ordering by arrival.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stride scheduling enforcing proportional shares.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A cache-affinity migration penalty.

hard.hint: Trace who blocks whom: H→L (lock), but M→L (preemption) extends H's wait.
hard.explanation: H, highest priority, ends up waiting for M, a lower job, because M stretches L's lock hold.
hard.deepDive: Fixed priorities break down when locks couple jobs across levels. The Mars Pathfinder reset was this exact pattern. Bounded blocking requires either preventing M's preemption or boosting L. Inheritance, covered next, is the standard boost.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Convoy needs no locks or priorities — just a long job ahead of shorts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stride paces by tickets/passes, unrelated to lock blocking chains.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Affinity is about cache warmth on multicore, not priority blocking.

hard.prompt: To fix the L/M/H inversion above, the kernel temporarily runs L at H's priority until L releases the lock. What is this?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Priority inheritance: L borrows H's priority to preempt M and exit quickly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Priority boost of all jobs to top MLFQ queue every 100ms.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Lottery ticket inflation for L permanently.

choices.label: D
choices.body: EDF rescheduling by earliest deadline.

hard.hint: Ask whose priority L runs at during the critical section, and when it drops back.
hard.explanation: L inherits H's priority, so M cannot preempt; on unlock L drops to its own priority and H proceeds.
hard.deepDive: Inheritance bounds H's blocking to one critical section instead of M's whole burst. Chains nest transitively if L itself blocks on another lock. Priority ceiling variants pre-assign bounds to avoid deadlocks. Without this, real-time priorities are unenforceable with locks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MLFQ boost is periodic anti-starvation, not lock-aware temporary borrowing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Permanent inflation distorts shares; inheritance is scoped to the lock hold.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: EDF reorders by deadline but does not itself unblock lock holders.

hard.prompt: Real-time jobs with deadlines: A deadline 10, B deadline 5, C deadline 8 (all ready). EDF runs which order?

choices.label: A
choices.body: B, C, A (earliest deadline first)

choices.label: B
choices.body: A, C, B (latest deadline first)

choices.label: C
choices.body: Shortest burst first regardless of deadlines

choices.label: D
choices.body: Round-robin fixed quanta ignoring deadlines

hard.hint: Sort by deadline numbers ascending; that sorted order is the EDF schedule.
hard.explanation: Deadlines sorted are B=5, C=8, A=10, so EDF runs B then C then A.
hard.deepDive: EDF is dynamic: priority is urgency, recomputed as jobs arrive with new deadlines. It differs from SJF (burst) and fixed priority (static rank). Optimality holds only under the feasibility condition examined next.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Latest-first maximizes lateness; it inverts EDF's rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Burst-first is SJF/SRTF, which can miss urgent deadlines for short lax jobs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deadline-blind rotation provides fairness, not timeliness.

hard.prompt: Two periodic tasks each need 2 units every 3 units (U = 2/3 + 2/3 = 1.33). What does EDF do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Misses deadlines (overloaded: U > 1 means no schedule meets all deadlines, EDF included).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Meets all deadlines because EDF works under any overload.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Meets all deadlines by switching to SJF burst order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Meets all deadlines if quanta are removed (MLFQ needs no quanta).

hard.hint: Add utilizations: demand 4 per 3 exceeds capacity 3 per 3 — can any scheduler fit?
hard.explanation: Demand exceeds capacity (1.33 > 1), so deadlines necessarily miss; EDF cannot conjure CPU.
hard.deepDive: EDF is optimal only up to U ≤ 1 on uniprocessors: if EDF misses, nothing could succeed. Overload needs admission control or degraded modes, not a smarter order. Assuming EDF survives overload is the classic real-time misconception.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No algorithm meets all deadlines with U > 1; EDF's optimality is bounded by feasibility.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SJF ignores deadlines, so it cannot rescue an overloaded deadline set.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Removing quanta does not create capacity; MLFQ concepts are irrelevant to feasibility.

hard.prompt: Which statement about EDF vs fixed-priority (Rate Monotonic) is true for periodic tasks on one CPU?

choices.label: A
choices.body: EDF can use up to 100% CPU (U ≤ 1); RM guarantees only ~69% in the worst case.

choices.label: B
choices.body: RM uses 100% while EDF stalls at 69%.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both ignore deadlines and optimize maximum turnaround.

choices.label: D
choices.body: EDF needs no deadlines because tickets encode urgency.

hard.hint: Recall the Liu & Layland bounds: dynamic deadlines achieve full utilization, static periods do not.
hard.explanation: EDF's dynamic urgency attains the U ≤ 1 feasibility bound; static RM can miss even at U ≈ 0.7 adversarially.
hard.deepDive: RM's simplicity (priority by period) costs schedulable utilization in pathological phasings. EDF adapts per-job urgency to reclaim that gap. Both still need inheritance protocols when sharing locks. Overload still requires admission regardless of choice.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This swaps the bounds; RM is the conservative one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both are deadline schedulers; max-turnaround is not their objective.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tickets are lottery/stride shares, not EDF deadlines.

hard.prompt: System: interactive editors + batch compiles on 4 CPUs + one soft real-time audio task (deadline 10ms, needs 2ms). Which design fits all, using ideas in order?

choices.label: A
choices.body: MLFQ with affinity-aware per-CPU queues + steal on idle, and admit/guard the audio task (reserve 20%) with inheritance on its locks.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Pure FCFS single queue; EDF works overloaded so audio is safe.

choices.label: C
choices.body: SJF with exact bursts for all; SJF optimizes max so audio never misses.

choices.label: D
choices.body: RR with 0.001ms quantum and migrate every tick; MLFQ needs no quanta.

hard.hint: Compose prior fixes: MLFQ for mix, affinity+steal for multicore, reservation+inheritance for real-time.
hard.explanation: MLFQ separates interactive/batch, per-CPU+steal scales with affinity, reservation keeps U ≤ 1 for audio, inheritance bounds lock blocking.
hard.deepDive: No single policy covers batch, interactive, multicore, and real-time alone. Reservation-based admission prevents the overload failure EDF would otherwise hit. Inheritance closes the inversion hole that priorities alone leave. Together they synthesize the chapter's chain end to end.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: FCFS convoys interactives and EDF provably misses when overloaded.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Bursts are unknowable for editors and SJF targets average, not deadlines or max.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Microsecond quanta drown in switch overhead and per-tick migration thrashes caches.

hard.prompt: P1: base=10000 limit=2000. P2: base=30000 limit=2000. P1 accesses virtual 100, then OS switches to P2 which accesses virtual 100. Results?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Same physical 100 in both — virtual equals physical.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both trap — address 100 is reserved for the OS.

choices.label: B
choices.body: P1 → physical 10100, P2 → physical 30100; same virtual, different physical.

choices.label: D
choices.body: P1 → physical 30100, P2 → physical 10100 (swapped).

hard.hint: Check-then-add per process: is 100 < 2000? Then physical = which base + 100 for P1 vs P2?
hard.explanation: OS swaps base/bound on switch (PCB-saved); same virtual maps to base+virtual per process.
hard.deepDive: Context switch here is two stores: save outgoing base/bound into its PCB, load incoming pair into registers — the Ch1-2 PCB-pointer idea extended to memory. Trace P1's access 100: 100 < 2000 passes, 10000+100 relocates to 10100; after the switch the same virtual 100 with P2's base maps to 30100. One virtual, two physicals — relocation plus isolation in a single switch.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Ignores base — without +base there is no relocation or isolation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 100 is well within 2000; nothing reserved about low virtual addresses here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bases are not swapped — each process uses its own base from its PCB.

hard.prompt: `char *p = malloc(32); free(p); *p = 'x';` No new malloc shown, but heap is in use. Worst-case consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Safe — freed memory is zeroed and unmapped so reuse traps.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Safe — it behaves exactly like a leak with no corruption.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Guaranteed immediate segfault on the very next line.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Dangling-pointer bug: the block may be re-malloc'd elsewhere, so the write corrupts a live object / enables exploits.

hard.hint: Combine Q7 (free recycles) + Q15 (reuse): if malloc hands that block to new code, who does `*p` now overwrite?
hard.explanation: Use-after-free writes into recycled heap, corrupting whoever now owns the block.
hard.deepDive: Free does not scrub the pointer or fence the bytes — `p` still aims at a recyclable block, like a hotel key that still opens the room after checkout. If another malloc takes that room, `*p = ...` silently rewrites the new guest's data, far from the original bug. The fix discipline is ownership: null the pointer, or better, define exactly one owner who frees exactly once.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No zero/unmap guarantee in C allocators — the bytes sit reusable in the free list.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Worse than a leak — a leak wastes, use-after-free actively corrupts live data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: May crash, may silently corrupt — no guaranteed immediate trap without sanitizers.

hard.prompt: Stack region 8KB, each `f` frame 64 bytes, `f` recurses infinitely. How deep before stack overflow?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ~8 calls — one frame per KB.

choices.label: B
choices.body: ~128 calls (8192/64); the 129th push overflows the stack region.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Unlimited — stacks grow into heap automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exactly 1 call — recursion is forbidden on stacks.

hard.hint: Capacity ÷ per-frame cost = depth. 8KB is 8192 bytes; each frame 64 bytes. Divide, then what does one more call do?
hard.explanation: Stack capacity / frame size = max depth; exceeding it overflows (fault/collision).
hard.deepDive: Overflow math is just division with a trap at the end: bytes reserved divided by bytes per frame caps live depth. 8KB/64B ≈ 128 frames — call 129 deep and the stack pointer crosses its bound into unmapped space (or heap) and faults. Real stacks add guard pages to fail fast here instead of silently colliding with the heap gap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Inverted the division — depth is capacity/frame, not frames/capacity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stacks do not annex heap silently — overflow faults or collides; growth needs OS guard/extension.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Recursion is legal — each call legitimately pushes a frame until space runs out.

hard.prompt: Function needs a 10MB buffer, or must return a buffer to its caller. Stack frame or malloc'd heap?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always use stack — it is faster so size/lifetime do not matter.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always use heap — stack frames are deprecated.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Use heap/malloc when size is large/runtime-known or lifetime must outlive the return; else bounded locals can live in the frame.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Store return addresses on the heap for safety.

hard.hint: What happens to a frame's bytes on return? If the data must survive, or might overflow 8KB, where must it live?
hard.explanation: Match lifetime/size to owner: frame for call-scoped bounded locals, heap for large/dynamic/escaping data.
hard.deepDive: Frames are hotel rooms: checkout (return) clears them automatically, so sleeping there after checkout (returning a stack pointer) is a dangling-room bug, and moving in oversized furniture (multi-MB array) floods the floor. Heap is a rented storage unit: you choose when to vacate with free, so it fits big or long-lived data at the cost of manual bookkeeping. The rule is ownership-duration, not speed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Speed does not fix overflow or dangling — 10MB blows a typical stack; returned stack memory dangles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Stack is not deprecated — call-scoped locals belong there with zero bookkeeping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Return addresses live in frames by calling convention; heap-storing them breaks unwind.

hard.prompt: Page size 4KB. Segments used: code 3KB, heap 5KB, stack 1KB, each page-rounded. Total internal waste?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 7KB: code wastes 1KB (4-3), heap wastes 3KB (8-5), stack wastes 3KB (4-1).

choices.label: B
choices.body: 0KB — segmentation has no internal waste.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 15KB — sum of all segment sizes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 4KB — one page per segment regardless of use.

hard.hint: Round each segment UP to 4KB pages first: 3→4, 5→8, 1→4. Then waste = allocated − used per segment. Sum?
hard.explanation: Internal waste = sum over segments of (pages*pageSize - used).
hard.deepDive: Compute per segment: round each up to whole pages, subtract used — padding is billed per owner. Code 3KB→4KB wastes 1, heap 5KB→8KB wastes 3, stack 1KB→4KB wastes 3, totaling 7KB that no other segment can borrow. That per-owner rounding bill is the signature of internal fragmentation: shrinking pages (smaller quanta) is the only structural fix.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Page rounding always wastes unless exactly full — segmentation over pages still pads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Total waste is padding only, not the data itself.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Undercounts — heap 5KB needs two pages (8KB), not one.

hard.prompt: Allocator coalesces adjacent free blocks. Which fragmentation does this help, and why not the other?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It fixes both equally by compacting all memory.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It fixes internal waste by shrinking page size.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It has no effect on either kind.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It fixes external (merges adjacent frees into bigger runs) but not internal (padding inside owned pages stays).

hard.hint: Where does coalescing operate — inside your owned page, or in the free gaps between blocks? Which kind lives there?
hard.explanation: Coalescing merges free gaps (external) but cannot reclaim padding inside allocated units (internal).
hard.deepDive: Coalescing is parking-lot maintenance: joining adjacent free spots into longer runs helps the next bus (big contiguous ask) but does nothing about half-empty cars already parked (owned-page padding). That asymmetry is the diagnostic: if total-free ≥ request yet allocation fails, you have external and coalescing/compaction helps; if waste scales with page size, you have internal and need smaller quanta. One fix never cures both.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No compaction of owned pages happens — internal padding is untouched.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Denies a real effect — merging frees directly grows max contiguous free run.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Confuses the fixes — shrinking quanta helps internal; coalescing helps external.

hard.prompt: Why mark stack (and heap data) non-executable (NX) while code is executable?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stack must be executable so returns run faster.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Stack/data marked non-executable trap injected code; only code segment executes — blocks classic buffer-overflow exploits.

choices.label: C
choices.body: X bit lets the scheduler execute processes in priority order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: X bit removes all fragmentation on the stack.

hard.hint: Attack: overflow stack with malicious bytes, then jump there. Which permission bit turns that jump into a trap?
hard.explanation: NX enforces data-vs-code intent: injected stack/heap bytes cannot be fetched as instructions.
hard.deepDive: The NX (no-execute) bit turns the stack from a launchpad into a dead end for attackers: overflowed bytes may still land there, but jumping to them faults instead of running a smuggled shellcode. This is per-segment protection grown up — intent (data, not code) enforced by hardware on every fetch. Real exploits then pivot to return-oriented tricks, proving the bit raised the bar rather than ending the war.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Executable stacks enable exploits; speed comes from caching, not X on data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scheduling priority is unrelated to fetch permission.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Execute bits trap fetches; they do not rearrange or compact memory.

hard.prompt: Two processes use shared `libc` code but separate data. Correct sharing + protection setup?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Share the stack read-write so threads share locals.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Share code read-write so processes can patch bugs jointly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Map one physical code copy read-only+executable into both; keep each data/heap/stack private read-write (non-executable).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Share all segments fully so virtual equals physical.

hard.hint: Two rules at once: share only immutable (which segment?) with which perms, and keep mutable (which?) private?
hard.explanation: Share immutable code R-X; privatize mutable state RW — memory savings with isolation intact.
hard.deepDive: The mature pattern combines both ideas: share what is immutable (code/lib, R-X, one physical copy) and privatize what mutates (data/heap/stack, RW-, per-process frames). Each process sees the library at its own virtual address yet executes shared physical bytes — saving DRAM without breaking isolation. Making shared code writable would let one crash or attack rewrite everyone's execution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Shared stacks alias return addresses/locals across processes — corruption, not a feature (threads are the separate exception).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: W sisters — writable shared code lets one process corrupt all sharers; code must be R-only.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Full sharing abandons virtualization/isolation — the Ch1 motive this chapter implements.

hard.prompt: Why do stack locals need no `free` while heap blocks do? State the ownership rule.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Heap needs no free because the OS scans and frees garbage automatically.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Stack reclaims by popping on return (no free needed); heap needs explicit free with clear ownership, else leaks/dangling.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both need manual free per variable or both leak identically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Stack frames leak until process exit; heap pops automatically.

hard.hint: Which region's bytes vanish at the `ret` instruction? What does that imply for who must clean the other region?
hard.explanation: Stack lifetime = call scope (auto-pop); heap lifetime = manual (owner frees once).
hard.deepDive: Ownership is the synthesis of the chapter: stack lifetimes are tied to call scope, so the return instruction is an automatic free — bounded, LIFO, zero bookkeeping. Heap lifetimes are programmer-defined, surviving any return, so exactly one owner must free exactly once — flexible but leak/double-free/use-after-free prone. Choosing stack vs heap is thus choosing who decides death: callee-return or human-owner.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: C has no GC — un-freed heap stays live until exit; the scan-and-free is a managed-language idea.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Conflates the two — only heap needs manual free; stack pops deterministically.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reversed — stack pops promptly, heap lingers until freed/exit.

hard.prompt: Same VA 0x12345678. Compare splits for 4-KB vs 1-MB pages. What does it prove?

choices.label: A
choices.body: VPN = 0x12, offset = 0x345678 (24-bit offset)

choices.label: B
choices.body: VPN = 0x12345, offset = 0x678 with 4-KB pages; with 1-MB pages VPN = 0x123, offset = 0x45678

choices.label: C
choices.body: Page size never changes the split

choices.label: D
choices.body: PID occupies the top VPN bits in both cases

hard.hint: How many hex digits are 12 vs 20 offset bits? Re-split the same VA.
hard.explanation: Offset width follows page size: 12 bits vs 20 bits for the same VA.
hard.deepDive: Same VA splits differently by page size: 1-MB pages need 20 offset bits (5 hex digits), leaving VPN 0x123. Comparing both splits of one address proves the split point is log2(page size), not a fixed constant. Large pages thus shrink tables but coarsen protection and inflate internal waste.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 24-bit offset would be 16-MB pages, not 4 KB.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Directly contradicted: offset = log2(page size) moves with page size.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: PID is never VA bits; tables are per-process.

hard.prompt: PTE: valid = 0, present = 1, RW = 1, dirty = 0. A load hits it. What happens and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Write-back the page and resume the store

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fetch from disk; it is demand paging

choices.label: C
choices.body: Trap as illegal access (valid = 0 dominates); never consult present/dirty

choices.label: D
choices.body: Allow it; supervisor bit overrides valid

hard.hint: In what order should hardware test bits? What if the entry is garbage?
hard.explanation: Validity is checked first; other bits are don't-cares when valid = 0.
hard.deepDive: Valid = 0 short-circuits everything: the VPN is unmapped so present, RW, and dirty are meaningless. Hardware must check valid first and trap to the OS, which segfaults. Designs that check permission or residency first risk leaking or fetching for addresses the process never owned.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Write-back applies to dirty evictions of valid pages, not to invalid accesses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Disk fetch requires valid = 1; invalid has no backing to fetch.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Supervisor/user is checked after valid; it cannot resurrect an unmapped VPN.

hard.prompt: PTE: valid = 1, present = 1, RW = 1, U/S = 0 (kernel-only). User-mode store hits it. Result?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fault — user store to a kernel-only page; trap to OS (segfault/kill)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Succeed — RW = 1 allows all writes

choices.label: C
choices.body: Page fault to disk — present must be 0

choices.label: D
choices.body: Succeed — TLB caches override permission

hard.hint: RW says writable-by-whom? Which bit says user vs kernel?
hard.explanation: U/S denies user access to kernel page even though writable; RW alone is insufficient.
hard.deepDive: User/supervisor is a second permission axis orthogonal to RW: kernel pages are RW = 1 but U/S = supervisor, so user stores trap despite writability. This is how one table protects the kernel mapping in every address space. Meltdown/Spectre history shows why this bit's enforcement point matters.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ignores the privilege axis; RW without U/S check would expose the kernel.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Present = 1 so resident; this is protection, not paging I/O.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TLB entries cache permission bits too; they cannot grant what the PTE denies.

hard.prompt: Two-level page table, no TLB vs TLB hit: memory refs per load?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 1 ref — TLB always hits

choices.label: B
choices.body: 2 refs — same as single-level

choices.label: C
choices.body: 3 refs for a hit, 2 for a miss

choices.label: D
choices.body: 3 refs per access without TLB (2-level walk + data); TLB hit cuts to 1

hard.hint: Count one read per table level, plus the data itself. Then add a TLB hit path.
hard.explanation: Levels add refs linearly: L levels → L + 1 refs; TLB converts common case to 1.
hard.deepDive: A two-level walk reads directory then table then data: two translation refs plus data. Without locality that triples DRAM traffic, which is exactly why TLBs with >99% hit rates are mandatory. This cost model justifies TLB reach, ASIDs, and huge pages as first-order performance, not micro-optimization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Assumes 100% TLB hits; misses and cold starts still walk.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Forgets the directory level; that is the single-level cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inverts hit/miss costs; a hit is cheapest.

hard.prompt: Why is linear-table space overhead the dominant cost for small sparse processes?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Linear tables waste no memory on sparse spaces

choices.label: B
choices.body: A 10-KB process in a 4-GB space still pays a ~4-MB linear table — larger than itself

choices.label: C
choices.body: Walk cost drops to zero with big tables

choices.label: D
choices.body: Inodes shrink the table

hard.hint: Compare table bytes (virtual-sized) to process bytes (use-sized) for a tiny program.
hard.explanation: Virtual-proportional metadata vs use-proportional data — sparse pays most.
hard.deepDive: Table cost tracks virtual size while process cost tracks used bytes, so tiny sparse processes drown in metadata. A 10-KB footprint paying megabytes of table is the canonical absurdity. Multilevel trees fix it by allocating table pages only for populated VPN ranges.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Opposite: sparse pays for every hole VPN.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Bigger tables cost more refs/space, never zero refs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: inodes are filesystem metadata, unrelated to page-table size.

hard.prompt: Synthesize seg-vs-paging across fragmentation, sparsity, and sharing.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Paging wins on external frag + sparse validity, loses table space; segmentation wins sparsity metadata, loses external frag + coarse sharing

choices.label: B
choices.body: Paging always wins on every axis

choices.label: C
choices.body: Segmentation always wins; paging is obsolete

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither handles sparsity; need inodes

hard.hint: List three axes: frag, sparse metadata, sharing grain. Who wins each?
hard.explanation: Trade is frag type vs metadata vs sharing granularity; hybrids blend strengths.
hard.deepDive: No scheme dominates: paging's fixed frames kill external fragmentation and express holes per page but pay table space; segmentation's bounds describe holes free but fragment memory and share coarsely. Naming the axes — fragmentation, sparsity cost, sharing granularity — is the synthesis that motivates hybrids and multilevel paging as Pareto compromises.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ignores linear-table blowup on sparse spaces.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ignores external fragmentation that motivated paging.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: inodes index files, not address-space sparsity.

hard.prompt: 32-bit space, 4-KB pages, 4-B PTEs. Code 1 MB + heap 1 MB + stack 16 KB under hybrid seg-paging. Approx table bytes vs 4-MB linear?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 4 MB always, same as linear

choices.label: B
choices.body: 0 bytes — segments need no tables

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only populated segments pay: e.g. 3 small segments → 3 small tables, holes free

choices.label: D
choices.body: One entry per byte of segment

hard.hint: Size each segment's table as segment-bytes / page-size × entry-size. What about gaps?
hard.explanation: Per-segment tables ∝ segment size; unallocated inter-segment space costs zero.
hard.deepDive: Hybrid table bytes scale with segment size, not address-space size: a 1-MB segment with 4-KB pages needs 256 entries (~1 KB), not 1M. Summed over live segments this is orders smaller than linear for sparse programs. The residual cost is one table page minimum per segment plus the segment-check step.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the linear cost hybrid avoids; hybrid pays per segment.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Live segments still need entries for their VPNs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Entries are per page, not per byte.

hard.prompt: Under hybrid seg-paging, in what order are segment-bounds and PTE-permission checks applied, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bounds-check segment, then page-lookup within it — illegal cross-segment refs trap before memory is touched

choices.label: B
choices.body: Skip bounds; page tables alone protect

choices.label: C
choices.body: Store PID in VA upper bits, then walk

choices.label: D
choices.body: Consult the inode for segment permission

hard.hint: Which check is cheaper and broader? Should it run first?
hard.explanation: Segment check first (coarse), PTE check second (fine); both must pass.
hard.deepDive: Two-stage protection composes: segment bounds give coarse isolation between stack/heap/code, PTE bits give fine per-page RW. A wild pointer crossing segments fails fast at stage one even if some PTE alias looks plausible. This layering is why Multics-style hybrids influenced x86 segmentation plus paging.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tables alone lose inter-segment isolation; bounds add a cheap outer fence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real misconception: PID is register state, not address bits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Real misconception: inodes never mediate memory protection.

hard.prompt: How does page size trade internal fragmentation against table size?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Larger pages always reduce total waste

choices.label: B
choices.body: Smaller pages always reduce total waste to zero

choices.label: C
choices.body: Table size is unaffected by page size

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bigger pages shrink tables but grow average last-page waste (~page/2 per segment)

hard.hint: If waste averages half a page per segment, what happens when the page doubles?
hard.explanation: Waste ∝ page size; table ∝ 1/page size — cannot minimize both with one size.
hard.deepDive: Expected waste per segment is half a page if sizes are uniform mod page, so total ≈ s·P/2. Doubling P halves entry count but doubles expected waste — a direct quantity trade. Designers pick 4 KB as a middle ground, then add huge pages for TLB reach where waste is acceptable.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Forgets the waste side; tables shrink but tails grow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Smaller pages shrink waste but explode entry count — and waste never hits zero unless aligned.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Entry count = space/page, so size always matters.

hard.prompt: 64-KB pages. Segments ≈ 48 KB + 40 KB + 32 KB. Approx total internal waste?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ~4 KB

choices.label: B
choices.body: ~72 KB (16 KB + 24 KB + 32 KB tails)

choices.label: C
choices.body: 0 — 64-KB pages eliminate frag

choices.label: D
choices.body: 192 KB (3 full pages)

hard.hint: Round each segment up to 64 KB first. How much tail each?
hard.deepDive: Each small segment wastes most of a 64-KB page: 48-KB wastes 16 KB, 40-KB wastes 24 KB, 32-KB wastes 32 KB, totaling ~72 KB. That is ~16x the waste with 4-KB pages for the same data. This blowup is why huge pages are opt-in per region, not global.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the 4-KB-page regime; 16× bigger pages → ~16× waste.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Bigger pages maximize, not eliminate, internal waste.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Waste is tails only, not whole pages; full pages are fully used.

hard.prompt: How does fork use PTE protections to share-then-split memory (copy-on-write)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mark all PTEs read-only forever

choices.label: B
choices.body: Copy every page at fork time

choices.label: C
choices.body: Parent + child alias same PFN read-only; on write, trap, copy frame, install writable private PTE, resume
