choices.label: D
choices.body: Share one page table between parent and child

hard.hint: How could the OS detect the first write to a shared page and split just in time?
hard.explanation: Alias R/O, fault on first write, copy that page only — lazy privatization.
hard.deepDive: Copy-on-write starts as sharing then lazily privatizes: aliased read-only PTEs make the first store to each page trap. The OS copies that page only, flips the faulting PTE writable to the new PFN, and resumes — amortizing fork cost to touched pages. Dirty and RW bits implement the trap-and-split without app involvement.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Permanent R/O would break all writes; COW flips to writable after copy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Eager copy is correct but slow — COW's point is avoiding it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tables must stay per-process so later splits diverge; only PFNs alias.

hard.prompt: You computed ~512 GB for a 48-bit linear table. What is the architectural conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ~4 MB — same as 32-bit

choices.label: B
choices.body: ~8 MB

choices.label: C
choices.body: ~1 GB

choices.label: D
choices.body: ~512 GB, so a flat array is impossible — need multilevel / segmented tables

hard.hint: Compare your computed bytes to a machine's RAM. What design must follow?
hard.explanation: Virtual-proportional sizing breaks past 32 bits; hierarchical tables pay per used branch.
hard.deepDive: 2^36 PTEs × 8 B ≈ 512 GB per process dwarfs DRAM, ruling out any linear design on 48-bit spaces. Multilevel trees allocate only populated branches, collapsing sparse holes to null pointers. This single number justifies the entire x86-64 4-level and ARM table architecture.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Misses 2^16 growth from 32→48 bits (65536×).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Only doubles entry size; ignores 2^16 more entries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Undercounts by 512×; check 2^36 × 2^3 = 2^39.

hard.prompt: ASIDs, global pages, and shootdowns: what still forces a TLB flush?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ASID-tagged entries can stay resident across switches; only unmap/protect changes need shootdown, plus global kernel entries never flush

choices.label: B
choices.body: ASIDs mean the TLB never needs any flush ever again

choices.label: C
choices.body: Global bit forces user pages to be shared

choices.label: D
choices.body: Shootdowns are needed on every TLB hit

hard.hint: Separate two flush causes: process switch vs a mapping becoming invalid while CPUs run.
hard.explanation: ASIDs skip switch flushes, but mapping changes still need cross-CPU shootdowns; global pages are exempt.
hard.deepDive: With ASIDs, entries from multiple processes coexist, so switches skip the flush. But correctness still requires invalidation when mappings change: munmap/mprotect must shoot down stale entries on all CPUs running that ASID (IPI). The global bit exempts kernel mappings shared by all spaces from flushing. So ASIDs remove switch flushes, not coherence flushes -- the stretch subtlety.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Unmap/protect still stale-caches without shootdown; ASIDs only fix the switch case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Global marks shared kernel pages, never user pages.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Hits use valid entries; shootdowns happen on unmap/protect, not on hits.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: TLB=2ns, mem=100ns, two-level tables, TLB miss rate 8%. What is the expected page-walk contribution to EAT?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 16 ns (0.08 x 200ns for two table reads)

choices.label: B
choices.body: 200 ns

choices.label: C
choices.body: 8 ns

choices.label: D
choices.body: 100 ns

hard.hint: Add three layers: always-pay base, sometimes-pay walk, rarely-pay disk -- compute each separately.
hard.explanation: Walk contribution is 16 ns: 8 percent times two table reads of 100 ns each.
hard.deepDive: Compose EAT term by term: always-pay base, sometimes-pay walk, rarely-pay disk. Here the walk term is 8 percent of 200, which is 16 ns. This decomposition keeps multilevel plus swap problems organized.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 200ns is the cost of one miss, not weighted by the 8% rate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 8ns uses one table read instead of two levels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 100ns is a single memory read, unrelated to the miss-rate weighting.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: When do huge pages help vs hurt?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Huge pages remove page tables and faults

choices.label: B
choices.body: Huge pages cut TLB pressure and table levels for dense regions but waste memory on small sparse segments and still need tables

choices.label: C
choices.body: Huge pages always beat small pages for every workload

choices.label: D
choices.body: Huge pages make swapping free

hard.hint: Ask where huge pages win (large dense) vs lose (tiny sparse): what happens to leftover bytes?
hard.explanation: Huge pages trade fewer entries and TLB slots for internal fragmentation; tables remain but shallower.
hard.deepDive: A 1GB x86-64 huge page maps with one directory entry where small pages need three levels plus 262k PTEs, and one TLB entry covers 1GB. But a 4KB stack in a 2MB page wastes ~2MB, and swapping granularity coarsens. OSes therefore use huge pages for heap/code monsters and small pages elsewhere (THP does this adaptively). The misconception to kill is removal: tables shrink, they do not vanish.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Tables persist (fewer levels) and not-present huge pages still fault.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sparse/small workloads fragment badly under huge pages.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Paging a 2MB page costs more I/O per fault, not less.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: Why does Clock only approximate LRU? Give the mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Clock may evict a different page than true LRU because one ref bit cannot encode full recency order

choices.label: B
choices.body: Clock and LRU are identical on all traces

choices.label: C
choices.body: Clock needs future knowledge

choices.label: D
choices.body: LRU needs no per-access bookkeeping

hard.hint: Construct two pages both with ref=1 but different last-touch times: what can each policy distinguish?
hard.explanation: One bit per page loses ordering among recently-touched pages, so Clock only approximates LRU.
hard.deepDive: LRU keeps total recency order; Clock keeps one visited-recently bit per page. Two pages both with ref=1 are indistinguishable to Clock, so hand position breaks the tie arbitrarily while LRU would evict the older. On scans and loops this diverges visibly. Clock trades exactness for O(1) software cost with hardware-set bits -- usually good enough.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Identity fails on any trace with multiple ref=1 pages; hand order decides.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Future knowledge is OPT, never Clock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Exact LRU needs timestamps or stacks updated on every access -- its real cost.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: Why are LRU/OPT immune to Belady while FIFO is not?

choices.label: A
choices.body: LRU can fault more with more frames

choices.label: B
choices.body: OPT is implementable with a large TLB

choices.label: C
choices.body: LRU and OPT are stack algorithms: the set with N frames is always a subset of N+1, so faults never increase

choices.label: D
choices.body: FIFO never shows Belady if run slowly

hard.hint: Think nested sets: when does the small-memory resident set sit inside the big-memory one?
hard.explanation: Stack inclusion guarantees monotonic improvement; FIFO lacks it, LRU/OPT have it.
hard.deepDive: Stack property means the N most-recently-used pages are identical regardless of capacity, so growing from N to N+1 can only turn faults into hits. LRU satisfies this by definition; OPT satisfies it via future-distance ordering. FIFO's queue order depends on capacity history, breaking nesting. This proof is why LRU is Belady-immune and FIFO is not.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: LRU immunity is the theorem; claiming otherwise repeats the misconception.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No hardware reveals the future; OPT stays a yardstick.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Speed never changes victim choice; the anomaly is capacity-dependent, not timing.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: How does enhanced Clock (ref + dirty bits) pick a victim?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always evict the page with ref=1

choices.label: B
choices.body: Prefer (ref=0,clean) over (ref=0,dirty) over (ref=1,clean) over (ref=1,dirty): skip recently used and avoid writebacks

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ignore the dirty bit entirely

choices.label: D
choices.body: Write back clean pages

hard.hint: Two goals compete: keep hot pages and avoid disk writes -- which (ref,dirty) combo is cheapest to lose?
hard.explanation: Enhanced Clock orders victims by (ref,dirty) to jointly minimize locality loss and writeback I/O.
hard.deepDive: Enhanced Clock does multi-pass sweeps encoding (use,dirty) classes: 00 beats 01 beats 10 beats 11. It would rather evict an untouched clean page than a touched dirty one, saving both locality and disk writes. Implementation scans up to four rotations, clearing ref bits as it goes. This merges the replacement-trace and demand-swap ideas: recency plus writeback cost.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Evicting ref=1 discards hot pages; second chance exists to protect them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ignoring dirty treats a writeback the same as a drop, wasting disk I/O.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clean pages need no writeback by definition.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: How does page-fault-frequency (PFF) control use working sets?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fix W=1 for all programs

choices.label: B
choices.body: Count only code pages

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disable paging

choices.label: D
choices.body: Track fault frequency: high rate means W too small or overcommitted, so grow frames or suspend; low rate allows shrink

hard.hint: What observable signal tells you the current window/allotment mismatches locality?
hard.explanation: PFF uses fault rate as the working-set sensor to resize allotments or throttle multiprogramming.
hard.deepDive: Page-fault-frequency control adapts per process: faults above an upper threshold grow its allotment (or page the working set in faster), below a lower threshold shrink it. Globally, if no frames satisfy all targets, suspend a process rather than thrash. This turns working-set theory into a control loop, the ancestor of modern reclaim pressure feedback.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: One window cannot fit both tight loops and giant scans.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Data pages dominate working sets; code-only misses most faults.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Disabling paging removes oversubscription at the cost of the entire VM benefit.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: System is thrashing with 10 runnable jobs. Best recovery?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Suspend (swap out) a process to let survivors' working sets fit, rather than adding tiny slices to everyone

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shrink every process equally and hope

choices.label: C
choices.body: Overclock the CPU

choices.label: D
choices.body: Flush all TLBs

hard.hint: If every fair share still overflows, does fairness or exclusion restore progress?
hard.explanation: Thrashing recovery reduces multiprogramming by suspending victims until working sets fit.
hard.deepDive: When summed working sets exceed RAM, no fair split avoids thrashing -- each process faults constantly. Medium-term scheduling swaps a whole process out, donating its frames so the rest fit and CPU rebounds. Throughput with N-1 running beats near-zero with N thrashing. This is admission control: run fewer jobs well instead of many jobs badly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Equal shrinking keeps everyone below working set and prolongs collapse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: CPU speed cannot fix disk-bound fault storms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TLB flushes worsen miss cost and ignore the residency problem.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: Evict clean-hot vs dirty-cold: how to choose?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always evict the dirty cold page

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always evict the clean hot page

choices.label: C
choices.body: Prefer evicting clean pages unless hot (recently used); a cold dirty page may beat a hot clean one once writeback cost is weighed

choices.label: D
choices.body: Evict random pages to be fair

hard.hint: Compare total future I/O for each candidate: probability of refetch times read cost, plus certain writeback if dirty.
hard.explanation: Victim choice weighs reuse likelihood against writeback cost; clean-but-lukewarm often beats cold-and-dirty.
hard.deepDive: Real victims balance two costs: refetch probability (recency) versus writeback I/O (dirty). A barely-warm clean page is often cheaper to drop than an ice-cold dirty page needing a write plus later read. Enhanced Clock encodes this as class order. The stretch insight is cost-aware replacement: faults and writebacks have different prices, so recency alone is insufficient.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Always-dirty ignores writeback storms on write-heavy workloads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Always-clean can evict the hottest page and spike faults.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Random ignores both signals the OS already tracks for free.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: Demand paging vs prefetching/swap clustering: tradeoff?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Prefetching always helps and never causes thrashing

choices.label: B
choices.body: Demand pages in only faulted pages (minimal I/O, maximal faults); prefetching can cut faults but steals frames and risks thrashing

choices.label: C
choices.body: Demand paging reads the whole program at start

choices.label: D
choices.body: Swap space makes RAM unnecessary

hard.hint: What happens to neighbors' frames if speculative reads are wrong under memory pressure?
hard.explanation: Prefetch trades fewer faults for extra I/O and frame pressure; demand is conservative but fault-heavy.
hard.deepDive: Demand paging is lazy-optimal for I/O volume but pays a fault per cold page. Prepaging/clustering reads neighbors speculatively, amortizing disk seeks and faults when locality holds. Mispredicted prefetch pollutes frames and can tip a tight system into thrashing. Modern readahead therefore adapts to sequential patterns and pressure -- speculation gated by evidence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Wrong prefetch directly causes the pollution that triggers thrashing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Whole-program load is eager loading, the opposite of demand.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Swap backs overflow; every access still runs from RAM frames.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: What are inverted table hash costs?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Hash collisions chain multiple (pid,vpn) entries per slot and shared pages need extra alias handling, slowing lookups

choices.label: B
choices.body: Inverted tables make collisions impossible

choices.label: C
choices.body: Inverted tables remove the need for a TLB

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hashing makes all lookups O(1) worst-case

hard.hint: What happens when two translations hash to one slot, or one frame is shared by two keys?
hard.explanation: Hashing buys size proportional to RAM but pays collision chains and awkward sharing.
hard.deepDive: Different (pid,vpn) pairs hash to the same slot, so each bucket chains entries and lookups walk the chain comparing tags. Shared pages map one frame from many (pid,vpn) keys, needing alias lists or extra tables. Pathological hashing degrades to linear search. Forward tables avoid both by indexing directly on VPN per process at the cost of size.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hashing guarantees collisions; chaining handles them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The TLB still caches inverted lookups, which are slower without it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Chains make worst-case linear, not constant.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: What does ASLR actually guarantee, and how does it interact with fork/COW?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ASLR prevents buffer overflows

choices.label: B
choices.body: COW means fork never shares memory

choices.label: C
choices.body: Inverted tables eliminate page faults

choices.label: D
choices.body: ASLR randomizes base addresses to force attackers to guess, but bugs remain exploitable on guess/leak; COW/ASID interactions only affect sharing and tagging, not entropy

hard.hint: Does hiding an address remove the underlying overflow, or just the attacker's certainty?
hard.explanation: ASLR raises exploit cost via randomization without fixing overflows; COW/ASIDs are orthogonal mechanisms.
hard.deepDive: ASLR shifts stack/heap/mmap bases per exec so hardcoded gadget addresses fail, but info leaks or brute force (especially 32-bit) defeat it -- it is mitigation, not a fix. Fork inherits the layout (same entropy) unless re-exec randomizes again; COW shares the randomized pages efficiently; ASIDs merely tag cached translations under any layout. Do not confuse randomization with memory safety.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ASLR mitigates exploitation; only bounds checking/fixing the bug prevents overflow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: COW is defined by post-fork sharing; it shares until first write.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Residency still governs faults regardless of table direction.

source.chapterTitle: Advanced VM: TLB, Tables, Swapping, Replacement

hard.prompt: A thread function does int x = 42; pthread_exit(&x); After join, can the parent safely use *(int*)retval?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Return a pointer to a local (stack) variable; the caller reads it after join

choices.label: B
choices.body: The stack frame may be reused or unmapped after return, so the pointer dangles

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stack addresses are in a separate address space and fault on access

choices.label: D
choices.body: Join copies the whole child stack to the parent, so it stays valid

hard.hint: Forget threads: what happens when any function returns a pointer to its local? Apply that across join.
hard.explanation: The pointed-to frame is gone after return, so the pointer dangles and may be overwritten.
hard.deepDive: A thread's stack is private and its frames are recycled after the function returns. The address still points into the shared space but its contents get overwritten. Heap or global storage survives the return, which is why safe handoff uses them. This is the same dangling-pointer rule as ordinary function returns, applied across threads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This is the bug itself; the local dies with the frame before the parent reads it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stacks share the address space; the fault is reuse, not a separate space.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Join copies only the void* value, never the stack contents.

hard.prompt: Why is M:N rarely used despite combining M:1 flexibility with 1:1 parallelism?

choices.label: A
choices.body: User-level scheduling plus kernel cooperation for blocking and parallelism, which complicates the runtime

choices.label: B
choices.body: No multiplexing is needed; M:N maps threads directly in hardware

choices.label: C
choices.body: No scheduler at all; threads run in fixed round-robin burned into hardware

choices.label: D
choices.body: One kernel stack per process shared by all user threads

hard.hint: Ask what must happen when one user thread blocks but others should keep running on limited kernel threads.
hard.explanation: M:N needs two cooperating schedulers and a blocking protocol, adding major runtime and kernel complexity.
hard.deepDive: M:N needs a user scheduler for fast switches plus a way to keep kernel threads running when one user thread blocks. That requires scheduler activations or similar kernel hooks. Getting the protocol right proved hard to build and debug. The complexity is why Linux, for example, standardized on 1:1 NPTL instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No model is magic; every model needs multiplexing, and M:N needs two levels of it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scheduling is essential and harder here, not absent; hardware does not fix the order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Each kernel thread needs its own kernel stack; sharing one would corrupt blocking state.

hard.prompt: Fix this race: for(i=0;i<5;i++) pthread_create(&t[i],NULL,fn,&i); so each thread prints its own i.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pass &i from the loop; sharing is safe because ints are small

choices.label: B
choices.body: Copy the integer into a global and let threads race on it

choices.label: C
choices.body: Sleep in the loop so threads finish before i changes

choices.label: D
choices.body: malloc one int per thread, store i there, pass that pointer, free it after join

hard.hint: Ask what lifetime the argument needs: until the child reads it. Which storage outlives one loop iteration?
hard.explanation: Private heap slots give each thread its own stable copy with a lifetime beyond the loop iteration.
hard.deepDive: Each thread needs a distinct, stable argument lifetime covering creation through its read. A per-thread heap slot provides exactly that. The creator must not reuse it until after join, and someone must free it to avoid leaks. Casting the integer to void* also works but heap slots generalize to structs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: This is the original race; size does not matter since the address is shared.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A shared global keeps the race; all threads still read one mutating location.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sleep is timing luck, not ordering; join is the only correct ordering.

hard.prompt: A child computes an int result. Which parent code correctly retrieves it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: pthread_join(t, &res); int v = *(int*)res; with res pointing to heap or global set by the child

choices.label: B
choices.body: Child does pthread_exit(&local); parent uses *(int*)retval after join

choices.label: C
choices.body: Read a shared global immediately after create without joining

choices.label: D
choices.body: pthread_join(t, res); passing res instead of &res

hard.hint: Check the signature void** : what level of indirection must you pass, and when is the value ready?
hard.explanation: Join writes the child's void* through a void** slot; the data it points to must outlive the thread.
hard.deepDive: Join takes a void** so it can write the child's void* exit value into the caller's variable. The pointed-to data must outlive the child, hence heap or global. Reading before join races with the child's write. Passing res instead of &res gives join the wrong address to store through.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Returning a stack address dangles; the frame is gone before the parent reads it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Without join there is no happens-before; the global may be unread or half-written.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Join needs the address of your pointer (&res); passing res corrupts memory.

hard.prompt: 4 requests each need 50-ms blocking I/O plus 5-ms CPU on one core. Compare serial (~220 ms) to 4-threaded time.

choices.label: A
choices.body: About 220 ms, because threads serialize all waits

choices.label: B
choices.body: About 55 ms, because four 50-ms waits overlap plus small CPU pieces

choices.label: C
choices.body: About 12 ms, because threads divide one wait by the thread count

choices.label: D
choices.body: About 0 ms, because enough threads eliminate waiting

hard.hint: Add serial first (4 x 55), then stack the 50-ms waits vertically and add the 5-ms CPU slices.
hard.explanation: Overlapped waits cost roughly max(wait) plus CPU slices (~50+ms), not the 220-ms serial sum.
hard.deepDive: Four requests each wait 50 ms on the device while needing 5 ms of CPU. Overlapped, the waits coincide so elapsed time is near one wait plus the serialized CPU slices. Serial code would pay four full waits plus CPU. The gap grows with more concurrent blocking requests.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Serialization is the non-threaded case; threads overlap the BLOCKED waits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One wait stays 50 ms; threads never subdivide a single device latency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Waiting never vanishes; overlap only hides concurrent waits behind each other.

hard.prompt: Contrast CPU-bound scaling: 8 threads on 1 core versus 8 threads on 8 cores (1:1 model)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both scale linearly with threads because threads always create CPUs

choices.label: B
choices.body: Neither scales because the kernel never runs threads in parallel

choices.label: C
choices.body: Single-core: no speedup for CPU-bound; multicore with 1:1: near-linear speedup until cores saturate

choices.label: D
choices.body: Single-core always beats multicore because switches are free

hard.hint: Separate resource from mechanism: what resource does CPU-bound work need, and which setup adds more of it?
hard.explanation: CPU-bound speedup needs extra cores; threads alone cannot invent cycles on one core.
hard.deepDive: CPU-bound work speeds up only with more execution units. On one core total cycles are fixed, so extra threads add overhead. On multiple cores 1:1 threads run truly in parallel, scaling with cores. Once threads exceed cores, speedup flattens and switching costs dominate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Threads never create CPUs; only additional cores add compute capacity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The kernel does run 1:1 threads in parallel on multicores; that is the point of 1:1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Switches cost cycles and single-core cannot parallelize; multicore wins for CPU-bound.

hard.prompt: N threads each increment shared counter M times with no locks. What final value range do you expect as N and M grow?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Exactly N*M always, because hardware serializes increments

choices.label: B
choices.body: More than N*M because threads amplify each other

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always 0 because races crash the process

choices.label: D
choices.body: Between M and N*M, often far below N*M, motivating locks or atomics

hard.hint: Scale up the 2-thread lost-update picture: more pairs overlapping means more collapsed increments. What fixes it?
hard.explanation: Lost updates accumulate with more threads and iterations, so the count falls short and needs synchronization.
hard.deepDive: Every overlapping load-add-store pair loses at least one update. With many threads and many iterations, overlaps are frequent, so the deficit grows. The result stays above M since each thread contributes something. The gap between observed and N times M quantifies the race and justifies the next chapter on locks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hardware does not serialize plain loads and stores; that is what atomic or locked code adds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Races only lose updates here; nothing duplicates an increment.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Races corrupt values, not crash; the process survives with a short count.

hard.prompt: How do pthread implementations typically detect per-thread stack overflow?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Unmapped guard pages that fault on touch, catching overflow at the boundary

choices.label: B
choices.body: Compiler bounds checks on every stack push

choices.label: C
choices.body: Infinite virtual regions that can never overflow

choices.label: D
choices.body: Copying the stack to disk on every call

hard.hint: Ask how to turn silent neighbor-smashing into a loud fault: what memory trick faults on touch?
hard.explanation: Guard pages turn silent corruption into a prompt fault by leaving the page past the stack unmapped.
hard.deepDive: Pthreads place an unmapped guard page past each fixed stack end. Touching it raises a fault instead of silently corrupting a neighbor. The fault kills the process but pinpoints the overflow. Without guards, overflows would silently smash adjacent stacks or heap and be far harder to debug.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bounds checks on every push would be costly; guards give detection with zero per-access cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No infinite regions exist; each stack is a bounded slice of the shared space.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Stacks are never paged to disk per call; guards are a virtual-memory protection trick.

hard.prompt: Two threads racing on counter++ show a lost update. What makes that increment a critical section?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Any single machine instruction, which is always atomic

choices.label: B
choices.body: The whole program between create and join

choices.label: C
choices.body: Any code that never blocks on I/O

choices.label: D
choices.body: A load-add-store sequence that must appear atomic, requiring locks or atomics

hard.hint: Generalize counter++: which code pattern needs all-or-nothing execution even though it is several steps?
hard.explanation: A critical section is shared-state code needing indivisibility; counter++ needs a lock or atomic to be safe.
hard.deepDive: A critical section is code touching shared state where interleaving changes the result. counter++ is the minimal example: its three steps must execute as one indivisible unit. Marking it critical tells the runtime to enforce mutual exclusion. That requirement is the bridge from observing races to studying locks in the next chapter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Single instructions are not always atomic across cores; and counter++ is three instructions anyway.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Create-to-join spans the whole thread, far more than the shared update needing protection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Blocking is irrelevant; the hazard is interleaved memory access, not I/O.

hard.prompt: Design a hybrid spin-then-block lock. What is the principled policy?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spin when the holder runs on another core and the hold is shorter than a context switch; otherwise block.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always spin because blocking syscalls are deprecated.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always block because spinning is never correct.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Spin on single-core to let the holder run sooner.

hard.hint: What bounds the useful spin: the cost of what alternative?
hard.explanation: Spin briefly for the fast-handoff case, then block — matching wait cost to expected hold time.
hard.deepDive: Two-phase locks spin briefly then block, capturing both regimes: nanosecond handoffs stay in userspace while long waits surrender the CPU. Pure spinning collapses under preemption and single-core execution. Pure blocking pays a microsecond switch even when the lock would free in nanoseconds.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Blocking is essential for long waits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Spinning is correct and faster for very short waits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Single-core spinning prevents the holder from running.

hard.prompt: A per-node-locked list insert briefly holds no lock while stepping forward and loses updates. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fine-grained locking can never deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Throughput always beats coarse locking regardless of workload.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Code size is the only cost of fine-grained locking.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A thread drops the predecessor lock before securing the successor, letting a concurrent delete unlink the target — use lock coupling with a fixed order.

hard.hint: Is there any instant where the node you are about to modify is protected by no held lock?
hard.explanation: Releasing too early opens a deletion window; couple predecessor and successor locks across each step.
hard.deepDive: The window between releasing pred and acquiring curr lets another thread splice curr out, so the updater then modifies a detached node — a lost update despite holding a lock at each instant. Coupling (holding both across the step) closes the window while keeping distant segments parallel. Ad-hoc release-and-reacquire is the canonical fine-grained correctness pitfall.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Inconsistent order deadlocks via AB-BA.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Under low contention, lock overhead can make it slower.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ordering and window-closing discipline are the real costs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

hard.prompt: Why do Mesa-style CVs mandate `while (!pred) wait()` even with perfect signal placement?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spurious wakeups are impossible on correct hardware.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Re-checking in a while loop makes spurious wakeups harmless: the thread simply sleeps again.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Spurious wakeups prove the predicate-handling code is buggy.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An if-guarded wait handles spurious wakeups if signal is replaced by broadcast.

hard.hint: If wait can return with the predicate still false, which guard shape survives?
hard.explanation: Spurious wakeups are allowed; only a predicate loop distinguishes a real wakeup from noise.
hard.deepDive: Mesa runtimes may return from wait without any signal (implementation races, page faults, multiprocessor effects), so the wakeup-predicate link is never trustworthy. The while loop treats every wakeup uniformly — real, stolen, or spurious — by re-testing before proceeding. This is why if-guarded waits are always wrong under Mesa semantics.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Spurious wakeups are explicitly permitted by POSIX.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: They are a documented runtime behavior, not an app bug.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Broadcast multiplies spurious-style wakeups; only the loop saves you.

hard.prompt: Compare Hoare immediate-handoff vs Mesa竞争 (compete-after-signal) for implementers and users.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Hoare signaling is impossible to implement.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The signaler must exit the monitor before the waiter runs in every scheme.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Immediate Hoare handoff preserves the signaled predicate but adds context-switch urgency; Mesa defers with re-competition and requires re-checks.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mesa gives stronger guarantees than Hoare.

hard.hint: Who pays, and when: an immediate forced switch, or later re-competition plus looping?
hard.explanation: Hoare buys predicate certainty with an urgent switch; Mesa buys implementability at the cost of re-checks.
hard.deepDive: Hoare's urgent handoff keeps the predicate true at waiter resume, simplifying reasoning but forcing an immediate switch and complicating nested monitor calls. Mesa's wake-then-compete is cheaper to implement on real schedulers at the price of mandatory while loops. Production runtimes chose Mesa, so portable code always re-checks even when Hoare-style reasoning feels cleaner.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hoare monitors existed historically (e.g., Brinch-Hansen).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes one Hoare variant; others hand off directly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Hoare's guarantee is strictly stronger.

hard.prompt: Bursty N-producer queue shows missed wakeups: a consumer sleeps though items arrive. What robust fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A `nevents` generation counter tested in the wait predicate, so late-signal wakeups from an older burst re-sleep.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Removing all while loops for lower latency.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Signaling before enqueueing to wake consumers earlier.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Replacing the mutex with a spinlock held across the wait.

hard.hint: What predicate stays true even if the signal arrived a microsecond too early?
hard.explanation: Fold production events into the predicate with a generation counter; signals become pure hints.
hard.deepDive: Bursty producers can signal between a consumer's predicate test and its wait, and multiple consumers can steal the single new item — both are lost-wakeup shapes. A monotonic generation or sequence number folds every production event into the predicate itself, so no wakeup is load-bearing: the waiter sleeps only if its observed generation is current. Combined with while loops this closes both the missed-signal and steal races.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Holding a spinlock across a wait deadlocks producers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: If-guarded waits cannot survive steals or spurious wakeups.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Early signal recreates the lost wakeup.

hard.prompt: Two producers each see one free slot and both insert, overflowing a 1-slot buffer. Root cause?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It guarantees each producer gets equal buffer share.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It removes the need for empty/full counts.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It is always faster than a single lock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Two producers can both pass the not-full test then overflow the last slot — the put must be atomic with the reservation under the mutex.

hard.hint: Between 'buffer has space' and 'my item occupies it', what stops a second producer interleaving?
hard.explanation: Not-full checks must atomically reserve the slot; split check-then-put overflows under concurrency.
hard.deepDive: Testing not-full outside the mutex opens a check-then-act race: both producers observe one free slot and both insert. The fix reserves the slot (decrement or index bump) while holding the mutex, or uses the empty semaphore's atomic wait as the reservation. Flow-control counts only work when acquiring the count and occupying the slot are one atomic step.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Fairness needs extra queuing; the bug is atomicity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Counts are still required — they were just used non-atomically.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Split designs are often slower and here incorrect.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

hard.prompt: A worker that never acquired the lock calls unlock/post on an error path. Contrast mutex vs binary semaphore.

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are identical; semaphore wait tracks the owner like a mutex.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A mutex has an owner (only the locker may unlock; others unlocking is an error), while any thread may post a semaphore — so a stray post can silently admit extra holders.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Semaphores cannot be used for mutual exclusion at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mutexes cannot block; only semaphores block.

hard.hint: If a thread that never waited calls post/unlock, which primitive complains and which silently opens the gate?
hard.explanation: Mutexes enforce unlock-by-owner; semaphores accept posts from anyone, so misuse silently over-admits.
hard.deepDive: Mutex ownership enables error detection (recursive-lock or foreign-unlock faults) and priority-inheritance protocols that need to know whom to boost. Semaphores lack this: any thread's post increments the count, so a misplaced post inflates admissions without any error. This is the semaphore-equals-mutex-with-owner misconception — the missing owner is precisely the semantic gap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the exact misconception: semaphores track no owner.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Binary semaphores can exclude, but without ownership safety.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both block; ownership is the difference.

hard.prompt: Read-mostly cache starves writers under reader-preference. What fixes writer starvation while keeping read parallelism?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reader-preference, because writers are rare so starvation is impossible.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No lock at all, relying on atomic pointer writes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A fair turnstile/fifo (or writer-preference with reader drain): block new readers once a writer waits, then admit the writer when active readers drain.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Strictly serialize all readers with a mutex.

hard.hint: What must happen to readers that arrive *after* the writer started waiting?
hard.explanation: Gate new readers behind a waiting writer; admit the writer once in-flight readers drain.
hard.deepDive: Continuous readers keep the read-hold count nonzero, so a pure reader-preference writer waits forever. A turnstile records a waiting writer and deflects newly arriving readers to a queue until the writer completes, bounding writer delay by one read generation. Writer-preference mirrors the risk toward readers, so real systems add FIFO or bounded-bypass fairness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Rarity does not bound the worst case; one steady stream still starves.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reclamation and multi-word updates still need coordination.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Serializing readers destroys the read-parallelism goal.

hard.prompt: What is the ABA problem in a CAS-based lock-free stack pop?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Thread 1 reads top=A, preempted; thread 2 pops A, pops B, frees A, pushes A again (top=A); thread 1's CAS succeeds but B is lost — top pointed to A twice with different successors.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two threads pushing different values at the same time always corrupt the stack.

choices.label: C
choices.body: CAS failing spuriously even with no contention.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A fence placed on the wrong side causing a segfault.

hard.hint: Can the top pointer hold the same address yet mean a different stack? When does memory reuse make that happen?
hard.explanation: Recycled address A matches CAS but its successor changed, so the pop silently drops intervening nodes.
hard.deepDive: ABA fools address-equality into implying unchanged structure: the pointer matches but the `next` chain behind it changed while A was recycled. The popping CAS therefore splices out B silently. Fixes use tagged pointers (address+counter), hazard pointers or epoch reclamation to prevent recycling, trading a little space or latency for recycling safety.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Concurrent pushes retry safely; ABA is about pop plus recycling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Spurious CAS failure is a different (architectural) effect.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fences order memory; they do not segfault by placement.

hard.prompt: Which fix actually addresses ABA (vs the Peterson-scales and fence-fixes-everything misconceptions)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ABA is impossible if you use a mutex anywhere in the program.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Adding more fences always fixes ABA.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Making the stack larger prevents ABA.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Tag the pointer with a monotonic counter (double-wide CAS) or guard reclamation with hazard pointers/epochs so A cannot be recycled while observed.

hard.hint: Does the bug come from operation order, or from the same address meaning two different allocations?
hard.explanation: Disambiguate recycled addresses with tags, or stop premature recycling with hazard/epoch protection.
hard.deepDive: ABA is a recycling problem, not an ordering problem: fences change visibility order but not the fact that address A was freed and reused. A tag makes each (address, era) pair unique so a recycled A fails the CAS. Hazard pointers and epoch reclamation instead defer the free until no observer holds a reference, eliminating the reuse window entirely.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: An unrelated mutex does not stop recycling of the stack's nodes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fences order visibility; they do not make addresses unique.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Size only shrinks the window; reuse still occurs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Correct.

hard.prompt: Where do memory fences/barriers go in a flag-based handoff (`data=x; ready=1` / `while(!ready){}; use(data)`)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No fences are ever needed on x86 because it is sequentially consistent.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Acquire fence on lock/CAS-load success, release fence on unlock/CAS-store: operations inside cannot leak out, and the flag's visibility is ordered with the data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Full fence after every instruction for safety.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fence only the data accesses, never the flag.

hard.hint: Which direction must ordering flow: data before flag on one side, and flag before data on the other?
hard.explanation: Release on unlock publishes data with the flag; acquire on lock subscribes — the minimal correct pairing.
hard.deepDive: Release semantics on unlock publish all prior writes before the flag becomes visible; acquire semantics on lock ensure later reads observe that published state. This pairs exactly like message-passing: data-then-flag on the sender, flag-then-data on the receiver. x86 gives some of this free for aligned stores but weaker ISAs (ARM/RISC-V) need explicit barriers, and over-fencing everywhere destroys the performance lock-free code seeks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: x86 is TSO, not SC; and weaker platforms need explicit barriers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Fencing everything is correct but needlessly slow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unordered flag alone lets data and flag visibility swap.

hard.prompt: A teammate claims Peterson's algorithm 'just works for N threads on any hardware.' What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Peterson's algorithm scales cleanly to N threads with one shared turn variable.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Peterson needs no fences even on relaxed memory.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 2-thread Peterson needs N-thread generalization (filter/tournament) plus fences on relaxed hardware; plain N-way flag+turn is broken.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Peterson outperforms TAS spinlocks at high core counts.

hard.hint: What breaks first when a third thread arrives, or when flag and turn stores become visible out of order?
hard.explanation: Peterson is 2-thread and SC-assuming; N threads need filter/tournament structure and fences on weak memory.
hard.deepDive: Peterson's two-thread construction relies on sequential consistency of its flag and turn variables; on relaxed hardware the loads and stores reorder and mutual exclusion collapses without fences. Scaling to N needs a filter lock (N-1 levels) or tournament tree, adding O(N) space and traversal cost. Modern practice prefers queued locks (MCS/CLH) that spin locally instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is the exact misconception: 2-thread Peterson does not generalize by widening.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Relaxed memory reorders flag/turn without fences.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correct.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Peterson spins remotely and scales poorly vs queue locks.

hard.prompt: R1:2 copies 0 free; R2:2 copies 1 free. P1 holds R1 waits R2; P2 holds R1 waits R2; P3 holds R2 waits R1. Deadlock?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock, because the graph has a cycle.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlock, because total Need exceeds Available.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Starvation of P3 due to FIFO ordering.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No deadlock: free R2 copy lets P2 finish, cascading releases.

hard.hint: Isolate what P2 waits for: is any copy of exactly that pool free?
hard.explanation: The R2 free copy breaks the apparent cycle via P2's completion.
hard.deepDive: Multi-pool graphs need per-pool accounting: R1 has 2 copies both held, R2 has 2 copies with 1 free. P2 waits only for R2, so the free copy satisfies it despite the apparent cycle P1->R1->P3->R2->P1. After P2 finishes, its R1 copy unblocks P1. Drawing arrows without counts invites the false-positive.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Cycle without counts is the classic false positive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Total Need always exceeds Available in busy systems; sequencing matters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No scheduler priority is given; all waits are symmetric.

hard.prompt: Large codebase with nested locks wants prevention with least concurrency loss. Best trade-off?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Atomic acquisition always beats ordering on concurrency.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Ordering preserves concurrency but needs a known global order and discipline.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Preemption of mutexes is trivial with no rollback cost.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Detection prevents deadlock without runtime cost.

hard.hint: Compare what each fix holds or requires: which holds locks longest?
hard.explanation: Ordering is the concurrency-friendly fix, paid for with discipline.
hard.deepDive: No prevention is free: atomicity holds locks longer, ordering demands design discipline and complete lock sets, preemption needs rollbackable state. Ordering usually wins for modular lock code because waiters hold less. But a missed order edge silently reintroduces cycles, so teams enforce it with lockdep-style checking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Atomicity holds extra locks early, hurting concurrency versus ordering.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mutex rollback is generally infeasible for arbitrary critical sections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Detection allows deadlock then pays detector plus recovery cost.

hard.prompt: Avail [CPU 2, Disk 1]. Alloc P0[1,0] P1[1,1] P2[1,0]; Max P0[3,2] P1[2,2] P2[2,1]. Safe sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.body: P0,P1,P2 because lowest Alloc goes first.

choices.label: C
choices.body: P0,P2,P1 because Max decides order.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Unsafe, no sequence works.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Safe via P2 first because it holds most.

hard.hint: Compute Need=Max-Alloc per resource, then test who fits Avail [2,1].
hard.explanation: P1 or P2 must lead since P0 Need [2,2] exceeds Avail [2,1] on disk.
hard.deepDive: Compute Need: P0 [2,2], P1 [1,1], P2 [1,1] with Avail [2,1]. P1 and P2 both fit but P0 does not, so P0 cannot lead. Running P1 first yields Avail [3,2], then P0 fits, then P2. Any witness suffices; lowest-Alloc or biggest-Max heuristics do not define safety.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Alloc order is irrelevant; Need versus Avail decides.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A cascade exists via P1 first, so unsafe is wrong.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P2-first also works but holding most is not the reason; fit is.

hard.prompt: Same state Avail [2,1]. P0 requests [1,1]. Grant or deny?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deny: residue Avail [1,0] fits neither P0 Need [2,2] nor others fully.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Grant: Avail still covers P1 so all is fine.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Grant because single-resource intuition says small requests are safe.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Deny because Banker never grants CPU requests.

hard.hint: Subtract the request from Avail and from P0 Need, then search for any fittable Need.
hard.explanation: After the grant no Need fits the residue, so the safe witness is destroyed.
hard.deepDive: Simulate P0 requesting [1,1]: Avail falls to [1,0]. Remaining Needs are P0 [1,1], P1 [1,1], P2 [1,1], none fitting [1,0] on disk. Hence no leader exists and the state is unsafe. The request is small yet fatal, showing size alone never proves safety. Denial preserves the prior safe state.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One survivor is insufficient; the full sequence must survive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Multi-resource safety cannot reuse single-resource intuition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Banker grants many CPU requests; this denial is residue-specific.

hard.prompt: Banker says a state is unsafe. Is the system deadlocked?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Unsafe and therefore already deadlocked.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Unsafe but not yet deadlocked; deadlock only if risky requests are granted.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Safe because no thread has blocked yet.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Deadlocked because Available is zero.

hard.hint: Does unsafe describe the future risk or the present stuck threads?
hard.explanation: Unsafe is fragility, not stuckness; blocking has not occurred yet.
hard.deepDive: Unsafe means no order guarantees completion, not that threads are stuck now. Deadlock requires actual circular waiting with no satisfiable demand. An unsafe state may still run fine if threads release early or request benignly. Banker denies to avoid entering such fragile states. Conflating unsafe with deadlocked causes false alarms.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Unsafe precedes possible deadlock; stuckness needs an irreducible wait.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Lack of blocking does not make it safe; no witness sequence exists.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zero Available is common and often safe via release cascades.

hard.prompt: Deadlock between a DB transaction and a thread in a mutex critical section. Best recovery?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Kill is always best because it is simplest.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Preemption is always best because nothing is lost.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rollback is unnecessary if you kill carefully.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Preempt DB transaction with log rollback; killing a lock holder corrupts state.

hard.hint: Which victim state can be restored: logged transaction or raw critical section?
hard.explanation: Logged work can be rewound; raw mutex state cannot be safely killed.
hard.deepDive: Recovery must match resource semantics: preempt plus rollback suits logged transactions, while killing a mutex holder leaves shared state inconsistent. Kill is simple but lossy; preemption needs checkpointing. The choice hinges on whether victim state can be restored. OSTEP frames this as kill versus preempt-plus-rollback trade-off.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Simplicity ignores corruption of mutex-guarded invariants.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Preemption loses work unless rollback exists; it is not free.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rollback is exactly what makes preemption safe for the DB side.

hard.prompt: Server opens user-chosen files in unpredictable order; mutex rollback infeasible. Best strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Detection plus kill: waits are unpredictable and preemption is infeasible.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Atomic acquisition of all files to maximize concurrency.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Strict ordering of file opens to guarantee zero detector cost.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ignore deadlock because files are preemptible.

hard.hint: Can you name all files up front to order them? If not, what remains?
hard.explanation: Unpredictable file sets defeat static prevention; detection fits.
hard.deepDive: When lock sets are dynamic and rollback is hard, prevention over-constrains or fails, so periodic detection with kill-and-retry is pragmatic. Atomic acquisition serializes unrelated files; ordering is brittle when paths are computed at runtime. Files can be closed and reopened, making kill-recovery acceptable. Match the strategy to feasibility, not ideology.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Atomicity across arbitrary files kills concurrency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ordering needs a knowable total order; user paths defeat it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Files via mutexes are not safely preemptible mid-update.

hard.prompt: Trace: high-priority threads repeatedly acquire the lock and finish; low-priority T waits 30s and never acquires. Which?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock: all threads blocked with no progress.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Starvation: low-priority thread never runs while others do.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Livelock: all threads spin with no progress.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Safe state: Banker guarantees progress.

hard.hint: Who makes progress: nobody, everybody-spinning, or everybody-except-one?
hard.explanation: System progresses but one thread never wins: unfairness, not a cycle.
hard.deepDive: Starvation shows asymmetric progress: the system advances but one victim never gets the resource. Priority schedulers or unfair locks cause it without any cycle. Unlike deadlock, killing a random thread rarely helps; aging or fairness fixes it. Traces with one starved but others looping completions signal starvation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Deadlock needs zero progress on all parties, but here others finish.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Livelock needs busy spinning by all with zero commits; here commits occur.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Banker safety is about resource grants, not scheduler priority.

hard.prompt: Pair 1 spin-retries in lockstep; Pair 2 parks in lock(A)/lock(B) cyclically. Correct fixes?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deadlock, because two threads wait.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Livelock, because backoff always deadlocks.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Livelock resolved by randomized backoff; deadlock needs ordering.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Starvation, because ordering fixes priority.

hard.hint: Map symptom to cure: spinning-symmetry versus parked-cycle?
hard.explanation: Spinning collision wants jitter; parked cycle wants ordering.
hard.deepDive: Symmetric try-and-backoff collides in lockstep, which is livelock, fixed by jittered retries. True ordered-wait deadlock with blocking lock() calls does not retry and needs cycle-breaking such as ordering. Misclassifying wastes the fix: backoff never breaks a parked cycle, ordering never breaks spin symmetry. Diagnose via CPU-busy versus parked stacks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Two waiting is insufficient; spin versus park decides the class.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Backoff causes or reflects livelock; it is not deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ordering addresses cycles, not priority unfairness.

hard.prompt: dirA/file is hard-linked as dirB/alias on the same FS, then renamed dirA/file → dirA/new. What still opens the data via dirB/alias?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes — both names point to the same inode; rename only edits dirA's directory file

choices.label: B
choices.body: No — rename invalidates all other hard links to the inode

choices.label: C
choices.body: No — hard links auto-convert to symlinks on rename and then dangle

choices.label: D
choices.body: Yes, but only if the data blocks were duplicated at link time

hard.hint: Rename removes one directory entry and adds another — does it touch the inode or sibling entries?
hard.explanation: Rename is namespace-only; the inode and other links are untouched.
hard.deepDive: Contrast with a symlink dirB/slink → 'dirA/file', which would dangle after this rename because it stores the old path string. Hard-link immunity to renames is the operational test distinguishing the two link types, and why cross-FS hard links are forbidden.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rename affects one entry only; sibling links persist.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Link type never morphs on rename.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No duplication ever occurs for hard links.

hard.prompt: Two processes share an offset (after fork) and each does lseek(fd,0,SEEK_END)+write. Why can data still be lost, and what fixes it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Seek-then-write races: both seek to same EOF then overwrite; O_APPEND makes placement atomic

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shared offsets corrupt the inode size field permanently; only reformatting fixes it

choices.label: C
choices.body: fork closes the file in the child; reopen with O_SYNC fixes it

choices.label: D
choices.body: lseek clears O_APPEND automatically, so nothing can fix it

hard.hint: Two steps (seek, write) with a shared cursor — what interleaving puts both writes at one offset?
hard.explanation: Non-atomic seek+write races; O_APPEND seeks atomically per write.
hard.deepDive: Even with a shared offset, the TOCTOU window between lseek and write allows both to compute the same EOF. O_APPEND moves the position-to-EOF inside the write syscall under a lock. pread/pwrite avoid the shared cursor entirely by taking explicit offsets.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Size field is not corrupted; blocks simply overlap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Fork preserves descriptors; closing is not the issue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: lseek does not clear flags; O_APPEND is the fix.

hard.prompt: VSFS inode: 12 direct + single + double indirect, 4KB blocks, 4B pointers. Max file size?

choices.label: B
choices.body: 13 blocks total (~52KB)

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unlimited; indirects chain indefinitely

hard.hint: Sum the three tiers: directs + one indirect's fan-out + one double's fan-out-squared.
hard.explanation: Additive across tiers: 12 + 1024 + 1M blocks times 4KB.
hard.deepDive: Single contributes 1K blocks (4MB), double contributes 1M blocks (~4GB); directs are rounding error at scale. Reaching tail data costs up to 3 extra reads. This mirrors two-level page tables: small mappings cheap, large mappings possible.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Counts pointer slots instead of blocks they address.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Multiplies tiers that should be added.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Depth is fixed at double-indirect here; no chaining beyond.

hard.prompt: 1M × 4KB-block VSFS with 256B inodes needs how many bitmap blocks (inode + data), roughly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 1 inode-bitmap block (32K inodes capacity) + 32 data-bitmap blocks (1M bits)

choices.label: B
choices.body: 1M bitmap blocks — one per data block

choices.label: C
choices.body: Zero — bitmaps are stored inside each inode

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1024 + 1024 blocks regardless of FS size

hard.hint: Bits needed = entries; bits per 4KB block = 32768 — divide entries by that.
hard.explanation: Bitmap size scales with capacity: 1M/32768≈31 → 32 blocks for data.
hard.deepDive: This shows metadata overhead explicitly: ~33 blocks per 1M-block disk is tiny, but must sit at known locations. Growing the disk without growing bitmaps caps allocation — a classic mkfs sizing question. Inode count is an independent mkfs choice bounding file count.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One bit per block, not one block per block — 32768× overestimate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Bitmaps are FS-global, not per-inode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 1024 is the pointer fan-out, unrelated to bitmap sizing.

hard.prompt: Crash occurs after data-bitmap set + data written, but before inode is updated to point at the block. Effect after reboot?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Leaked block: marked allocated in bitmap but unreachable from any inode

choices.label: B
choices.body: The file transparently gains the new data on next open

choices.label: C
choices.body: The bitmap bit is auto-cleared because link count is nonzero

choices.label: D
choices.body: All directory entries pointing to the file are deleted

hard.hint: Allocation has two halves: claim the block, then publish the pointer — what if only the first persists?
hard.explanation: Unreferenced-but-marked blocks leak until fsck frees them.
hard.deepDive: Reverse order (pointer before bitmap) is worse: two inodes could claim one block. This ordering dilemma motivates journaling or careful write ordering (and fsck repair). fsck detects leaks by cross-checking bitmaps against all inode pointers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Unpublished pointers are invisible; no inode means no access path.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No auto-clear exists without a journal or fsck scan.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Directory entries are untouched by this data-path crash window.

hard.prompt: A 500MB file on FFS with 8MB cylinder groups. How is it placed?

choices.label: A
choices.body: First blocks in the directory's group, then spilled across other groups in large contiguous runs

choices.label: B
choices.body: Entirely within one group by compressing blocks to fit

choices.label: C
choices.body: One block per group round-robin to balance load

choices.label: D
choices.body: All inodes in group 0 and all data in the last group

hard.hint: Locality is preferred but a file bigger than one group cannot fit — what is the graceful exception?
hard.explanation: FFS keeps the head local then allocates large extents elsewhere.
hard.deepDive: Spilling in big runs preserves mostly-sequential bandwidth while avoiding one-group overflow. Pure round-robin would destroy sequentiality with a seek per block. This is the standard locality-vs-capacity tradeoff: optimize the common small-file case, degrade gracefully for huge files.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A file cannot exceed its group's capacity; overflow is mandatory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Per-block striping maximizes seeks — the opposite of FFS policy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Splitting all inodes from all data reintroduces long seeks.

hard.prompt: Benchmark: reading 100 small files in one directory is 10× faster on FFS than on a FS scattering inodes far from data. Best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Co-location turns per-file open+read from 2 long seeks into nearby/short seeks within one group

choices.label: B
choices.body: FFS caches filenames inside inodes, saving directory reads

choices.label: C
choices.body: FFS needs no bitmaps, saving one I/O per file

choices.label: D
choices.body: Small files need no data blocks on FFS

hard.hint: Count seeks per file under each layout: inode location vs data location distance?
hard.explanation: Locality cuts seek distance per file; transfer size is identical.
hard.deepDive: With 100 files the seek savings multiply: scattered layout pays a full-stroke seek per inode and per block, while grouped layout pays short seeks plus contiguous transfer. Filenames still live in the directory and bitmaps still exist — neither is eliminated.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Names never live in inodes, on FFS or otherwise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Bitmaps are still consulted for allocation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Small files still consume at least one block (with internal fragmentation).

hard.prompt: Freeing a 3-block file: bitmap shows blocks free but one block is later double-allocated to two files. Likely bug?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Freed a block twice / freed a block never owned (cleared a bit belonging to a live file)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Decremented the link count instead of clearing the bitmap

choices.label: C
choices.body: Called fsync on the file before freeing

choices.label: D
choices.body: Removed the directory entry before freeing blocks

hard.hint: Bitmaps have no refcount — what happens if free is called on the wrong block number?
hard.explanation: Bitmap free is blind clearing; freeing a live block corrupts allocation.
hard.deepDive: Unlike link counts, bitmaps cannot detect double-free. Correct free order is: remove directory reachability, verify last link/refs gone, then clear exactly the owned bits. Journaling and fsck cross-checks catch such corruption after the fact.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Link-count ops affect naming lifetime, not bitmap double-alloc directly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: fsync ordering affects durability, not double allocation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unlink-before-free is actually the correct order.

hard.prompt: App creates 'dir/new' + writes data, fsyncs the file, but not dir — then crashes. After reboot, what may be true?

choices.label: A
choices.body: File data durable but name missing: directory entry never persisted

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both file and name guaranteed durable because file fsync covers the directory

choices.label: C
choices.body: File permissions revert to 777 on recovery

choices.label: D
choices.body: The data bitmap is guaranteed consistent without fsck

hard.hint: File fsync flushes inode+data of the file — does it flush the parent directory's data blocks?
hard.explanation: Directory durability needs its own fsync; file fsync is insufficient.
hard.deepDive: Create/rename mutate the parent directory file, a separate object with its own blocks. Databases and mail servers fsync the directory after creates for this reason. Without it the file becomes an allocated-but-unnamed orphan after crash.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Core misconception: file fsync does not flush parent directory state.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Permissions never change on crash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bitmap consistency still needs ordering/journaling.

hard.prompt: Which fsync discipline gives a crash-safe file replace via rename?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Write tmp, fsync tmp, rename tmp→final, fsync directory

choices.label: B
choices.body: Write final directly with no fsync; rename is always atomic so data is safe

choices.label: C
choices.body: Rename first, then write tmp and fsync the directory only

choices.label: D
choices.body: chmod 777 before writing to avoid permission checks on recovery

hard.hint: Durability needs data on disk before the new name, and the new name on disk before acknowledging — what two fsyncs do that?
hard.explanation: fsync data before publishing the name; fsync dir after publishing it.
hard.deepDive: Atomic rename guarantees readers see old-or-new, not half-files — but only if the tmp data was durable first. The directory fsync makes the rename itself durable. Skipping either yields truncated or vanished files after crash despite atomicity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Atomicity ≠ durability; undurable data can still vanish.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Publishing before data is durable exposes garbage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Permissions are irrelevant to crash atomicity.

hard.prompt: Unlink('dir/f') with link count 1 must persistently:

choices.label: A
choices.body: Remove dir entry, decrement link count to 0, clear inode + data bitmap bits (deferred until no open refs)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Zero all file data blocks immediately before removing the name

choices.label: C
choices.body: Clear the data bitmap but leave the directory entry for reuse

choices.label: D
choices.body: Delete the superblock entry for the file only

hard.hint: Reverse of create: unpublish the name, drop the count, then reclaim — what defers the last step?
hard.explanation: Namespace removal precedes reclamation; open holders defer bitmap clearing.
hard.deepDive: Zeroing data is unnecessary — clearing bitmap bits suffices since future allocs overwrite. Leaving the entry would dangle to a freed inode. Crash between entry-removal and bitmap-clear yields a leak that fsck reclaims, the safe failure direction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Secure erase is a special case; normal unlink just frees bookkeeping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Leaving the entry creates a dangling name to freed metadata.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No per-file superblock entry exists.

hard.prompt: rename('a', 'b') where 'b' exists must be atomic (readers see old-b or new-a, never half). Implementation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Point 'b' at a's inode and remove 'a' as one atomic dir update (journaled); free b's old inode after

choices.label: B
choices.body: Copy a's data blocks to b's blocks byte-by-byte then delete a

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete 'b' first, sync, then much later link 'a' to 'b'

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unlink both names then recreate 'b' from scratch on reboot if crashed

hard.hint: Renames only swap pointers (directory entries), not data — how do you make the swap indivisible?
hard.explanation: Rename is pointer surgery on directory entries, journaled as one transaction.
hard.deepDive: No data moves; only namespace changes, so it is fast. The old b inode's link count drops and is freed after the atomic swap. A crash mid-rename must recover to either mapping — the journal replays or rolls back the transaction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Data copy is unnecessary and non-atomic; renames move names, not bytes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Two-phase without atomicity exposes a window with no 'b'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deleting both loses data on crash — the unsafe direction.

hard.prompt: A log-heavy HDD workload writes 10k random 4KB updates/sec. Why might LFS beat FFS here but lose on SSD?

choices.label: A
choices.body: LFS batches to sequential segments saving seeks; on SSD cleaning/GC adds write amplification

choices.label: B
choices.body: LFS encrypts writes making HDD faster

choices.label: C
choices.body: SSD seeks are longer so LFS always wins there too

choices.label: D
choices.body: FFS cannot write small files at all

hard.hint: Compare what each device hates: seeks vs extra erased writes.
hard.explanation: Sequential log wins where seeks dominate but pays cleaner plus FTL double-copy on flash.
hard.deepDive: On HDD, one segment write replaces 10k seeks, a 100x win. On SSD, random writes are already cheap, while LFS cleaning and SSD GC multiply each logical write into several physical ones. Modern flash file systems therefore tune segment size to erase blocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: LFS performs no encryption; the win is sequentiality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SSDs have zero seeks, so sequential batching buys little.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: FFS writes small files fine, just with more seeks per file.

hard.prompt: RAID-5 (4x1TB) vs RAID-1 (2x2TB) both give ~3TB? Actually 4x1TB RAID-5 = 3TB; 2x4TB RAID-1 = 4TB. Which survives 2 concurrent disk failures?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Neither guarantees it; both tolerate only 1 (RAID-1 pair both dying also fails)

choices.label: B
choices.body: RAID-5 survives any 2 failures via double parity

choices.label: C
choices.body: RAID-0 survives 2 failures

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both survive any 2 failures

hard.hint: Count independent parities/copies: how many independent losses can each reconstruct?
hard.explanation: Single parity or single mirror each reconstruct at most one loss; a second kills data.
hard.deepDive: RAID-5 has one parity equation per stripe, solving for one unknown disk. RAID-1 has two copies, surviving one copy loss. Surviving two arbitrary failures needs two parities (RAID-6) or triple mirroring. Rebuild windows also expose a second failure.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Double parity is RAID-6, not RAID-5; RAID-5 has one parity per stripe.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: RAID-0 has no redundancy and dies on the first failure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two-fault tolerance needs two independent redundancies, which neither has.

hard.prompt: Why do small random writes perform worst on RAID-5 (4+1) compared to RAID-1?

choices.label: A
choices.body: RAID-5 needs read-modify-write of data+parity (4 I/Os per small write)

choices.label: B
choices.body: RAID-5 encrypts parity on every write

choices.label: C
choices.body: RAID-1 needs parity recomputation

choices.label: D
choices.body: RAID-5 has no capacity for small writes

hard.hint: To update one stripe block, what must be read before new parity can be written?
hard.explanation: Small write must read old data and parity, then write new data and parity.
hard.deepDive: This 2-read/2-write penalty quadruples I/O per logical write and serializes on parity. Full-stripe writes avoid it by computing parity from all new data. RAID-1 just writes two copies with no parity math, so it wins small-write latency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Parity is XOR, not encryption; cost is extra I/O, not crypto.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: RAID-1 has no parity at all; it only duplicates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Capacity is unrelated; the penalty is I/O amplification.

hard.prompt: A student claims: 'With DMA, the disk controller runs my user program to process data during transfer.' What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: DMA only copies bytes; CPU still runs all code, driver handles completion

choices.label: B
choices.body: DMA is slower than polling so claim understates it

choices.label: C
choices.body: User programs always run on the disk

choices.label: D
choices.body: Interrupts are illegal with DMA

hard.hint: Separate data movement from execution: what fetches instructions?
hard.explanation: Only the CPU fetches/executes; DMA is a memory-copy engine programmed by the driver.
hard.deepDive: Confusing offload with execution is a classic misconception. The driver sets source, destination, and length, then the DMA engine shuffles bytes while the CPU schedules other work. A completion interrupt wakes the driver, which wakes the blocked process.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DMA is faster in CPU terms precisely because it removes per-byte polling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: User code never leaves the CPU; devices expose registers, not execution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DMA completion is normally signaled by an interrupt; they cooperate.

hard.prompt: Request stream keeps arriving near track 50 while head serves there (SSTF). Request at track 5 waits 10s. What fixes it with what cost?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Switch to SCAN; bounds wait by one sweep but adds travel vs SSTF average

choices.label: B
choices.body: Switch to FCFS polling to encrypt faster

choices.label: C
choices.body: Add DMA to eliminate seeks

choices.label: D
choices.body: SSTF already guarantees no starvation

hard.hint: SSTF minimizes average but what happens to a far request under continuous near arrivals?
hard.explanation: SSTF starves distant requests; SCAN forces periodic sweeps to the edge.
hard.deepDive: SSTF is optimal greedily for average seek but has unbounded worst-case wait. SCAN trades slightly higher average travel for a bounded one-sweep wait. This average-vs-fairness tradeoff is why real elevators use SCAN variants with aging.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: FCFS polling is unrelated to seek starvation and adds no fairness bound efficiently.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA moves data post-seek; it cannot move the arm or reorder the queue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SSTF provably can starve outliers under adversarial arrivals.

hard.prompt: Sequential streaming workload reads 1GB contiguously. Why might aggressive SCAN reordering hurt vs simple FCFS?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stream already sequential; reordering adds CPU/queue delay with no seek saving

choices.label: B
choices.body: SCAN encrypts sequential data

choices.label: C
choices.body: FCFS increases seeks on sequential streams

choices.label: D
choices.body: Streaming needs DMA user execution

hard.hint: If arrivals are already in track order, what work does the scheduler add?
hard.explanation: No reordering benefit exists, only scheduling overhead and possible prefetch disruption.
hard.deepDive: Elevators win on random queues with conflicting positions. A single sequential stream has maximal locality already, so sorting is pure overhead and can split prefetches. Modern schedulers detect sequentiality and bypass reordering.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scheduling never encrypts; overhead is queueing, not crypto.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: FCFS preserves arrival order, which is already optimal for a sequential stream.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DMA moves the stream but runs no user code.

hard.prompt: Crash during 3-block append (D, I, B). Student says journaling fixes it by encrypting blocks and any order works. What is the correct fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Write-ahead: log D+I+B + commit durable before home; order matters, no encryption

choices.label: B
