choices.body: Encrypt D+I+B in any order then crash is impossible

choices.label: C
choices.body: Poll the disk faster to prevent power loss

choices.label: D
choices.body: Use RAID-0 to make 3 writes atomic

hard.hint: What must be durable before the commit word, and does secrecy help atomicity?
hard.explanation: Atomicity comes from ordered write-ahead plus commit, not secrecy; order is the fix.
hard.deepDive: Journaling = encryption is a real misconception; the journal is plaintext redo info. Only TB->log->commit->home lets recovery distinguish complete from torn transactions. RAID-0 striping widens the failure domain and adds no atomicity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Encryption provides confidentiality, not crash atomicity; unordered writes still tear.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Faster polling cannot stop power loss mid-sequence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RAID-0 increases loss risk and provides no multi-block atomicity.

hard.prompt: Metadata journaling logs only inode/bitmap, not file data D. Crash after journal commit but before D reaches home. What is visible?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Metadata points to D but D holds stale/garbage (ordered mode needs D-before-commit to limit this)

choices.label: B
choices.body: File data guaranteed correct because commit implies data durable

choices.label: C
choices.body: Entire transaction vanishes including metadata

choices.label: D
choices.body: DMA replays the missing data automatically

hard.hint: If D was never logged, what source does recovery have for D after commit?
hard.explanation: Replay restores metadata only; unlogged data may be stale, so ordering D first matters.
hard.deepDive: Ordered journaling forces data to home before logging metadata+commit, narrowing exposure to garbage pointers. Full data journaling logs D too, giving exact data recovery at 2x write cost. Commit atomicity still needs barriers so the device honors log-before-commit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Commit covers only logged blocks; unlogged D has no durability promise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Committed metadata replays; it does not vanish — that is the garbage-pointer risk.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DMA never replays file systems; journal replay does, but only for logged blocks.

hard.prompt: Circular journal of 100 slots is full with uncheckpointed commits. New transaction arrives. What must happen?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stall new writes, checkpoint oldest to home, then reuse tail slots

choices.label: B
choices.body: Overwrite head immediately; old commits unneeded

choices.label: C
choices.body: Run fsck instead of checkpointing

choices.label: D
choices.body: Encrypt the log to make room

hard.hint: The log is the only durable copy until home is updated: can you drop it early?
hard.explanation: Log space reuses only after checkpoint; otherwise stall and flush oldest first.
hard.deepDive: Overwriting live log entries would destroy redo sources for crashes before home writeback. Checkpoint pressure thus throttles throughput when the log is small or home writes are slow. Sizing the journal trades memory/disk overhead against stall frequency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Overwriting uncheckpointed commits loses committed data on next crash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: fsck is a full-scan fallback, not steady-state log reclamation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Encryption does not free slots; only home writeback does.

hard.prompt: LFS cleaner must pick between segment A (90% live) and B (10% live). Snapshot pins many blocks in A. Which to clean and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Clean B; cost per free byte is lowest, and snapshots make A expensive to move

choices.label: B
choices.body: Clean A; fullest segments always free most space

choices.label: C
choices.body: Overwrite both in place to avoid copies

choices.label: D
choices.body: Delete the snapshot implicitly by cleaning A

hard.hint: Cost = live bytes copied per free byte gained: which segment gives cheap free space?
hard.explanation: Cleaning B copies 10% to free 90%; A copies 90% to free 10% and fights snapshot pins.
hard.deepDive: Greedy cleaning by utilization minimizes write amplification. Snapshots pin blocks alive, raising effective liveness and deterring cleaning of snapshotted segments. Cost-benefit policies also weigh segment age since cold live data stays dead longer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fullest segments cost the most copies per freed byte — the worst choice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: In-place overwrite breaks LFS append-only and snapshot sharing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cleaning never deletes snapshots; refcounts keep pinned blocks alive.

hard.prompt: LFS crashes with only the last partial segment unwritten and imap plus checkpoint region intact. How does recovery + snapshot interact?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Roll back to last checkpoint, roll forward live log tail; snapshots share via imap roots so survivors persist

choices.label: B
choices.body: Replay elevator queue to reconstruct files

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decrypt the checkpoint to rebuild DMA state

choices.label: D
choices.body: Must full-copy disk because LFS cannot recover

hard.hint: LFS recovery is log recovery: where is the last consistent root, and what follows it?
hard.explanation: Checkpoint gives consistent imap root; log tail replay restores post-checkpoint appends.
hard.deepDive: Because LFS never overwrites in place, pre-checkpoint state is inherently consistent. Only the tail needs scanning, unlike fsck full scans. Snapshot roots are just pinned imap versions, so they survive as long as cleaner preserves their blocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The disk queue is volatile; recovery uses checkpoint plus log contents on disk.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No encryption or DMA state is involved; imap and segments suffice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Log-structured layout is designed for fast roll-forward, not full copy.
